articles.title: FT: Estonia moving troops closer to Russia in 'active defense' push
articles.body:
FT: Estonia moving troops closer to Russia in 'active defense' push
Estonia is moving its armed forces closer to the Russian border and building up its long-range strike capabilities, the Financial Times wrote in an overview of the state and strategy of the Estonian Defense Forces.
Estonia is permanently stationing its troops closer to the Russian border and acquiring weapons capable of striking deep inside its neighbor's territory as the NATO eastern flank country prepares for possible Russian aggression after the war in Ukraine ends, the Financial Times (FT) reported Monday, citing Estonian defense officials.
Estonia's military and intelligence chiefs do not believe Moscow intends to launch a full-scale war with NATO within at least the next two years, but they believe their hostile neighbor is preparing for a possible future conflict with the small Baltic country, the FT noted.
Estonian officials fear the Kremlin could take an opportunistic gamble, such as launching a smaller-scale incursion aimed at testing NATO's collective defense clause. They say neither Estonia nor NATO can currently credibly deter such a scenario. This has prompted Estonia, which has no air force of its own and therefore relies on NATO to protect its airspace, to shift to an active defense strategy, the newspaper wrote.
"We have to start from the border and win from the first battles," said Col. Tarmo Kundla, commander of the 1st Infantry Brigade, the country's main fighting force.
As part of the new strategy, his unit will be permanently relocated from Tapa, about 130 kilometers from the Russian border as the crow flies, to Jõhvi, just 50 kilometers from the border. New facilities are currently being built there to house the brigade's soldiers.
"Deterrence is not working," said a senior Estonian military intelligence official. "The critical period to address that, for all of us in the Baltic states, is in the next one to four years."
The Financial Times noted that Estonia's defense minister has said in public remarks and ministry documents: "Credible deterrence requires us to make aggression against us unthinkable. Our aim is clear: to keep the enemy and the destruction of war away from Estonian territory."
At the same time, the newspaper noted that Russian state media consistently portrays Estonia as a hostile and Russophobic country intent on drawing Moscow into a direct confrontation with NATO. The Kremlin has threatened Estonia, including with a nuclear attack, should the country ever host NATO nuclear weapons on its territory.
According to the Financial Times, the Estonian government incorporated the concept of active defense into its national defense policy in May. Since then, the country's small but well-trained military has begun a quiet but far-reaching reorganization.
Elite units are now being permanently moved from Estonia's main military base in Tapa to positions farther east, closer to the Russian border.
In addition to the new base in Jõhvi, a base capable of accommodating up to 1,000 military personnel is also being built in Narva. It is planned to permanently house 200 soldiers, but will be able to accommodate another 800 in a crisis.
As Estonia increases its defense spending — which, according to official figures, will rise 42 percent this year to €2.4 billion or 5.4 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) — the country is also changing the types of weapons it procures.
Over the past year, Estonia has signed contracts to acquire nine U.S.-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system (MLRS) platforms, including M57 ballistic missiles with a range of up to 300 kilometers. The country is also in the process of acquiring nine South Korean Chunmoo multiple launch rocket systems, which likewise have a range of about 300 kilometers.
In a conversation with the FT, a senior officer based in Tapa pointed out that St. Petersburg is 260 kilometers from Estonia.
"We are in the process of changing everything," said a military policy official at Estonia's defense ministry. "The reality is that the [Estonian defense planning] has been the same for the last 10 years. But Russia is already planning to double its forces across our border."
In the decade following Russia's 2014 invasion of Crimea, Estonian military planners developed a defense doctrine shaped by the country's history and geography. Under this approach, in the event of a Russian invasion, Estonia's conscript-based forces would mobilize rapidly and wage a highly tactical, almost guerrilla-style defensive war, using their extensive knowledge of the country's swampy and forested terrain to wear down Russian forces and inflict heavy losses until NATO reinforcements arrived, the FT wrote.
But after observing Russia's actions in Ukraine, Estonia's military leaders have concluded that such a plan would not work. In their assessment, the Kremlin does not care about its own losses.
Estonia has also observed that once the Russian military gained control of territory in Ukraine, it did not give it up, but fought to hold it even after everything there had been destroyed. Given Estonia's population of 1.3 million and territory of 45,000 square kilometers, that is a troubling conclusion, the FT noted.
The newspaper pointed out that while Estonia has a trained reserve force of up to 230,000 people, equivalent to almost one-fifth of the population, only 4,200 personnel are in permanent active service. Under Estonia's defense plans, in wartime or a prewar situation, this force can be supplemented by 39,500 high-readiness reservists, each of whom must report within hours to a specific unit with which they have trained. A further 40,000 trained reservists are available for mobilization without predetermined assignments.
Changing the defense doctrine to prevent the loss of any territory is therefore difficult, particularly because Estonian military intelligence assesses that Russia would seek to preserve the element of surprise for as long as possible in any act of aggression.
Estonia now plans to fight for every square centimeter of its territory from the border onward and to strike Russia hard hundreds of kilometers behind the front line from the first day of an invasion.
"Militarily this is very demanding," said Kundla. "We cannot shape the enemy [by retreating or tactically luring them into situations]. We have to build our lines today. It is forward defense."
According to the Financial Times, Estonian military intelligence is particularly concerned about some form of limited action against a target near the border — especially in predominantly Russian-speaking Narva. Seizing Narva would make little sense if the goal were a full-scale conquest of Estonia, but officials said it could serve as a provocative test of NATO's resolve aimed at dividing the alliance.
In such a scenario, Russia's goal would be to cast doubt on NATO allies' willingness to come to Estonia's aid by presenting the attack as a fait accompli.
Estonia hopes NATO allies will also play an important role in the country's new defense posture and help deter such an attack. The United Kingdom has already committed to increasing the size of its military contingent in Estonia from the current 800 troops to 1,200 by April next year.
The FT noted that when British units took part in this year's Estonian Defense Forces exercise Spring Storm, they brought something new with them. According to British military officials, these were Nyan attack drones designed to conduct deep strikes after being launched from the combat zone. Like the MLRS systems, the Nyan drones have a range of 300 kilometers. This puts most of Russia's major military bases in the surrounding region, as well as the city of St. Petersburg, within striking range.
Despite growing concern about Russian aggression in Europe, particularly because of the Kremlin's hybrid sabotage campaign, Estonia's security establishment still believes the country has time to adapt its defenses and deter its neighbor, the FT noted.
But there is one major source of uncertainty: Ukraine. As long as the war continues, Russia's military remains tied down in Ukraine. But if a ceasefire is established or a lasting peace takes effect, NATO officials fear the threat to the Baltic states will become much more serious, as tens of thousands of battle-hardened Russian troops could then be redeployed to the border. Russia would also have a vast defense-industrial machine operating at full capacity. "We were afraid of the war [in Ukraine]," said one senior Estonian intelligence official. "Now we are afraid of the end of the war."
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski, Mait Ots
Source: Financial Times

articles.title: What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say Ukraine brought peace to world? Norwegian professor who nominated Zelenskyy and Ukrainians for 2026 Nobel Peace Prize takes on tough questions
articles.body:
It is rare to hear a European say "I'm sorry" to the Ukrainians. Dag Øistein Endsjø, who nominated the Ukrainian people and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy for the Nobel Peace Prize 2026, shared it several times during our interview.
Mr. Endsjø is a professor of religious studies at the University of Oslo in Norway. He comes across as intelligent and reserved. But when he talks about Europe not helping Ukraine as much as it could, his eyes give away deep personal emotions.
"Just thank you for keeping us safe. Thank you for the extreme sacrifice you've been making for all of us. And I'm sorry that my government and the other governments haven't done enough," he said, speaking to me not as a journalist but as one of the Ukrainians.
These words reach cut through, because tens of millions of us live under daily psychological and physical terror, feeling forgotten and betrayed.
At the same time, Professor Endsjø names things as they are, even when it is uncomfortable. When the full-scale invasion began, he says, he doubted Ukraine would hold. And he admits that Norway has profited from the war: by its own Finance Department's calculation, about €106 billion in additional revenue from higher oil and gas prices.
He was honest with us. Our questions were sharp too, even those about US President Donald Trump's chances to win this year's award, and he answered them the way he answers everything: straight.
Do you think people who fight the war can be nominated for a Nobel Peace Prize?
People who defend themselves, yes! Who defends a free and democratic state against unprovoked aggression, yes, I think so.
Many say Ukraine should stop fighting and negotiate. Wouldn't a peace prize reward the war?
It's not a reward for the war, because the war could stop tomorrow if Russia just found out they didn't want to break international rules and could pull out. This is not about continuing the war. On the other hand, the war would stop the moment Ukraine threw out Russia. That, regrettably, seems to take more time.
This is not, in any way, about rewarding or promoting war as such. This is about standing up against war, because not standing up against war has only provoked more war and aggression from Russia.
Russia is attacking free and democratic countries unprovoked. They started in 2008 with Georgia, and then moved on to Ukraine, and as so many others point out, they have their plans.
"Moldova, if Ukraine hadn't been able to resist this invasion, would also have been under Russian rule now for sure. Poland and the Baltics would have been under extreme pressure, maybe also invaded," Mr. Endsjø says.
If there was a moment when you thought that Ukraine might lose the war?
Yes, in the beginning, when I saw those lines of tanks heading for Kyiv, I was afraid that everything was lost. Also noting the lackluster reaction from the free world and how they only came with condemnations and no ammunition, just a flight out.
If Ukraine is defending peace, why is the war getting closer to Europe's borders?
That is because of Russia. If Ukraine hadn't defended itself and just given up, the war would have been even closer to Europe. We would be even more under threat with probably even more degrees of sabotage and terrorist attacks around in Europe.
Does Ukrainian resistance escalate the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia?
No. The other way around. If Ukraine had given up, it would have been a more direct threat to NATO countries.
But some politicians say that in this case, Russia will just negotiate and sell energy as it did in the past
Yes, while sabotaging and even murdering people around in Europe, and acting like a state of terrorism. So, no, it would remain aggressive. You can listen to various prominent Russians on Russian TV. You know, you're not allowed to say anything on Russian TV unless the government approves it...
People are again and again threatening Finland, Poland, Britain, and the Baltic. Just as they made up these fake republics in Luhansk and Donetsk in 2014, they have tried to do the same in Estonia and Latvia already.
So if it hadn't been for Ukraine and Ukraine's resistance, the risk of direct war between NATO and Russia would have been even greater. Because Ukraine keeps Russia at bay.
If Ukraine agrees to a ceasefire, will you consider this a failure or a victory?
I, as a non-Ukrainian but fellow European, like any other European, have no right whatsoever to tell the Ukrainians what to do.
If the Ukrainians themselves find that this most horrible war is too much, and you want a ceasefire and you want to stop, and it's not for me to criticize. It's not for any European to criticize. We cannot tell the Ukrainians what to do after that horrible sacrifice you've made already.
I only hope that Europe and the rest of the free world will assist Ukraine even more, so that you will be even more successful in throwing out the Russian occupation army of the entire of Ukraine, including Crimea.
What if Russia uses nuclear weapons? Can we say that Ukraine brought the world to peace?
They will not use nuclear weapons. If they wanted to do it, they would have done that already. China and India are completely clear that they will not accept any use of nuclear weapons, so that would mean that Russia would be completely isolated and completely devastated economically in weeks. So that's not going to happen.
Putin says the war ends if Ukraine gives up Donbas. Why give a Nobel Peace Prize to a country that refuses?
This is just a proposal from Putin and American so-called negotiators. They're supposed to be negotiating, but this is not a negotiation. This is just about trying to make Ukraine give up without even a fight, which Russia is unable to do, and, incredibly, in some way, try to force Ukraine to give up its rightful ownership of its occupied territories.
This is just appeasement, just as what Chamberlain did in 1939 and what Europe has done again and again in 2008 and 2014. This would be a completely terrible mistake.
"Ukraine deserves the Nobel Prize, no matter how long they keep on fighting against this horrible aggression by this dreadful kleptocracy," Mr. Endsjø says.
Europe says Ukraine keeps the peace for everyone. Can it then demand that Ukrainian refugees go back and fight?
I, as a European, think that other Europeans cannot demand anything of the Ukrainians, whoever they are. This must be up to the Ukrainian people and the Ukrainian government.
Do people in Norway still genuinely believe that Ukraine can win this war, dragging on for so long?
I think so. Very many do believe that. But this depends on whether the West keeps on, and the free world continues to support Ukraine. Here in Norway, we are in a particular situation because, as our own Finance Department calculated last year, we have earned an extra 106 billion euros from the war (additional government revenues generated by high energy prices — ed.) due to higher oil and gas prices.
We don't support you as much as we should. We should have given you those 106 billion euros.
Why should someone in Europe care whether Ukraine wins or loses?
That is the point: that this is a war against the free world from a horrible dictatorship. More or less, you can call it a kleptocracy — that's the most, I guess, the most precise definition of Russia today. It's not a democracy whatsoever. It's most of all a kleptocracy where the top leaders just steal whatever they can get their hands on.
If Ukraine had fallen, it's not just that that would be horrible for Ukraine as such, but that would mean also that Russia would have had its hands on all the immense resources Ukraine has. Also, all the million men and women who probably would have been forced into the Russian army, and made it an even more dangerous enemy to the West.
So this is about the survival of all of us. Ukraine is the free world. We belong together. Ukraine should have been in NATO and the EU a long time ago.
If Russia says it only wants Donbas, why not just give it to them and let the war end?
This is like World War II all over again. They say: "If we only get Donbas, we're going to at least have proper negotiations."
Donbas, that is the Ukrainian Sudetenland. That's just what the West forced Czechoslovakia to do in 1938 and 1939. The Sudetenland wasn't just a nice little border region. It was the defense line of Czechoslovakia. So the moment the Germans got that, they were defenseless against the full-scale invasion that followed in the months afterward.
"Donbas, it's not just a small border region. It's the most important line of defense," Mr. Endsjø says.
Forcing Ukraine to give up anything whatsoever is rewarding the Russian aggression.
But I have to give Putin right in one thing when he says: "We are, you know, continuing World War II." That's true, because you have to remember what Russia did in World War II. They started it together with Nazi Germany in 1939. They occupied the Baltic countries, they occupied Moldova, they occupied half of Poland, they split Poland with Nazi Germany, and they tried to occupy Finland.
When Norway was invaded by Nazi Germany, Russia congratulated Germany. They were on Germany's side. The only thing that made Russia shift sides in World War II was the German invasion. What did they do after World War II? They didn't liberate any country - they occupied. They just changed one occupation for another.
"Eastern Europe wasn't liberated before 1990 and 1991. That's the actual end of World War II, when the Russian occupation of Eastern Europe ended," he stresses.
They even talk about the northern parts of Northern Norway. In 1945, they did have designs. They wanted Svalbard and the northern islands. They had plans to take the regions closest to Norway, which were also part of the Soviet Union. They want everything they have ever had, and they want it back.
Trump has made no secret of his desire for the Nobel Peace Prize. Could the Committee deny Ukraine the award simply to avoid provoking him?
Trump has been nominated for the Peace Prize several times, but I don't think he really has a chance. What I did note is that last year's recipient, Mrs. Machado from Venezuela, was probably chosen partly due to it. I don't criticize the prize, as she is a democratically elected leader, a good candidate, and a good recipient.
"But I believe part of the reason she got it was that the Nobel Committee wanted a recipient who would not provoke President Trump," he says.
I consider that they are going to worry about that again, about whether the recipient is going to provoke Trump or not. You never know what his reaction will be anyway. I don't think they really see him as a serious candidate — someone who just started an immense war in Iran, drawing the whole world economy down.
My nomination has gone viral — there are thousands of posts online. I usually don't get 750,000 views on my Facebook posts, but I did with my post about Ukraine. I really do believe that Zelenskyy and Ukraine are the most worthy recipients at this point in time.
If continuing the war means more Ukrainians will die, why not negotiate to stop the killing? Zelenskyy says Ukraine plans to fight further. Does it bring peace, really?
It does. Look at Norway in 1940. It was peace, but it wasn't peace. It was an occupation. It was killing, it was murder, and even worse in other parts of Europe. What happened in Norway was nothing compared to what happened in Poland, the Baltics, Ukraine, and Belarus.
Thank God the current Western leaders understand this: they are not going to force Ukraine to give up, to let millions of people live under horrible occupation, and give up more land. They stand by Ukraine now, and I hope they will support it even more, especially Norway.

- Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022
- Ukraine keeps finding ways to replace its MiG-29s. It’s running out of MiG-29s to find

articles.title: FP-7 expands Ukraine’s strike capabilities against Russia: expert names potential targets
articles.body:
FP-7 expands Ukraine’s strike capabilities against Russia: expert names potential targets
Kyiv • UNN
Tactical ballistic systems could give Ukraine an additional tool for striking Russian command posts, warehouses, logistics hubs and air defense systems.
The first combat use of the FP-7 opens up new opportunities for Ukraine to strike military targets at a considerable distance from the front line. The emergence of tactical ballistic capabilities makes it possible to plan strikes on command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, air defense systems, and other important facilities supporting Russian forces. Military expert Ivan Stupak expressed this opinion in an exclusive comment to UNN.
Ukraine used the FP-7
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy published a video of the launch and reported the first combat use of the Ukrainian FP-7 ballistic missile. At the same time, Ukraine has not disclosed exactly where or against what target the missile was used.
The FP-7 was developed by Fire Point, a leading Ukrainian defense company. It is a ballistic missile designed to strike targets at a distance of up to 250 km and deliver a payload weighing up to 200 kg. Such a system is a cheaper response to the U.S. ATACMS.
The emergence of such weapons expands Ukraine’s ability to operate against the Russian rear, since tactical ballistic capabilities make it possible to reach facilities that the enemy is trying to move farther away from the combat zone.
The very emergence of such a weapon is a very important development. Ukraine becomes stronger when it has not merely an individual missile, but the ability to plan its use
What targets could the FP-7 potentially strike
Potential key targets for such weapons could include command posts, ammunition depots, logistics hubs, air defense systems, and other military facilities.
According to Ivan Stupak, the creation of the FP-7 is a "strong card" that Ukraine either did not previously have or had in a much more limited form.
In his view, the mass or at least regular use of such missiles could potentially affect the situation on particular sections of the front, as well as how Russian troops deploy their forces and infrastructure.
The Russians are already being forced to withdraw some of their forces, equipment, repair bases, depots, and other facilities farther from the front line. условно, if they place them more than 100 kilometers away, while the Ukrainian missile has a range of about 200 kilometers, then a significant portion of such facilities potentially falls within the strike zone. And here intelligence is extremely important. If we see a facility, understand its coordinates, know its importance to the Russian army, and have a missile with which we can engage it, then we gain the ability to strike the enemy’s rear much more effectively
Logistics infrastructure could become a separate area of focus. The aggressor country’s forces require a constant supply of ammunition, fuel, equipment, and spare parts.
It is possible to strike depots, command posts, repair bases, and other facilities that support the Russian grouping at the front. The more such facilities fall within range, the more difficult it will be for the Russians to organize their logistics
Potential targets could also include facilities in the fuel and energy sector if they have military significance and are within the missile’s range.
At the same time, Ivan Stupak emphasized that the effectiveness of strikes against protected facilities would depend on the missile’s accuracy and the power of its warhead.
What serial production will provide
The military expert emphasized that a stable supply of missiles would allow the military command to plan their use over a longer period and distribute the missiles according to priority targets.
Let us imagine a situation—the command knows for certain that from the 1st to the 30th of the month, it has ten missiles at its disposal. Then it is a completely different story. The military can plan which targets are of the greatest value, which facilities need to be destroyed first, and which can be left for later. For example, Alabuga, where Russian attack drones are produced, could be designated as one of the priority targets. If we accumulate ten missiles over the course of a month, we can plan to use them against such facilities. And if the warhead and accuracy make it possible to strike fortified structures, that is an entirely different level of capability
Therefore, important factors include not only the missile’s range, but also its production rate, accuracy, and the effect of its warhead.
After the first large-scale deployments, we will see much more. We will see how accurate the missile is, how powerful its warhead is, how effectively it overcomes air defenses and, most importantly, how quickly Ukraine will be able to ramp up production
In his opinion, the FP-7 is a "very promising prospect" for Ukraine, but its real impact will become clear after combat experience has been accumulated.

articles.title: Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Is Iran losing control of the Strait of Hormuz?
As Iran and the US take tentative steps towards a deal to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, there may be signs that Tehran's biggest source of leverage is being eroded.
Iran has long viewed its ability to paralyse the strategic chokepoint as its own version of a nuclear bomb, a Trump card which, if used, could trigger a global energy crisis of historic proportions.
Immediately after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) did just that, moving decisively to block the strait and trapping a fifth of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas inside the region.
But its ability to apply the thumbscrews to the global economy has been threatened in recent weeks as the US military facilitates covert oil shipments through the strait and Arab producers reconfigure export routes.
More oil is now leaving the region than at any point during the seven-month war, weakening Tehran's hand as it tries to negotiate permanent control over the strait.
Arab oil exports are rebounding
Middle Eastern crude exports excluding Iran returned to pre-war levels in September despite Iran and its allies escalating attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and Saudi Arabia's oil infrastructure.
Estimates by data tracking platform Kpler indicate that Arab countries shipped at least 16.5 million barrels of oil out of the region per day during the month.
Much of the rise was powered by Saudi Arabia, which responded to the attack on its Red Sea pipeline last month by surging exports through the strait.
Shipping data tracked by Bloomberg shows that the kingdom's Hormuz shipments rose to more than three million barrels per day in the first three weeks of September, more than triple the amount in August.
Exports through Hormuz have slowly ticked up since June, when the Pentagon launched a coordinated effort to get energy supplies onto the global market. Backed by US air cover, Gulf states have snuck millions of barrels of oil through the narrow stretch of water by using shadow fleets to evade Iranian fire.
The US attempt to prise open the waterway has dovetailed with moves by Arab states to find new ways of getting their oil out of the region. Saudi Arabia has re-routed its crude to the Red Sea via its East-West Pipeline while the UAE has relied on its terminal at Fujairah on the other side of the strait. Iraq has trucked millions of barrels of oil across the Syrian desert to the Mediterranean.
"Iran appears to have lost significant leverage over the Strait of Hormuz," said Ria Reddy, Iran team deputy lead at the American Enterprise Institute's Critical Threats Project.
"If commercial vessels can continue to transit the strait at high rates despite Iranian threats, Iran has less ability to use the strait to compel the US and other states to accept its demands," she told The New Arab.
The rise in Arab oil exports isn't the only way in which Tehran's control has slipped. The US blockade has turned the tables on Iran, trapping its oil in the region and depriving it of billions of dollars of vital revenues.
Dozens of its ships have been struck by US forces, in what the Trump administration has described as a "tanker for tanker" policy aimed at deterring IRGC attacks on maritime traffic.
Energy crunch continues
With no end in sight to the war, the millions of barrels of oil now making their way out of the region have had little impact on global prices, which continue to be influenced by heightened geopolitical risk and spiralling freight rates.
The unlocking of Hormuz has coincided with a 57% surge in the price of Brent, which peaked at $110 in mid-September following the Houthi takeover of Yemen's Red Sea coast and the crucial Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Neither has it helped to curb shortages of fuels such as gasoline and diesel, whose prices have surged to record highs due to ongoing bottlenecks at refineries worldwide.
The US-led effort also appears not to have had the same success with raising gas shipments from Qatar, which remain far below pre-war levels. Last month, gas prices in Europe and Asia climbed to their highest levels since 2022 amid supply fears ahead of the winter.
All of this means that Iran continues to have a large say over the trajectory of the global economy, despite millions of barrels of crude now transiting the strait every day.
"Resumed oil exports in the Strait of Hormuz is not synonymous with stabilisation," Burcu Ozcelik, a senior research fellow for Middle East security at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), told The New Arab.
"Iran still retains the capability to resume retaliatory drone and missile strikes on Gulf critical infrastructure and oil production sites," she said.
Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies (INSS), said that although the US has weakened Iran's control of the strait, it has so far failed to achieve its overarching goal of stabilising the global energy market.
"Iran retains the ability to target tankers, threaten commercial shipping, and make passage through the strait increasingly difficult and expensive," he said.
"As a result, Washington's operational achievements have yet to produce the economic outcome it ultimately needs. Oil prices remain elevated, in part because of higher insurance premiums, tanker shortages, and the continuing risk to commercial shipping."
Tanker war
Iran's sporadic attacks on ships have prevented a normalisation of maritime traffic in the strait, keeping freight rates at record highs, extending the freeze in the insurance market, and maintaining pressure on oil prices.
September saw a notable uptick in attacks on tankers, with 21 vessels confirmed hit by Iranian projectiles, up from 12 the month before, according to data collected by conflict monitor ACLED.
"September has seen the largest number of successful Iranian attacks on commercial ships since March, when the war was at its peak," Valentin d'Hauthuille, ACLED's Middle East regional team lead, told The New Arab.
Washington has for the moment gained the upper hand in the strait, but Iran's continued ability to threaten ships raises questions about the long-term viability of its escort operation, he said.
That said, the US's destruction of its coastal radars and surveillance systems is making it increasingly hard for it to use them. There are signs that the damage is forcing it to resort to cruder means of disrupting maritime traffic.
"Iran appears to have adopted less effective methods of tracking and attacking vessels, including the use of fast attack craft to visually identify targets and shore-based rocket launchers to deploy mines," the Critical Threats Project's Reddy said.
"These adaptations suggest that Iran faces greater difficulty identifying, targeting and consistently disrupting shipping at scale."
Widening the battlefield
Iran's say over the future of the strait extends beyond what happens in its immediate neighbourhood to other parts of the region, where its allies have been able to further tighten global energy markets.
Oil and gas prices spiked last month after Houthi forces and Iraqi paramilitaries mounted a one-two punch on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea exports, in the same day taking over the Bab al-Mandeb strait and disabling Aramco's East-West oil pipeline.
Since the ceasefire in Yemen collapsed in July, the group has struck several refineries on the kingdom's Red Sea coast and closed the chokepoint to Saudi-linked ships.
However, horizontal escalation has had limited success for the Axis of Resistance, with Arab producers proving resilient to these multi-pronged attacks and swiftly finding new export routes when one is closed down.
Oil traders may have been spooked by September's attack on the Saudi pipeline, but, in the end, it made little impact on the kingdom's ability to export. Aramco was able to quickly divert flows to Hormuz and brought the pipeline back online in only two weeks.
It also involves a degree of risk which Iran has thus far not been willing to fully take on. Iran has refrained from targeting the UAE since signing the ill-fated peace deal in June, allowing shipments to Fujairah to continue. Neither has it tried to disrupt Iraq's overland shipping route through Syria, a move which would only anger Baghdad and risk pushing it further into America's orbit.
War of attrition
Despite the intense US bombing campaign, the IRGC is believed to still possess thousands of drones and a sizeable missile inventory. There are also signs that China is shipping components to Iran's military to help it maintain production lines and replenish its stockpiles.
This means that, unless there is an end to the war or the US can accomplish the unlikely feat of fully destroying its offensive capabilities, Iran will likely be able to disrupt shipping for many months to come.
The sustainability of the US's operation is less certain. It may be succeeding in getting more oil through the strait at the moment, but it remains an open question about how long it can keep this up.
Months of deployment are putting US forces under increasing strain, with commanders recently warning that continuing the war is unsustainable. Missile interceptor stockpiles are dangerously low, naval forces are fatigued, and the concentration of assets in the region is harming the military's readiness elsewhere around the world.
Moreover, the cost of the operation is currently running at around $2 billion every month, according to the Congressional Budget Office. The Pentagon has put the total cost of the war at more than $45 billion up to the middle of September - and that's without factoring in the costs of replenishing missile inventories and repairing the damage at US bases.
Despite this, the Pentagon appears to be preparing to resume the full-scale war following November's midterm election, last week dispatching another carrier strike group and up to 10,000 additional troops to the region.
The Trump administration is hoping that economic pressure will push Tehran into accepting its conditions for an agreement and recently renewed its attempts to collapse Iran's economy.
The new wave of sanctions dubbed Operation Economic Outcast, together with the naval blockade, has piled more pressure on Iran's economy, sending inflation surging to 73% year-on-year in September and the Iranian rial plunging to a record low of 2.7 million to the dollar.
Meanwhile, the economy shrank more than 10% year-on-year between 21 March and 20 June, while the vital oil and gas sector contracted more than 26%.
RUSI's Ozcelik said that, while large portions of the Iranian public appear to be backing the government's twin calls for resilience and resistance, that may change in the coming months as the economic crisis continues to intensify.
"Tehran may find it harder to convince large segments of the public that they are winning the war and that resistance against the US is worth the heavy toll on the cost of living, hyperinflation, and shrinking economic opportunities," she said.

articles.title: Germany warns of direct clash with Russia as Ukraine deploys AI guns against drones
articles.body:
Germany’s foreign intelligence chief warned Monday that the country faces a real risk of being drawn into a violent confrontation with Russia, saying Moscow is escalating its “shadow war” against European democracies and is prepared to intensify sabotage and other hostile operations.
“The confrontation we are in with Russia has taken on a new and more dangerous dimension,” Martin Jäger, head of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service, or BND, told lawmakers during the annual public hearing of the country’s intelligence chiefs.
“Moscow is betting on our weakness,” he said. “The danger of attacks against targets in Germany remains real.”
Germany’s domestic intelligence chief separately warned that Russia was prepared to carry out sabotage, disruption and killings as part of its campaign against Western countries.
Jäger cited an alleged attempted attack at Leipzig airport in August as an example of the threat. German authorities have said Russia sent an explosive drone to the international airport, where it was found near a parked Ukrainian cargo aircraft that reportedly carried military ammunition.
Germany has repeatedly accused Moscow of conducting a hybrid campaign against European countries involving drones, cyberattacks and other acts of sabotage.
Russia has consistently denied plans to attack NATO members.
“We are not threatening anyone and have no intention of attacking anyone, not in 2029, not in 2030 and not in 2050,” Russian President Vladimir Putin said Thursday. “But if we face aggression, we will have no choice but to respond.”
Jäger said Russia could carry out relatively limited military actions against the Baltic states of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia, though he did not expect Moscow to launch a major attack on NATO territory.
He also argued that Putin had passed the point at which he could simply end the war in Ukraine without placing his own rule at risk.
The war, Jäger said, is entering another increasingly dangerous phase, with even more severe Russian attacks expected during the coming winter.
Ukraine turns to AI against Russia’s new jet drones
The German warnings come as Russia has repeatedly struck homes, warehouses and bridges in Kyiv in recent days using a new generation of fast, relatively inexpensive jet-powered drones.
Their introduction caught Ukrainian defenses off guard. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has acknowledged that Kyiv is currently intercepting only about 60% of the new drones, relying heavily on F-16 and MiG fighter jets.
Ukraine is now racing to develop another answer.
Serhiy “Flash” Beskrestnov, an adviser to Zelenskyy on defense technology, said 12 automated firing positions have been deployed around Kyiv to intercept the new jet-powered Shahed drones.
He described the Ukrainian-developed systems as machine guns controlled by artificial intelligence and said additional units would be installed.
The new drones pose a particular problem because their speed makes them harder for existing Ukrainian interception systems to catch.
Kyiv claims 51% of Russian refining capacity disabled
Against the backdrop of the intensified Russian drone campaign, Zelenskyy has vowed to expand Ukrainian attacks on oil facilities deep inside Russia.
Moscow warned Monday that Kyiv would face consequences if the campaign intensified.
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said Sunday that recent long-range attacks on refineries across Russia, from the Moscow region to Siberia, had disabled 51% of the country’s oil-refining capacity.
The figure is a Ukrainian assessment and has not been independently confirmed by Russia.
The strikes contributed to a broad fuel shortage in Russia over the summer, forcing authorities to impose restrictions on gasoline sales.
Russian officials have not publicly released detailed figures on damage to the country’s oil infrastructure. Putin, however, acknowledged Thursday that the attacks had inflicted economic damage.
“They began attacking oil refineries and openly declared that their goal was to damage our economy,” Putin said at a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club. “Did they achieve their goal? Partially.”
He said the strikes had cost Russia about 1% of its gross domestic product.
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said the estimate on refinery damage was compiled by analysts from Ukraine’s intelligence services, General Staff and Defense Ministry.
“Damage to 51% of refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy’s economy, its ability to wage aggression and supply its forces,” he said. “Our deep strikes continue to carry the war into Russian territory.”
Russian drone attacks continue
Russian drone attacks inside Ukraine continued overnight.
One person was killed and six others were wounded in Kharkiv after drones struck the city, setting vehicles and an administrative building on fire and damaging residential buildings.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces had struck energy facilities and vessels used by the Ukrainian military in the Kharkiv region.

articles.title: NATO state preparing to strike St. Petersburg – FT
articles.body:
NATO state preparing to strike St. Petersburg – FT
Estonia is preparing to deploy weapons capable of striking the Russian city of St. Petersburg, the Financial Times has reported.
Amid unprecedented mis- and dis-information from NATO’s European members, Tallinn has presented the proposed buildup as a form of deterrence, should Moscow “test” NATO. However, Russia’s leadership has repeatedly stressed that it has no intention of attacking the US-led military bloc. Moscow has also warned that any direct conflict with NATO would likely escalate into nuclear war.
The British newspaper reported on Monday that Estonia is deploying additional troops along the Russian border and acquiring tactical missile systems capable of reaching St. Petersburg. They include US-made HIMARS and South Korean Chunmoo launchers, both of which can fire longer-range projectiles.
Estonia also trained with the UK during this year’s Spring Storm exercise using Nyan kamikaze jet drones, which can likewise reach Russia’s second-largest city from Estonian territory, according to the report.
The Baltic state has a standing army of just 4,200 troops, but plans to reinforce it with tens of thousands of reservists if tensions with Russia escalate.
Last month, Defense Minister Martin Herem said during a public lecture that Tallinn could not afford to keep mobilized troops in the field for long.
“I have jokingly said that if we get to the orange zone there and carry out mobilization, but Russia does not attack, then it would be economically more correct to attack ourselves,” he said. “Then at least we will know when it will start, and we will not waste food and air in vain”
Russian President Vladimir Putin responded to the remark with an idiom: “The circus has left, but the clowns remain.” He added that Moscow has no plans to attack Estonia or any other NATO member.
Commenting on the FT report, Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova echoed the president, saying it belongs in the funny pages.
Russian diplomats previously cited Herem’s remarks as examples of what they described as aggressive rhetoric by senior officials in NATO countries. The Russian Foreign Ministry has formally warned the bloc against attacking Russian territory or imposing a blockade on the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, saying the country’s response could involve “all weapons” in its arsenal.
While NATO poses as a purely defensive organization, it has a history of military interventions on foreign soil and does not rule out preemptive attacks. Last week, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said European members of the bloc should have been capable of attacking Iran themselves to eliminate what was described as a nuclear threat from Tehran. He argued that Europe’s military buildup should eventually allow it to conduct such operations without relying on the US.
Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania have all sharply increased military spending in recent years and are reportedly seeking additional procurement funds from the EU budget. According to Finnish newspaper Iltalehti, the three Baltic states have asked Brussels to urgently provide €500 million ($570 million) in additional funding, citing the scenario of Russia seeking to “test NATO.”

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Kharkiv devastated by Russian glide bombs, children among victims
articles.body:
Ukraine war latest: Kharkiv devastated by Russian glide bombs, children among victims
Key developments on Oct. 5:
- Children among dozens injured as Russian glide bombs hit Kharkiv, 5 dead
- New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
- Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says

At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, including children, injured after Russian forces struck Kharkiv with glide bombs on Oct. 5.
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram.
"As a result of the strikes… warehouse buildings are on fire, and residential buildings have been damaged. There may be people under the rubble of a residential building that was hit in the attack. A search and rescue operation is underway," he added.
Russian glide bombs, often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.
read also
New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
Automated machine gun turrets using artificial intelligence to aim have downed their first Russian jet-powered drones over Ukraine, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Oct. 5.
A day prior, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
"There are already cases of shooting down even jet UAVs, even 'Geran-5' from the those very turrets," Ihnat said on national television.
"The use of innovative technologies — artificial intelligence — has eliminated human error. Machine vision is used in the shooting down. Artificial intelligence allows you to target even jet-powered drones."
Since Russia started using jet-powered drones en masse against Kyiv toward the end of summer this year, they, especially the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, have presented an air defense problem for which Ukraine has not yet found a single solution.
read also
Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.
read also
Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country.
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.
read also
Ukrainian pilots to soon start training on French Rafale jets, Zelensky says
President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed further European assistance in phone calls with the French and Polish leaders on Oct. 5, as Ukraine braces for a new wave of Russian attacks while U.S.-led peace talks fail to make headway.
Zelensky revealed after his call with French President Emmanuel Macron that France is preparing fresh defense assistance for Ukraine amid relentless Russian strikes, with a new support package expected "soon."
"Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France. This is a significant step forward for Ukraine's combat aviation," he added.
Kyiv announced in 2025 that it aims to purchase 100 Rafale jets to bolster its growing fleet of Western-made aircraft. The Rafale is a 4.5-generation multirole fighter, considered one of the most advanced among European jets.
France is Ukraine's staunch ally in its war against Russian aggression and has provided Kyiv with long-range missiles and intelligence support, among other assistance.
Zelensky said that both sides are also "continuing to work on localizing the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine."

articles.title: Peeter Kaldre: A dangerous moment
articles.body:
Peeter Kaldre: A dangerous moment
As the United States scales back its military role in Europe, the continent faces a dangerous test: strengthening its own defenses while Russia intensifies its threats and war against Ukraine.
It is appalling that 500 million people (Europe) have to ask 300 million people (the United States) for protection against 140 million people (Russia). That is what NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said recently when the subject of reducing the U.S. military presence in Europe came up. Rutte is certainly not the first to put it this way, but it illustrates the situation European security now finds itself in.
How to shoot yourself in the foot
The U.S. plan to reduce its military contribution to NATO and delegate more responsibility to European countries is nothing new; nearly every U.S. administration has talked about it. Why should the United States have to defend wealthy Europe when Europeans themselves barely lift a finger for their own defense? The difference is that the Donald Trump administration has now begun to act and the first cuts are already taking place.
All this is happening at a time when Russia is waging a full-scale war in Europe against Ukraine and is increasingly threatening European countries that support Ukraine.
The September 15 issue of Foreign Affairs featured an article by three security experts — Franklin C. Miller, Eric Edelman and Walter B. Slocombe — pointing to the risks posed by such a U.S. plan. The authors refer to a new security strategy completed last year that calls for shifting the focus from Europe to Asia and the Middle East.
The article lists military capabilities that the Americans want to cut in Europe but that Europe will not be able to replace anytime soon. Its conclusion is that such a policy threatens America itself — in other words, the United States would be hurting itself.
The U.S. military presence in Europe prevents potential adversaries from growing stronger and becoming a threat to the United States. One example cited is that, for the first time in many years, the United States did not take part in a NATO exercise in the North Atlantic that practiced countering Russian submarines. Those same nuclear-armed submarines are designed to approach the U.S. coast...
The story of the Dead Hand
Now the United States is pulling back, but Europe is simply not ready to replace the Americans. One way forward is through so-called coalitions of the willing, one example being the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), led by the United Kingdom and comprising the Baltic and Nordic countries.
The JEF does not have to wait for NATO's Article 5 to be formally invoked; it can act immediately. Jamie Murray, commander of the British contingent stationed in Estonia, put it well: We are ready to go into battle immediately. There are currently 900 British troops in Estonia, with another 300 to be added next year.
We should also bear in mind that the United Kingdom has nuclear weapons, as does France. Although their combined arsenal cannot be compared with Russia's, the Kremlin still has to take it into account. In theory, NATO's collective defense provides for the possibility of using nuclear weapons, including in Estonia's defense. Finland's recent decision to allow nuclear weapons into or through the country in the event of a threat was a powerful statement.
Incidentally, Finland and Sweden seem to have been transformed since joining NATO. Sweden recently announced that if Russia attacks, Sweden will strike targets deep inside Russia.
As for nuclear weapons, Russia has recently begun threatening their use again. Some time ago, Vladimir Putin warned Europe at the Valdai forum that if European countries were planning to take action against Kaliningrad, Russia could resort to nuclear weapons.
There has also been renewed talk of the so-called Dead Hand, an underground system in the Urals that can launch nuclear weapons even if the country's political leadership has been eliminated. It is one of those "nice" Kremlin stories whose veracity cannot be taken for granted.
Nuclear weapons are, after all, Russia's last resort. It cannot defeat even Ukraine with conventional weapons, let alone prevail in a potential conflict with all of Europe. Before it comes to that, however, there are the so-called hybrid tools to try: sabotage, assassinations, election interference and so on. And, of course, brutal strikes against Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, along with disingenuous appeals to foreign countries to move their embassies out of Kyiv.
The aim is to frighten Europe into abandoning its support for Ukraine or at least scaling it back. Putin understands very well that if European support for Ukraine continues, it will be almost impossible for him to subjugate the country.
A very dangerous period lies ahead. Russia may be tempted to make some move against Europe before next month's U.S. congressional midterm elections. Those elections could significantly change Washington's hitherto lenient approach toward Russia.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

articles.title: Putin's escalating bombing campaign won't break Ukrainians' resolve. History shows that it's doomed to fail | Rajan Menon
articles.body:
Vladimir Putin’s army hasn’t made much headway in Ukraine this year, and his territorial goals – annexing four Ukrainian provinces – remain elusive, despite more than four and a half years of war. That explains his recent efforts to sap Ukrainians’ will to resist by launching relentless drone and missile strikes against their cities – targeting, among other sites, residential buildings, large open-air markets, shopping malls, the Dobrobut medical centre and the National Academy of Sciences, both in Kyiv. The capital has been hit the hardest, but other cities – Dnipro, Kharkiv, Kherson, Odesa, Mykolaiv, Sumy – haven’t been spared.
Air-raid sirens pierce the quiet of night. People scramble to shelters (assuming there are any nearby) or, in Kyiv, race to below-ground subway stations. Even walking along city streets, shopping, or filling up your car at a garage forecourt – which are prime targets – can lead to injury, or even death.
I got a taste of what these unremitting attacks are like during a September trip to Ukraine. One night in Mykolaiv, I counted more than a dozen alerts between midnight and dawn. In Kopyliv, about 31 miles west of Kyiv, I was having dinner in a restaurant when a deafening bang made the walls shudder. A drone had hit a building about 500m away; orange flames engulfed its roof within seconds.
Incidents like this are now part of daily life for Ukrainians, but are no less nerve-racking for that.
During September, Russia launched 3,177 jet-powered drones, mainly Geran variants, at Ukraine: nearly 12% more than in August, and a massive increase compared with 350 such strikes in June. Drones, jet-powered or not, are often supplemented by ballistic missiles such as the Iskander – devilishly difficult to intercept with its top speed of 5,600mph and ability to swerve in flight.
The purpose of Putin’s escalating bombardment is to make life so unbearable for Ukrainians that they conclude that the only way out is to satisfy his unfulfilled annexationist ambitions: his army occupies almost all of Luhansk, but has yet to conquer the regions of Donetsk, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia completely.
But his drone and missile campaign won’t force Ukraine to cave.
In December 2025, a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology poll revealed that Ukrainians’ resistance to trading land for peace remains strong. Three-quarters of those surveyed rejected a hypothetical deal that included these provisions: Ukraine’s withdrawal from the unoccupied part of Donetsk, recognition of Russia’s legal ownership of Crimea and Donbas, and the abandonment of its Nato aspirations. Asked separately whether they would approve a settlement that required ceding the unoccupied parts of the two southern provinces, two-thirds said no. These responses are all the more significant because by the end of last year, Russia had begun attacking Ukraine’s power grid as a brutal winter approached.
Putin might nevertheless calculate that a massive bombing operation this winter that turns off the lights, disrupts heating and damages waterworks and sanitation systems will break Ukrainians’ willpower, creating conditions for Russia to conclude the war with additional territory in hand. His calculation isn’t unreasonable, considering Ukraine’s severe shortage of ballistic missile interceptors, which reduced interceptions from 70% in March to 20% in July. It’s collaborating with a European coalition to develop the cost-effective Freya ballistic missile defence system, and will acquire the Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG missile defence system, which provides far easier mobility to aid rapid relocation and is now under development. Neither, however, will be deployed in sufficient numbers any time soon.
Still, the Russian leader’s strategy collides with some inconvenient facts, quite apart from Ukrainians’ proven toughness.
The historical record shows that bombing campaigns don’t crush morale; they strengthen it. Ukrainians won’t be the exception. They regard resistance to Russia as essential for national survival. When I’ve asked them why they continue to fight, the reply, in one form or another, is that the alternative is to forfeit their independence. One can dismiss this as bravado, but what matters is that Ukrainians hold this view.
Accompanying it is the widespread belief that Putin will use any deal to buy time and regroup before renewing his assault on Ukraine. This, too, makes Ukrainians wary of land-for-peace formulas, particularly those offered by Donald Trump and his two emissaries, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, whom they consider Putin partisans, rather than disinterested mediators.
Besides, Putin, too, is under pressure. According to the chief of the UK’s defence staff, his army has suffered 1.5 million casualties. And though Ukraine has a military manpower shortage, so does Russia, despite a population that’s 3.5 times larger; hence its reliance on North Korean soldiers and Asian and African mercenaries. Moreover, the Russian army has barely gained any additional territory this year. During the first six months of 2026, it captured only 28% as much land as it did in the same period last year, and its troop losses now exceed its monthly intake by 6,000.
Furthermore, Ukrainian drone attacks on Russia’s roads and rail lines traversing Ukraine’s occupied territory in the south have left its troops in Crimea, Kherson and Zaporizhzhia short of critical supplies. Most recently, Operation Vivaldi, conducted by Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, caught Russian troops by surprise in the Lyman sector of northern Donetsk, forcing them to retreat eastward.
The war has harmed Russia’s economy. The army’s huge appetite for manpower has created severe labour shortages that have hurt businesses. The 2027 budget draft allocates 35% of federal expenditures to defence. Ukraine’s strikes on refineries deep inside Russia had cut their throughput by about 30%, year on year, by June, creating chronic fuel shortages, widespread rationing, serpentine lines at petrol stations and a 21% surge in petrol prices since January.
Taken together, Ukrainians’ opposition to sacrificing land, the historical failure of bombing campaigns to shatter civilian morale and Russia’s own assorted problems suggest that Putin’s drones and missiles won’t force Ukraine to accept peace on his terms – even under the stress of winter.
- Rajan Menon is a professor emeritus of international relations at the City College of New York and a senior research scholar at Columbia University’s Saltzman Institute of War and Peace Studies

articles.title: Kremlin Downplays Estonia’s Troop Shift to Border, Plays Up Russia’s Intelligence Capabilities
articles.body:
The Kremlin on Monday said Russia’s intelligence services were capable of monitoring military movements along the country’s borders, brushing aside reports that Estonia is shifting troops closer to the Russian border.
“There should be no doubt that our Defense Ministry and other relevant services possess the necessary intelligence to properly monitor and assess the situation around our borders,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters during a daily briefing.
His comments come in response to the Financial Times detailing Estonia’s strategic pivot toward an “active defense” posture after observing Russia’s military tactics in Ukraine.
Under the updated doctrine, the Baltic nation of 1.3 million is moving primary combat units from northern Estonia’s Tapa to Jõhvi — 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the border with the Leningrad region.
Estonia is also constructing new facilities in the border city of Narva to house up to 1,000 troops during a crisis.
Instead of a doctrine involving efforts to “harry” invading Russian forces until the arrival of NATO reinforcements, Estonian military planners are now opting to “fight over every inch of territory.” The country is also acquiring drones and ballistic missiles capable of striking up to 300 kilometers (186 miles) inside Russian territory.
Estonia, a former Soviet republic that has long had strained relations with Moscow, has been at the forefront of countering Russian security threats and has strongly backed Ukraine since Putin ordered the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
The FT report comes amid escalating rhetoric between European officials and Russia.
Martin Jaeger, the head of Germany's BND foreign intelligence agency, said Monday that Germany faces a real risk of entering a “violent conflict” with Russia as Moscow expands its “shadow war” of hybrid attacks across Europe.
Jaeger warned that in the short term Russia could engage in “low-intensity military activities, particularly in the Baltic states.”

articles.title: Saudi-backed forces recapture key areas around strait from Houthis in Yemen
articles.body:
Forces of the Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen have recaptured several key areas around Bab al-Mandab strait from Iran-backed Houthi rebels, Yemeni officials said on Monday.
The officials said forces allied with the internationally recognized government have retaken the crucial town of Dhubab just north of the strait. They also captured the towns of Bab and Hadeid, said the officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak to reporters. Witnesses said they saw government tanks and forces entering the towns.
The government push came as part of a major offensive launched early Monday under an air cover by a Saudi military coalition, aiming to retake all territory held by the Houthis.
However, the offensive came just after the rebels said they had captured more territory in the south-western part of Yemen, taking the key town of Turbah in a blow to the Saudi-backed forces as they advanced toward the strategic provincial capital of Taiz, Yemen’s third-largest city.
The Saudi-led coalition spokesperson, Maj Gen Turki al-Malki, said 100 fighter jets were providing support to the forces of Yemen’s internationally recognized government fighting against the Houthis. He said the coalition had secured “air protection” of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait and destroyed hundreds of Houthi targets as part of the ongoing campaign.
Marco Rubio told reporters that it was expected that the Saudi-backed government in Yemen would hit back at the rebels to reclaim territory. Asked if the Saudi-led coalition coordinated the action with the United States, the US secretary of state said that Saudi Arabia and the US had a defense agreement but would not offer more details.
He said the Yemeni government was ousted from some of its territory by a Houthi campaign and the Saudis had come under attack, and “they have a right to defend themselves”.
The new push sets an ambitious goal for the embattled government, which recently lost swathes of the country’s Red Sea coastline and areas around the Bab al-Mandab strait – a chokepoint for international shipping – after a lightning offensive by the Iran-backed Houthis.
Yemen’s internationally recognised government has struggled to roll back the surge, even with the military support of Saudi Arabia. The Houthis have increasingly targeted Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, and on Sunday said they had attacked oil infrastructure in the capital again.
The statement came just hours after the Houthis cut a vital supply route linking the besieged city of Taiz with the government’s interim capital, Aden, according to four security sources.
The Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the city.
“We were informed that the Houthis had taken control of the al-Safiya area, where they cut the main road and took control of the police station,” a police source in the area said.
Three sources with the Yemeni military also confirmed Houthi control over the area and the supply route, with traffic along the road halted and the group now surrounding Taiz city. Fighting in the area was ongoing, they added.
Sources from both sides told AFP on Sunday that fighting in and around the western province of Taiz had killed more than 70 people over the past day.
Sources from the internationally recognised government reported that 34 government troops were killed – 20 on the edge of Taiz province in neighbouring Lahj – while Houthi military sources said 39 of their fighters were killed in fighting across Taiz and in border areas with Lahj.
Taiz city itself remains under the control of government forces but has long been besieged from the north, east and west by Houthi fighters and remains one of the main fronts in Yemen’s long-running civil war.
A Houthi military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said on Sunday the group launched ballistic missiles and drones at the Saudi energy company Aramco’s sites in Riyadh and in the Khurais area in the east, causing large fires.
The attacks were in response to what the Houthis claimed were 50 Saudi-led air and missile strikes in Yemen in the past 12 hours.
There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia.
Saudi oil exports were already under pressure due to Iran’s blockade of the strait of Hormuz in the Gulf.
The Houthi’s Al-Masirah TV channel reported Saudi strikes on Sunday in the northern governorates of al-Jawf and Saada, saying at least two people had been wounded.

articles.title: Estonia relocates troops closer to Russian border – FT
articles.body:
Estonia relocates troops closer to Russian border – FT
Estonia is redeploying a key brigade from the city of Tapa to Jõhvi, located 50 km from the Russian border, as it prepares for potential Russian aggression.
Source: European Pravda, citing Financial Times
Details: According to Estonian officials, the country is continuously moving troops closer to the border with Russia and procuring weapons capable of striking deep into Russian territory as it prepares for possible aggression by Moscow beyond Ukraine's borders.
The FT writes that Estonian military and intelligence chiefs do not believe Russia is seeking a full-scale war with NATO, at least not within the next two years. Meanwhile, they are convinced that Moscow is preparing for a possible future conflict with Estonia.
This has prompted Estonia, which has no air force of its own, to shift to an "active defence" strategy.
"We have to start from the border and win from the first battles," declared Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the First Estonian Brigade, the country's primary fighting force.
His unit is being permanently redeployed from Tapa to Jõhvi, where large new facilities are currently being constructed to house soldiers.
"Deterrence is not working. The critical period to address that, for all of us in the Baltic states, is in the next one to four years," noted an Estonian military intelligence representative.
Meanwhile, the Estonian Ministry of Defence emphasised that they must make aggression against the country "unthinkable".
"Our aim is clear: to keep the enemy and the destruction of war away from Estonian territory," the Ministry of Defence stressed.
In May, the Estonian government introduced the term "active defence" into its national security concept. Since then, the country's armed forces have initiated a quiet but radical reorganisation. Elite units are being continuously redeployed from Tapa, Estonia's primary military base, to positions closer to the Russian border. Additionally, a new base for 1,000 military personnel is under construction in the border city of Narva.
Over the past year, the country signed contracts to acquire nine American HIMARS multiple-launch rocket systems, M57 ballistic missiles with a strike range of up to 300 km and nine South Korean Chunmoo MLRS with a similar range. It should be noted that the distance from Estonia's border bases to Russia's St Petersburg is 260 km.
In the decade following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2014, Estonian military strategists developed a defence doctrine shaped by the country's history and geography. Under this approach, in the event of an attack, conscripts would rapidly mobilise and engage in a tactical, quasi-guerrilla defence to delay Russian troops and inflict casualties until NATO reinforcements arrived.
However, after observing Russia's actions in Ukraine, Estonian military leaders concluded that such a plan would not work. They now believe that the Kremlin pays no heed to casualties when fighting to hold captured territory, even after everything on it has been destroyed.
Estonia now plans to fight for every inch of territory and inflict powerful strikes against Russia hundreds of kilometres behind the frontline from the very first day of any invasion.
"Militarily this is very demanding. We cannot shape the enemy [by retreating or tactically luring them into situations]. We have to build our lines today. It is forward defence," stated Kundla.
Estonian military intelligence is particularly apprehensive about potential limited actions targeting a border objective – specifically, the small, predominantly Russian-speaking city of Narva. This could serve as a provocative test of NATO's resolve, aimed at fracturing the alliance.
Background:
- As reported, Estonia's defence spending in 2027 and beyond will exceed 5% of GDP, with total national defence expenditure reaching €2.2 billion.
- Neighbouring Lithuania, together with Poland, is developing an international civilian evacuation plan to be utilised should it become necessary to evacuate portions of the populations of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia across the border.

articles.title: ‘Muslim NATO’ activates force deployment over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.body:
‘Muslim NATO’ activates force deployment over Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
A three-nation military alliance dubbed the “Muslim NATO” has activated its collective-defense commitments and ordered the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia amid an escalating confrontation with Yemen’s Houthis.
Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan made the decision at an emergency meeting of the Mecca Defense Alliance in Riyadh on Monday after a series of Houthi attacks. In a joint statement they condemned the “attempted targeting” of the Islamic holy cities of Mecca and Medina, as well as attacks on Saudi cities and civilian and economic infrastructure.
The group decided to “move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defense commitments” and take measures to provide agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their “rapid deployment” in Saudi Arabia. It said the move was intended to boost military readiness and integration and strengthen the three countries’ “collective capacity to confront and counter threats.”
The Emergency Meeting of the Strategic Political and Defense Committee under the Makkah Alliance for Defense reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom and the holy sites. The committee agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the Alliance in response to the attacks and all those responsible for them.
— Khalid bin Salman خالد بن سلمان (@kbsalsaud) October 5, 2026
The alliance was formed in August under an agreement treating an armed attack on any member as an attack on all three, mirroring NATO’s Article 5 collective-defense principle.
