— Ministry of Foreign Affairs - Pakistan (@ForeignOfficePk) October 5, 2026
Yemen’s civil war has escalated sharply in recent weeks. A Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen’s internationally recognized government said on Monday that 100 fighter jets were taking part in Operation Dawn of Yemen, providing air cover for ground forces. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki said 324 “high-value targets” had been destroyed.
The Houthis, also known as Ansar Allah, are a Shiite armed group that has controlled the Yemeni capital of Sanaa and much of northern Yemen for more than a decade. They have accused Riyadh of carrying out extensive airstrikes and hitting civilian targets.
Yemen’s government announced a new campaign on Sunday aimed at retaking all Houthi-held territory. The move followed major gains by the group in September, when it captured swathes of the Red Sea coast and territory around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a key shipping route.
Government forces said on Monday that they had retaken several areas around the strait, including the town of Dhubab, which sits strategically along the strait. The Houthis have disputed reports of government advances.
The renewed fighting has killed hundreds of combatants on both sides and forced more than 145,000 people from their homes since September, according to UN figures.
Saudi Arabia first intervened in Yemen in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government after the Houthis had driven it from Sanaa the previous year. Large-scale fighting decreased significantly following a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
Fighting escalated again last month. The Houthis have accused Riyadh of imposing an illegal siege on Yemen, while Saudi Arabia says the group has stepped up missile, drone, and maritime attacks against the kingdom itself and shipping in the Red Sea.
The escalation comes as the Strait of Hormuz remains closed to most shipping and US-Iranian talks on ending the conflict have stalled.
Several Saudi allies have stepped up military support for the kingdom. Britain has agreed to provide air-to-air refueling for Saudi warplanes, while France is sending troops, radar, and air-defense systems to help protect the Red Sea oil hub of Yanbu.

articles.title: Macron slams Russia’s ‘irresponsible’ strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure
articles.body:
Macron slams Russia’s ‘irresponsible’ strikes on Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday slammed Russia's increased strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure. In a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Macron said he reviewed "the concrete support" Europe can provide Ukraine to defend itself against the attacks.
French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday condemned Russia ramping up strikes on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, calling it "irresponsible" after speaking with Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky on ways to bolster support for Kyiv.
Russia "has made the irresponsible choice to intensify its strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets", Macron said on X.
He said Zelensky and he reviewed "the concrete support we can provide" to help Ukraine intercept drones and defend itself against Russia's attacks.
"We will yield neither to intimidation nor to Russia's escalation," Macron said, accusing Moscow of "stubbornly refusing all calls for a ceasefire".
Moscow announced at the weekend that it would step up its strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure as winter approaches.
Zelensky has made repeated calls on Ukraine's Western allies for better air-defence weaponry to combat the increasingly deadly barrage of drone and missile strikes.
Kyiv has also expressed interest in producing Patriot missile systems under US licence in the future, though the status of any such arrangement remains unclear.
Over the weekend Russia issued a fresh warning to foreigners and diplomats to leave Kyiv, saying "massive" new airstrikes would hit the capital.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz travelled to Kyiv on Sunday to demonstrate his support and pledge additional financial assistance to Ukraine.
Read moreMerz unveils new aid for Ukraine as Russia strikes Kyiv during German leader's visit
Efforts to end Europe's worst conflict since World War II have been at a standstill, while both Moscow and Kyiv have vowed to intensify long-range attacks against military and related targets.
Russian drone strikes sink Turkish ship in Black Sea, Ukraine says
Macron's condemnation came as Russian drones carried out a deadly attack on a grain ship in the Black Sea, Zelensky said, after Romania reported a ship had caught fire and sunk near its coast with two crew killed.
"A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn," Zelensky said in a post on X, adding that the ship was Turkish-owned and Azerbaijani and Indian nationals were on board.

articles.title: Russia Repeatedly Tests Romanian Air Defense
articles.body:
A suspected drone fell near Romania’s border with Ukraine and started a fire on Friday, Oct. 2, without national air defense radars reporting an incursion, adding to concerns over NATO’s ability to detect and stop aircraft crossing its eastern frontier.
Romanian authorities were investigating the object’s origin. Their initial statement described it as possibly an aerial drone and did not confirm that it was Russian.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The alert came during Russian drone attacks on civilian sites and infrastructure across the Danube in Ukraine. At about 5 a.m., authorities received reports that an object had fallen near Plauru in northern Tulcea County. Firefighters and military teams secured the area. No casualties or material damage were reported.
Local Mayor Tudor Cernega told Euronews Romania that the object fell in a harvested field roughly 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Danube and 1.5 kilometers (0.9 miles) from homes. He said residents had received no air-raid alert that night.
Romania faced another alert early Monday, Oct. 5, when radar detected an aerial target near Vylkove on the Ukrainian side of the border. Two Spanish F-18 fighters scrambled from Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base, and authorities warned residents in northern Tulcea County at 2:34 a.m. No incursion into Romanian airspace was detected, and the alert ended at 3:23 a.m.
Repeated breaches, different responses
Recent incidents have included aircraft briefly entering NATO territory, drones disappearing from radar and debris recovered after explosions. Those events have not all produced shootdowns, but official accounts also record fighter deployments and other responses.
India Moves to Broker Black Sea Deal Between Russia and Ukraine
On the evening of Sept. 27, a drone entered Romania near Ceatalchioi and disappeared from radar approximately 10 minutes later near Somova, according to a Defense Ministry account carried by Agerpres. Two Romanian F-16s took off to monitor the situation. The statement did not report a shootdown.
On Sept. 29, the ministry confirmed finding a crater and drone fragments near Gropeni in Brăila County. Investigators established that an explosive payload had detonated on impact, causing a limited fire on agricultural land.
Poland reported a separate violation on Sept. 23, when a Russian military Mi-8 helicopter crossed from Kaliningrad near Braniewo. According to Polish operational command, reported by Notes from Poland, it penetrated no farther than 300 meters (about 980 feet) and remained in Polish airspace for 42 seconds. Poland scrambled fighters and placed ground forces on standby.
Earlier in September, Estonia reported drones entering its airspace after flying along its eastern border. Allied aircraft responded from Ämari Air Base. The foreign ministry’s statement linked the threat to Russia’s war but did not identify the drones’ operator.
NATO forces have also destroyed intruding drones. As Kyiv Post reported in July, Romanian forces shot down three drones over three consecutive days. Authorities identified the first as a Russian Shahed-type drone, and Bucharest subsequently expelled a Russian diplomat.
Pressure to strengthen drone defenses
On the Ukrainian side of the border overnight Oct. 1–2, the Air Force reported 108 incoming Russian drones, including 47 jet-powered Shaheds. It said air defenses shot down or suppressed 88, approximately 81% of the total. That figure combines different methods of neutralization and is not a count of aircraft physically shot down.
Across NATO’s eastern flank, repeated alerts have increased pressure to strengthen defenses against drones rather than rely on fighter deployments alone.
Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania reportedly requested €500 million ($570 million) in urgent EU assistance for drone defenses. Kyiv Post’s Sept. 23 report, citing Finland’s Iltalehti newspaper, said the three countries’ defense ministers had sent their request to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The reported request had not been publicly announced.
Sabotage allegations and NATO’s response
The airspace incidents come alongside allegations of Russian operations against European businesses supporting Ukraine.
On Sept. 29, Estonia accused Russian intelligence services of ordering an August arson attack on Milrem Robotics, a defense company in Tallinn. Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna said the perpetrators had been apprehended and that Estonia had summoned Russia’s ambassador. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov rejected the accusation as baseless.
In a separate maritime incident, Russian border guards held the cargo ship Västerbotten for several hours on Oct. 1 while it was heading to Estonia’s Sillamäe port. The Cypriot-flagged vessel was in Russian territorial waters and subsequently continued to its destination.
Estonia’s Transport Administration said Russia had not explained the detention. An official also noted that states can inspect ships in their territorial waters, so the detention alone did not establish an unlawful action.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said the alliance’s responses to Russian hostile activity will not always be public or match Moscow’s actions directly.
Speaking alongside Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius in Brussels on Sept. 29, Rutte said: “You will not always see them public. They will not always be symmetric. It will not always be tit-for-tat.”
Romania’s latest statements illustrate the continuing detection problem: a suspected drone fell near Plauru without a recorded incursion, while a separate radar alert three days later prompted fighter launches without a confirmed border crossing.

articles.title: Ukraine wants to aim Starlink at Russian targets—and build a version Elon Musk can’t switch off
articles.body:
Ukraine is working on a satellite system of its own, something similar to SpaceX's Starlink, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Interfax-Ukraine reported. He argued Kyiv should be free to turn Starlink on Russian military targets, warning that China and other states will share comparable satellite technology with Moscow within months. Ukraine's battlefield communications still ride on a network owned by Elon Musk, who has clashed with Kyiv and once limited its wartime use.
Low-orbit satellite internet has turned into a frontline utility that a single company or government can switch on or off, and both armies are now racing to own that link instead of renting it. Control of the network decides whose drones can see the battlefield and fly through the jamming to strike it—leverage Kyiv has gone without while its connection rode on hardware it does not run.
Working on a Starlink of its own
Zelenskyy said there was groundwork in place and that Ukraine was working on a system similar to Starlink. He called it fair for Ukraine to aim Starlink at military sites inside Russia. The timing is the reason, he said: some states will share the technology with Russia late this year or early next, and the Chinese are among them. Moscow is already fielding its own Starlink-style constellation, Rassvet, though for now it reaches Ukraine only in brief passes.
Ukrainian brigades detail Starlink crackdown: Russian terminals “became just bricks,” assaults disrupted
Ukraine's troops and drones lean heavily on Starlink, a network Kyiv neither owns nor controls. Musk has used that control against Kyiv before: in 2022 SpaceX refused a Ukrainian request to extend Starlink over occupied Crimea for a drone strike on Russia's warships, and it has since restricted the network's use for drone operations.
Sanctions, and satellites of its own
Zelenskyy has asked US President Donald Trump several times to sanction the Russian and Chinese companies building Russia's Rassvet network, most recently at the UN General Assembly in New York, he said in a recent Financial Times interview.
The EU sanctioned Russia’s Starlink rival but not the company that builds it. Experts call that the gap that matters
Denys Shtilerman, co-founder and chief designer at Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, told the Financial Times in May that the firm had launched two satellites this year and planned dozens more in 2027, aiming to reduce reliance on the US government and Western tech companies. To strike deep inside Russia and gather intelligence, he has said, Ukraine needs its own constellation covering all of Russia.

articles.title: Ansarallah sets Aramco sites ablaze as mercenaries commit war crimes in Yemen
articles.body:
Ansarallah sets Aramco sites ablaze as mercenaries commit war crimes in Yemen
TEHRAN — Yemeni armed forces fired a coordinated salvo of heavy ballistic missiles and long-range attack drones deep into the Saudi interior on Monday and Sunday, striking major Saudi Aramco installations in Jeddah, Riyadh, and the Khurais oil field.
The precision retaliatory operations ignited massive fires near strategic energy infrastructure, triggered civil defense alerts in Mecca and Taif, and forced flight cancellations across Saudi commercial airports.
Ansarallah official Mohammed al-Bukhaiti warned international airlines that Saudi airspace remains unsafe while the aggression continues.
Footage of burning Aramco sites has been broadcast, and satellite fire-detection data have corroborated blazes in Jeddah and south of Riyadh.
Yemeni military spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree confirmed that these strikes answered more than 50 Saudi air raids launched against civilian centers in Sanaa, Saada, Al-Jawf, and Taiz within a single twelve-hour period.
Mercenary war crimes at Dhubab Airport
While Saudi-backed media promoted tactical movements along the western coast near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaked video footage exposed the lawless conduct of foreign-funded proxies.
Verified recordings filmed at Dhubab Airport show members of the Saudi-backed Presidential Leadership Council and UAE-funded Southern Giants Brigades forces committing severe war crimes against captured Ansarallah prisoners of war.
The footage shows heavy military vehicles driving intentionally over bound captives, summary executions of unarmed detainees, and the gross mutilation of corpses. These visual records document grave breaches of international humanitarian law and highlight the total collapse of discipline among Riyadh’s auxiliary troops.
On the ground, claims by Presidential Leadership Council chairman Rashad al-Alimi regarding gains in Dhubab remain fragile and short-lived.
Historical experience across Taiz, Hodeidah, and Al-Jawf suggests that foreign-backed formations consistently crumble once immediate air support subsides.
Just last month, Yemeni forces demonstrated their tactical agility by liberating Mocha, Dhubab, and Perim Island in an eighteen-hour coastal push. Similar coalition offensives in 2018 stalled completely, and current frontline reports confirm that Ansarallah units have maintained control over essential supply routes while preparing decisive counterattacks to reclaim temporary proxy gains.
Western collusion and strategic failure
This ongoing aggression relies heavily on direct intelligence and logistical support from Washington and Tel Aviv.
American military officials have supplied targeting data for over 200 sites inside Yemen, alongside more than 100 U.S. advisers operating with coalition command.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reportedly offered military backing to support the campaign, following previous Israeli strikes on Sanaa leadership targets.
Yet years of advanced Western weaponry and foreign advice have failed to resolve Saudi Arabia’s core military vulnerabilities or secure its southern border.
The humanitarian cost of the Western-backed campaign continues to climb.
World Health Organization reports confirm over 5,000 casualties since August, alongside a threefold increase in cholera cases across targeted governorates.
Nevertheless, relentless aerial bombardment cannot protect Saudi energy infrastructure from long-range retaliation.
By establishing a direct equation between Saudi aggression and the vulnerability of Aramco facilities in Jeddah and Yanbu, Ansarallah has shattered the coalition’s security guarantees, proving that Riyadh cannot achieve through foreign airpower what it has failed to gain on the battlefield for over a decade.

articles.title: Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
articles.body:
Ukraine scrambles for money to fight war as Russian strikes batter economy
KYIV, Oct 5 - Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, is struggling to survive. Russian airstrikes have brought the city's huge steel plant and mines to a standstill, dragging the local economy to its knees.
Mayor Oleksandr Vilkul said the sprawling industrial city — which stretches along the banks of the Inhulets River — was doing everything possible to ensure its hospitals remain open, the lights remain on in kindergartens and schools, and buses keep running.
"In Kryvyi Rih, the situation is actually worse than anywhere else, apart from the front line itself," Vilkul, 52, a former mining executive, said in a video address.
The financial squeeze on the city of about 600,000 people underlines the challenges facing Ukraine as the government navigates its biggest budget crisis since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Last month, the city's largest employer — ArcelorMittal's hulking mining and steelmaking complex — suspended its operations following a series of Russian ballistic missile strikes that darkened its furnaces.
The prospects for next year, Vilkul said, are bleak.
"It's about survival. Right now, we need to survive," he said.
It's a scene played out across Ukraine's once-mighty steel industry, which accounted for a tenth of economic output before the war. Giant mills in Zaporizhzhia in the southeast and other industrial cities stand silent and exports have stopped.
An escalation in Russia's drone and missile strikes this summer destroyed factories and warehouses across Ukraine, damaged ports and railways, and forced shops and businesses to close, slowing the growth of the economy and tax revenue.
Meanwhile, the technology-driven war is becoming ever more expensive for Ukraine to fight.
Billions of euros in foreign loans have been delayed by failure to pass bills including unpopular tax reforms and anti-corruption legislation demanded by Ukraine's Western allies, leaving a gaping hole in state coffers.
Ukraine needs $56 billion to fund that gap this year —equivalent to about a quarter of its economic output. Of that, $27 billion is military spending.
To bridge the shortfall, Ukrainian officials met European partners in Brussels last week to discuss bringing forward disbursements due next year under a €90-billion ($101-billion) EU loan. The European Commission and Ukraine said they had identified funds to close the gap this year.
But three sources familiar with the talks said accelerating these payments risked increasing budget pressure next year - at a time when looming election campaigns in European allies including France and Poland could erode support for Kyiv.
Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi acknowledges the situation is "challenging". The government has been forced to freeze non-essential spending — including reconstruction of damaged buildings and infrastructure — to prioritise military spending, public sector wages and pensions.
"All resources should be channelled into critically important areas," Koretskyi told reporters.
WAR COSTS SOAR, DOMESTIC REVENUES FALL
Two years ago, a single day of fighting cost Ukraine $140 million, but that figure has jumped to $190 million, according to Roksolana Pidlasa, the head of parliament's budget committee. And that does not include direct military support to Kyiv from its Western allies.
Rising costs are driven partly by the need for expensive medium- and long-range weapons capable of striking Russia's oil refineries and military factories to reduce Moscow's ability to continue its war.
Plus, the wage bill for an expanded army is higher than ever before, and the state must support a growing number of military families of disabled or deceased soldiers.
"Expenditure will continue to rise," Pidlasa told a conference in Kyiv. "This is one more pragmatic reason why the US and Europe need to act faster to force (Russia) to end this war."
In the first nine months of this year, Ukraine spent more than $44 billion on defence alone, data showed. That does not include in-kind military support from allies.
In the same period, the government was able to raise only about $42 billion in tax revenue as the economy slowed.
Pidlasa said that in the first nine months of this year Ukraine's budget lost over 49.5 billion hryvnias ($1.1 billion) in tax revenue because of Russian attacks that not only damaged property and goods, but disrupted logistics and shut shops and businesses for hours at a time.
By the end of the year, the cumulative losses could rise to 70 billion hryvnias, the government estimates.
"We have not a temporary but a structural problem with the revenues at the very time when spending really requires resources," said Oleksandra Myronenko, an economist at the Centre for Economic Strategies, a Kyiv-based think tank.
Some Ukrainian businesses have started to scale back operations. Others have put capital expenditure on hold as the country braces for a difficult winter. Business sentiment and economic expectations are darkening.
Vasyl Khmelnytskyi, founder of an industrial park in the city of Bila Tserkva near Kyiv, said he had scrapped plans to build three new factories.
"The risks are simply too great right now — both for the business and for the people," he said in a Facebook post.
Ukraine's agricultural sector — its largest source of export revenues — has been particularly hard hit. Russian attacks on Ukraine's Black Sea ports led to a 36.6% fall in grain exports year-on-year in September.
About $40 billion in export revenue is at risk this year as a result of the blockade, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said.
Even with tens of billions of euros in foreign support, Ukraine's economy is expected to grow only between 0.5% and 1.5% this year, economists say — down from 1.8% in 2025.
FOREIGN AID IS DELAYED
During more than four years of intense fighting, Ukraine has been able to maintain macroeconomic and financial stability thanks to fiscal support from its Western partners, receiving nearly $200 billion since Russia's invasion.
But $29.5 billion in foreign aid is now at risk this year because of delays in passing reforms, Koretskyi said. The government has postponed about $900 million of capital spending until December, in the hope the legislation will be passed.
The aim is to pass all the required legislation in parliament by October 15, Koretskyi said.
"Only then we will get all the money," Koretskyi said. "This is absolutely vital. It needs to be done as soon as possible."
Legislators are now discussing the budget for next year. The government has proposed record defence budget spending of $110 billion. This figure does not include direct military aid.
Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has estimated that the unfunded budget gap for the next year is already more than $32 billion.
Part of the solution, Marchenko said, is to use frozen Russian assets in Europe to fund Ukraine's budget. EU countries immobilised some €210 billion of Russian central bank assets after Moscow invaded Ukraine.
"Ukraine continues to mobilise domestic resources, but the scale of Russia's war puts clear limits on our capacity," Marchenko said on X. REUTERS

articles.title: Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport
articles.body:
Houthis claim strikes on Riyadh airport
Yemen’s Houthis have claimed a direct missile strike on Riyadh’s main international airport as part of a large-scale barrage targeting airports, military bases and oil infrastructure across Saudi Arabia.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Monday night that the group, officially known as Ansar Allah, had carried out three operations using “a large number” of ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in response to intensified Saudi-backed strikes on Yemen.
The first attack targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh and achieved a “direct and precise hit,” Saree claimed, saying air traffic was disrupted. The second targeted Saudi Aramco’s refinery in Rabigh, where the group claimed a direct hit started fires. The third operation allegedly targeted Abha Airport, Khamis Mushait air base, the Aqeefah military camp and other “sensitive sites” in Najran and Jizan.
Saudi authorities have not addressed the specific claims of direct hits on the airport and refinery or said whether Houthi strikes caused disruption at King Khalid. The Foreign Ministry issued a broader statement condemning continued Houthi attacks on Riyadh and several other Saudi cities and “civilian and economic facilities,” while reiterating the kingdom’s right to respond.
#Statement | The Foreign Ministry expresses the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia’s strongest condemnation and denunciation of the terrorist Houthi militia’s continued targeting of civilians and civilian and economic facilities in the Kingdom; its blatant and repeated attacks against the holiest sites on earth—Makkah and Madinah— the capital Riyadh, and the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, Najran, Taif, and Yanbu; and its targeting of Saudi vessels in the southern Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
— Foreign Ministry 🇸🇦 (@KSAmofaEN) October 5, 2026
Loud explosions were reportedly heard in northern Riyadh near King Khalid airport. An AFP journalist reported hearing a “powerful explosion,” while residents said blasts shook windows in the area.
Saudi Arabia’s Interior Ministry has meanwhile renewed a warning that photographing, publishing or circulating information about missile and drone interception operations or impact sites could result in legal action. The same warning was originally issued earlier in the war. Saudi media republished it shortly after midnight amid the latest attacks.
The Houthis also warned international airlines against using Saudi airspace, declaring it a theater of military operations while exempting the airspace over Mecca and Medina. King Khalid airport remained operational, but Flightradar24 data showed substantial delays, with average delays reaching 38 minutes.
The group said the barrage was retaliation for 60 Saudi air and missile strikes on Sanaa and the provinces of Al-Jawf, Taiz, Hodeidah, Saada and Marib over the previous 24 hours, which it said caused civilian casualties. Saree claimed Saudi forces had carried out 1,576 strikes since the latest escalation began.
The exchange comes as Saudi Arabia and its Yemeni allies intensify a major counteroffensive against the Houthis. The Saudi-led coalition says about 100 fighter jets are providing round-the-clock air support as government forces attempt to retake territory lost along Yemen’s Red Sea coast and around the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait. The coalition claims to have destroyed 324 “high-value” Houthi targets.
Saudi-backed forces said on Monday that they had recaptured Dhubab and the nearby towns of Bab and Hadeid, with witnesses telling AP they saw government tanks and troops entering the towns. The Houthis have denied reports of a broader retreat, while fighting has also intensified around Taiz.
The US is also assisting the Saudi campaign with intelligence sharing, target identification and operational planning, American and regional officials told AP. The US Embassy in Riyadh has meanwhile warned Americans to remain vigilant for possible missile and drone attacks.

articles.title: Turkey weighs military support for Saudi Arabia under Mecca pact
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Turkey weighs military support for Saudi Arabia under Mecca defence pact
Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan are set to hold high-level defence talks in Riyadh on Monday as Ankara signals its readiness to support the kingdom against continued Houthi attacks under the countries' newly signed joint defence pact.
Foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs from the three countries will attend a meeting of the Political and Defence Strategic Committee established under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on 7 August.
The talks come as Turkey steps up its engagement with Saudi Arabia amid growing questions over what military support Ankara could provide Riyadh, including expanding defence industry, intelligence cooperation and expertise in drone warfare.
Turkey's foreign ministry said Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan, Defence Minister Yasar Guler and Chief of the General Staff Selcuk Bayraktaroglu would attend the meeting.
Fidan is expected to outline Turkey's position on consolidating the alliance and its next steps, as well as assess threats to peace and stability in the region and discuss developments impacting the three countries' shared security.
According to the ministry, Fidan will stress the importance of the alliance in providing a combined and effective response to threats and preventing regional crises.
He is also expected to reaffirm Turkey's "strong support" and solidarity with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks and stress that attacks targeting holy sites, including Mecca, are unacceptable.
Ankara is also expected to emphasise the importance of securing international trade routes and resolving regional conflicts through peaceful means.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar said on Friday that Iran had proposed political engagement with the Houthis, an initiative expected to be discussed at the emergency Riyadh meeting.
Dar said Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan would determine their next steps during the talks.
The alliance is also expected to establish its secretariat in Riyadh, with Pakistan nominating retired Lieutenant General Nauman Mahmood as its first secretary-general.
Mecca defence pact takes shape
The Political and Defence Strategic Committee, comprising the three countries' foreign and defence ministers and chiefs of staff, is responsible for directing activities under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.
It held its first meeting in Istanbul on 31 August, when officials discussed the technical work required to institutionalise the alliance.
The countries' foreign ministers also met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where they discussed regional developments and issued a statement condemning attacks on Mecca, which the Houthis denied carrying out, as well as attacks on Saudi civilian and economic infrastructure.
The military chiefs of Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan subsequently met in Riyadh on 25 September.
Saudi Arabia's defence ministry said the commanders reviewed threats facing the kingdom and discussed strengthening military cooperation, intelligence sharing and coordination between their armed forces.
They also agreed to begin translating commitments under the Mecca pact into "effective military cooperation".
Fidan later said regional developments and military threats facing Saudi Arabia from both the north and south had been discussed.
He said Turkey's chief of staff had briefed President Recep Tayyip Erdogan following the technical military talks in Riyadh, adding that the Turkish armed forces possessed the capabilities and expertise required to respond to threats.
Erdogan has stressed that the pact should not be viewed as an alliance directed against Iran, Israel or any other country.
In an interview with Newsweek, he said the agreement was based on Article 51 of the UN Charter, which recognises the right to self-defence. Under the agreement, an armed attack against one of the three countries is considered an attack against all parties.
Erdogan said the response would depend on the requirements of the country under attack and could range from intelligence, logistical and ammunition support to broader military assistance.
What could Turkey provide?
Attention has increasingly turned to what Turkish support for Saudi Arabia could look like in practice.
Fidan said on 20 September that Ankara would consider Riyadh's military requirements as it confronted continuing attacks, while stressing that Saudi Arabia should not be drawn into the conflict between the United States and Iran.
Turkey's growing defence industry could become a central component of that support.
Ankara has developed significant capabilities in drones, missiles, smart munitions and artillery, while its armed forces have accumulated experience in conflicts involving armed groups and irregular forces.
Turkey provided extensive military support to Azerbaijan during the 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh war and intervened in support of Libya's internationally recognised government in 2019, where Turkish drones helped shift the military balance.
It has also conducted repeated military operations in northern Syria and Iraq and exported drones to countries including Ukraine and Ethiopia.
Those capabilities have prompted speculation that Ankara could provide Saudi Arabia with military advice, intelligence support and advanced weapons without becoming directly involved in fighting.
Ufuk Necat Tasci, a professor of international relations at Canakkale Onsekiz Mart University, told The New Arab that Fidan's comments signalled that Ankara was positioning itself firmly alongside Riyadh.
"Politically, this statement indicates that Turkey will enter the equation in favour of Saudi Arabia. Time will reveal whether this intervention will be direct or indirect," he said. "Nevertheless, Turkey does not want to remain neutral towards the attacks on Saudi Arabia during this period, because this alliance, as is clear, has raised concerns in both Israel and Iran."
Drones and air defence
Merve Suna Ozel Ozcan, an international relations academic at Kirikkale University, cautioned against interpreting Turkey's position as signalling direct military intervention.
"Fidan's statement should be interpreted from the perspective of solidarity, not war or aggression," she told TNA.
She noted that defence industry cooperation was among the clearest areas in which Ankara could assist Riyadh, particularly through drone technology.
Turkey and Saudi Arabia already have an agreement involving the Bayraktar Akinci combat drone, with Turkish defence company Baykar and Saudi military industries pursuing local production and technology transfer.
Ozcan said the nature of Houthi warfare meant Saudi Arabia required more than additional advanced air defence systems such as the Patriot and THAAD.
Riyadh also needed additional defensive layers, she said, particularly cheaper systems capable of countering large-scale drone attacks.
Such cooperation could offer the clearest indication yet of how the Mecca agreement will move from a political commitment to a functioning defence alliance, as Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan seek to define how collective defence will work in practice.

articles.title: Air defense downs 172 of 205 Russian targets, hits at 13 locations – Air Force

articles.title: European Diplomats Defy Russian Warning and Stay in Kyiv
articles.body:
The German, Italian, Spanish and Swedish embassies in Ukraine said on social media that they would remain in Kyiv despite warnings issued by the Russian Foreign Ministry against foreign diplomats.
The four diplomatic missions said they and other heads of diplomatic missions in Kyiv had taken note of the Russian MFA’s threat toward diplomats and foreign citizens in Ukraine.
“Russia is bound by the Vienna Convention and international humanitarian law. We stay in Kyiv,” the embassies said in their social media posts.
EU Ambassador to Ukraine Katarína Mathernová said all European Union member state embassies would continue operating in Kyiv despite the Russian threats. The Polish and Estonian foreign ministries issued the same message.
The European Commission also responded to the Russian warnings, saying the EU would continue supporting Ukraine and increase pressure on the aggressor country.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on September 30 that debris had been discovered on the grounds of an embassy belonging to one of the Western countries in the city’s Shevchenkivskyi district following Russian strikes on Kyiv.
Russia has also struck Kyiv’s Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River, with the attack taking place as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in the Ukrainian capital on an unannounced visit to demonstrate Germany’s support for Ukraine.
A Russian drone hit the key crossing, marking the fourth straight day of Russian attacks on bridges used by tens of thousands of people traveling between the two banks of the city. Video showed vehicles crossing the bridge when the drone struck the roadway and exploded, while Klitschko said two people were injured.
The attack occurred shortly after Merz reached Kyiv, as Ukraine enters one of its most precarious periods since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
Germany has become Ukraine’s largest provider of military aid since Merz took office in May 2025, overtaking the United States as American support has declined.
Kyiv has faced almost continuous Russian attacks involving new jet-powered drones in recent weeks, with the intensifying campaign increasingly disrupting daily life and threatening the city’s power supply this winter.
During his visit, Merz announced that Germany would finance joint production of drones intended to intercept Russia’s jet-powered drones, saying recent technical advances were allowing production to move faster.
“This will quickly and tangibly strengthen Ukraine’s air defence,” Merz said. “And this strengthening is urgently needed.”
Air-raid sirens sounded repeatedly while Merz was in Kyiv, including during a visit with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to the badly damaged National Academy of Sciences building. A Russian drone attack on the building killed two people the previous week.
Zelenskyy told Merz that residents of Kyiv were enduring “terrible nights and days” because of the continuing attacks and called Russia’s adversaries “absolute barbarians”.
Merz said the destruction he saw demonstrated the futility of the war and stressed the need for continued support for Ukraine.
“We can see the entire pointlessness of this war at this place,” Merz said, adding that Ukraine “needs all our support in the coming weeks”. He also warned, “If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us.”
Russian forces had previously damaged Kyiv’s Northern Bridge and repeatedly attacked the Southern Bridge. Although both crossings remain standing, the repeated strikes and possibility of further attacks have led city authorities to restrict or suspend traffic on five of Kyiv’s six road bridges over the Dnipro, resulting in temporary closures and major traffic jams.
Severe damage to the bridges could produce a logistical crisis for Kyiv, a city of 3 million people whose Dnipro crossings were last destroyed on a large scale when Nazi German forces withdrew in 1943. More than one-third of Kyiv’s residents live on the left bank, while much of the city’s employment and infrastructure is located on the right bank.
The bridge strikes are part of a wider Russian campaign targeting civilian and industrial infrastructure across Ukraine. Recent attacks have hit logistics centers, railway lines, data centers, medical storage facilities and steel plants, while Russia has also maintained a sustained assault on Ukraine’s energy system that is expected to intensify during the winter.
“He [Putin] is counting on constant escalation. He wants this very much,” Zelenskyy said at a press conference with Merz. “This is an answer to everyone – to those who believe that all you have to do is simply ask Putin and he will end the war for real. It won’t happen, simply.”
Russia’s Foreign Ministry warned foreign nationals and diplomatic personnel on Saturday against staying in or traveling to Ukraine, saying those who ignored the warning would bear responsibility for any consequences.
A number of foreign ambassadors, including Germany’s, responded on social media that they intended to remain in Kyiv.
“The EU delegation is staying,” Mathernová wrote on X on Sunday. “Threatening us will not stop Europe’s support for Ukraine. It only reminds us why that support matters.”
Some pro-war commentators in Moscow reacted positively to the continuation of Russian strikes after Merz arrived. Prominent pro-war commentator Sergei Markov wrote that Russia had previously paused attacks on Kyiv during visits by European politicians but no longer did so.
The visit was Merz’s second to Ukraine since becoming chancellor. He has been one of Kyiv’s most vocal European supporters and has repeatedly warned about Russia’s hybrid campaign against other countries.
Germany formally accused Moscow last month of being behind a suspected plot targeting Leipzig/Halle airport, a major logistics hub for Western military aid to Ukraine.
At home, however, Merz is facing increasing opposition to his support for Ukraine as his approval ratings decline. Germany’s far left and far right have questioned continued assistance to Kyiv and called for Berlin to reduce its aid.
The pressure has increased as the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has made major electoral gains.
AfD co-leader Alice Weidel criticized Merz in a social media post over his visit and additional financial support for Ukraine, while arguing that Germany was facing a severe energy crisis and lacked money for pension and health insurance funds.
“Merz is travelling to Ukraine on Germany’s national holiday and promising further billions in German taxpayer money that is missing from the pension and health insurance funds, while Germany is mired in its worst energy crisis,” Weidel wrote.

articles.title: Ukraine and Germany Sign 15 Deals Worth €8.5B for Air Defense, Radars, and Interceptors
articles.body:

Ukraine and Germany Sign 15 Deals Worth €8.5B for Air Defense, Radars, and Interceptors
Ukraine and Germany have reached 15 agreements worth more than €8.5 billion covering air defense, drone interceptors, missiles, radars, artillery, unmanned ground systems, and energy support, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said following talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Zelenskyy in a Telegram post on October 4, the 15 agreements cover drone interceptors, small missiles, radars, unmanned ground systems, artillery, air defense, Patriot missile production in Germany, and support for Ukraine’s energy sector.
“As of today, we have 15 agreements and documents with the German side, and most of them concern security cooperation, production, relevant procurement, our orders for German industry, and joint projects in Ukraine. The total value of our agreements today is more than €8.5 billion,” Zelenskyy said.
The agreements include cooperation on drone interceptors, small anti-drone missiles, radars, artillery, unmanned ground vehicles, and additional air defense capabilities. Kyiv and Berlin will also work to increase production in Germany of missiles used by Patriot air defense systems, according to the Presidential Office.
Ukraine has also placed a major order with German defense manufacturer Diehl Defence for IRIS-T air defense systems. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry signed three memoranda with Diehl covering IRIS-T systems and missiles as well as ammunition. Separate agreements were reached with Hensoldt on radar procurement and Quantum Systems on testing and supplying interceptor drones.
Zelenskyy also reported positive testing of the German-Ukrainian Spear interceptor. Work is continuing on another weapon, the Nika small missile, designed specifically to counter Russia’s jet-powered Shahed-type drones and which has yet to undergo testing.
Germany separately announced a new support package for Ukraine worth more than €1.3 billion, which includes defense assistance and funding for Ukraine’s energy sector ahead of winter. Part of the funding will go toward producing new interceptors designed to engage jet-powered Russian attack drones.
“It includes weapons that will help us now, as well as support for our energy sector, which is very important, ahead of winter—an important energy package. This comprehensive package from Germany also includes funding for the production of new interceptors specifically against jet-powered ‘shaheds,’” Zelenskyy said.
Germany is also involved in FREYJA, a European anti-ballistic missile defense project led by Ukrainian company Fire Point, with Germany’s Hensoldt supplying radar technology. The system is expected to integrate FP-7.x interceptors, launchers, and TRML-4D radars.
The agreements also cover energy cooperation, including equipment for Ukraine’s power grid and projects with Siemens Energy involving gas turbines, infrastructure protection, and power generation.
The focus on faster interceptors comes as Russia increasingly uses jet-powered Shahed-type drones, which fly significantly faster than conventional propeller-driven variants and reduce the time available for interception. Zelenskyy said Russia launched around 900 jet-powered Shaheds in the week before Merz’s visit.

articles.title: Meet Kyiv’s New Jet-Drone Killer—12+ Sky Sentinel Turrets Are Already on the Hunt
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Meet Kyiv’s New Jet-Drone Killer—12+ Sky Sentinel Turrets Are Already on the Hunt
Russia’s attempt to outrun Ukraine’s air defenses with faster jet-powered attack drones is now facing a different kind of threat over Kyiv—an AI-guided gun system that does not need to chase its target to shoot it down.
More than 12 automated .50-caliber turrets deployed across Kyiv to counter Russia’s jet-powered attack drones are Ukrainian-made Sky Sentinel systems, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed in an exclusive comment to UNITED24 Media.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“These are Sky Sentinel systems. They are already on combat duty and are being used to counter Russian attack drones,” Ihnat told UNITED24 Media. “The systems have already demonstrated results in combat. There are confirmed cases of them successfully engaging and shooting down jet-powered UAVs,” he added.
Ihnat’s confirmation comes after he revealed earlier on October 5 that the automated turrets had already intercepted Russia’s Geran-5 jet-powered drone.
“There have already been shootdowns of even jet-powered UAVs, even the Geran-5, using those same turrets,” Ihnat said during Ukraine’s national telethon.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy first revealed the deployment a day earlier, saying that more than 12 automated “fifties” had already been installed in Kyiv, with another eight set to be deployed across the Kyiv region.
Sky Sentinel is a Ukrainian-developed automated anti-drone turret that uses machine vision and artificial intelligence to detect, track, and engage aerial targets.
The system combines a heavy machine gun with an automated fire-control module. Once a target is acquired, its optics track the drone while onboard software calculates its speed, trajectory, distance, and the lead required for an interception.
Unlike an interceptor drone, Sky Sentinel does not need to chase its target. It calculates where the UAV will be and fires toward that point, allowing it to engage fast-moving aircraft within its firing envelope.
Previously published specifications indicate that Sky Sentinel can engage aerial targets traveling at speeds of up to around 800 kilometers per hour, placing Russia’s jet-powered attack drones within its theoretical capability.
The Geran-5, now increasingly used by Russian forces, flies substantially faster than conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones. Its vulnerability to Sky Sentinel, however, depends on altitude and range.
At higher altitudes, a jet-powered drone may remain beyond the reach of heavy machine-gun fire. But as it descends toward a target or operates at lower altitude, it can enter the turret’s engagement zone.
At that point, the key factor is no longer whether a weapon can catch the drone, but whether it can track it and calculate a firing solution quickly enough. Sky Sentinel’s machine vision continuously follows the target while its software determines the interception point in real time.
The system had already seen combat before its deployment around Kyiv.
UNITED24 raised approximately $3.3 million for 22 Sky Sentinel systems. In August, five were delivered to Ukraine’s 636th Separate Anti-Aircraft Machine Gun Battalion operating in the Sumy region to strengthen defenses against Russian attack drones.
The system had already demonstrated combat effectiveness during earlier deployments, with a Sky Sentinel prototype reportedly destroying multiple Russian Shahed-type drones.
Sky Sentinel is designed as a relatively inexpensive final layer of air defense around critical infrastructure, bridges, military positions, and other high-value sites.

articles.title: Ukraine, Germany Sign €8.5B in Defense Deals, Merz Pledges More Air Defense Support
articles.body:
Kyiv and Berlin have agreed on joint weapons production, signing 15 contracts worth more than €8.5 billion ($9.5 billion), with a primary focus on air defense missiles and advanced drones.
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the agreements following a meeting with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Sunday, Oct. 4.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The deals cover a range of defense priorities, including strengthening Ukraine’s artillery capabilities, protecting energy infrastructure, and countering Russian drones.
What the new agreements entail
Key areas of cooperation include the development of small missiles, radars, and ground-based robotic systems. The package also includes the FREYJA project and an expansion of German production capacity for ammunition for the Patriot air defense system.
Zelensky said the Ukrainian defense orders would provide work for German companies while significantly strengthening the defense industries of both countries.
“Germany is helping us during this war, and now Ukraine is placing defense and other orders that will create opportunities for German companies. This will make a significant contribution to Germany’s economy.”
The agreements were announced during Merz’s unannounced visit to Kyiv, which came as Russia intensified attacks on Ukraine’s critical infrastructure, Der Spiegel reported.
Merz arrived by special train alongside German Minister for Economic Affairs Katharina Reiche and a 10-member delegation of business and defense-industry executives.
Russia Repeatedly Tests Romanian Air Defense
Speaking at Kyiv’s central railway station, Merz stressed that European security was directly tied to Ukraine’s ability to defend itself against Russia.
“If Russia is not stopped, its war machine will sooner or later turn against us,” he said.
Merz also reaffirmed Berlin’s commitment to supporting Ukraine, saying Kyiv could “continue to count on our help” as Russian attacks intensify ahead of the heating season.
According to German government officials cited by Der Spiegel, Merz plans to guarantee the rapid delivery of 1,000 newly developed interceptor systems designed to destroy jet-powered Shahed drones.
The visit came days after Merz described Ukraine’s air defense as its “weakest point” and said Germany was working with European partners to assemble additional military support ahead of the European Council summit in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
Merz has repeatedly argued that continued military support for Ukraine is essential to European security.
In a recent speech in Münster, he warned that a peace dictated by Russia would destabilize Europe, trigger new refugee flows, and leave the continent vulnerable to further Russian pressure.
His visit also came amid growing political tensions at home. Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), which opposes arms deliveries to Ukraine and calls for the resumption of Russian gas imports, has made significant electoral gains, including strong results in recent state elections.

articles.title: Three Russian Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine Killed in Tu-95 Crash
articles.body:
Three Russian officers linked by a Ukrainian database to the organization of missile strikes on Ukraine were among eight officers killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia’s Amur Region on Sept. 29, independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported.
The bomber crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo during a training flight from the Ukrainka airbase. Initial reports said six crew members were killed.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Mediazona later verified the identities of all eight people aboard and found that all had served in Russia’s strategic aviation forces. Six were members of the Tu-95MS’ regular crew, while two others may have been aboard as inspectors or passengers.
Three of the dead – Maj. Andrei Lobanov, Maj. Andrei Gerasimov and Lt. Col. Fyodor Pavlyukov – are listed by Ukraine’s “Book of Executioners of the Ukrainian People” project as participants in or organizers of Russian missile strikes on Ukrainian territory.
The project, launched after Russia’s full-scale invasion, maintains a database of Russian military personnel and other individuals it says are involved in crimes against Ukraine.
The information is collected and documented using publicly available data as well as information from Ukrainian law enforcement and intelligence agencies.
Mediazona said the three officers’ inclusion in the database links them specifically to Russia’s strategic aviation operations against Ukraine.
India Pushing for Bigger Role in Russia-Ukraine Talks
Most of the eight officers killed in the crash had previously served at the Engels airbase in Russia’s Saratov Region before being transferred to the Ukrainka base in Amur Region, Mediazona reported.
The Tu-95MS is one of Russia’s main strategic bombers used to launch long-range cruise missiles against targets across Ukraine.
The bombers were also among the key targets in the clandestine Ukrainian operation dubbed “Operation Spiderweb” in June 2025, in which dozens of Tu-95s on tarmacs were hit after Ukraine deployed drones that had been smuggled near airfields disguised as modular houses.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet Drones Kill 1, Injure 8 in Kharkiv Amid 205-Drone Overnight Barrage
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kharkiv late on Oct. 4 with three “Banderol” jet-powered drones, killing one person and injuring eight, including one critically, Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported.
The drones struck near residential buildings in the city’s Industrialnyi district, shattering windows in five buildings and damaging their roofs, Terekhov said.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Unfortunately, there is one fatality. In addition, eight people were injured, one of whom is in critical condition,” he said.
Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, said one of the strikes hit a high-rise building.
Ukraine’s State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported fires at an administrative building and an industrial facility. Several vehicles were also damaged.
According to Novosti.LIVE, the man killed in the attack was traveling in a car with a woman and a dog when the strike occurred. The woman survived but was taken to intensive care, while the dog was rescued from the vehicle and taken to an animal care center.
The Kharkiv strike came amid a large-scale Russian drone attack on Ukraine.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russia launched 205 strike unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) against Ukraine from 6 p.m. on Oct. 4, including 49 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, as well as Gerbera, Banderol/Dan-T and Parodiya decoy drones.
Ukrainian forces countered the attack using aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, electronic warfare and unmanned systems, as well as mobile fire groups.
Zelensky Vows Proportional Retaliation for Russian Bridge Strikes
As of 8 a.m. on Oct. 5, Ukrainian air defenses had shot down or suppressed 172 Russian drones, the Air Force reported.
“Impacts from enemy aerial assets were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at three other locations,” the report said.
The attack included the jet-powered Banderol drones that struck Kharkiv, where three drones hit near residential buildings in the Industrialnyi district, killing one person and injuring eight, according to Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov.
On the afternoon of Oct. 2, Russian forces attacked two districts of Kharkiv with guided aerial bombs. One of the bombs struck a private home, killing two people and injuring 42 others, including three children.
The attack damaged 23 private houses, an educational institution, office buildings, seven vehicles and power lines. Across the Kharkiv region, Russian strikes that day killed five people and injured 49, according to local authorities.
The latest air assault also comes amid warnings that Russia could intensify its attacks on major Ukrainian cities as winter approaches.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has previously warned that Russia could seek to isolate Kyiv, Kharkiv and Odesa from the rest of Ukraine through intensified attacks. He has also said Lviv, a key logistics hub near the Polish border, could become a target.
Zelensky said he had information that Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the removal of restrictions on conducting air strikes.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials cited by the Financial Times said Moscow was seeking to increase pressure on Kyiv and force it to accept Russian demands, including the ceding of territory in the Donbas, by early 2027.

articles.title: U.S. Withdraws All B-1B Strategic Bombers from RAF Fairford
articles.body:
The United States has withdrawn all B-1B strategic bombers deployed at the British RAF Fairford airfield.
The Pentagon and U.S. European Command (EUCOM) confirmed to Air & Space Forces Magazine the redeployment of the aircraft to their permanent bases in the United States.
On October 4, 12 B-1B Lancer bombers previously stationed in the United Kingdom left the air base throughout the day.
“We can acknowledge now that all U.S. bombers that were deployed to RAF Fairford have re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” the U.S. defense agency said in a statement to TWZ.
The Pentagon emphasized that the redeployment does not affect U.S. strategic bombers’ ability to conduct combat missions. B-1Bs, B-2s, and B-52s can carry out long-range combat missions directly from the continental United States.
The redeployment took place amid a counterterrorism investigation surrounding the airfield.
On September 27, British law enforcement received reports of three suspicious vehicles traveling toward RAF Fairford. Police detained five men aged between 23 and 25 near Welford. Police later released all five detainees on bail with restrictions, but they remain subjects of the investigation.
Britain’s Counter Terrorism Policing said they are investigating several possible lines of inquiry, including the possibility that the detainees may have been acting on behalf of a foreign state.
On September 30, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were indications of Iranian involvement in an alleged plot to carry out a terrorist attack near RAF Fairford.
On October 1, police detained another man in London as part of the investigation. The British-Iranian national was suspected of preparing a terrorist attack. On October 3, he was released on bail, while the investigation remains ongoing.
However, as of now, British law enforcement has not publicly presented evidence conclusively establishing Iran’s involvement in the incident.
RAF Fairford plays an important role in U.S. strategic bomber operations in the Middle East. At the beginning of hostilities with Iran, the British government officially allowed the United States to use RAF Fairford for designated operations against Iranian missile forces.
The UK government said that U.S. operations from British bases were aimed at destroying Iranian missiles that posed a threat to allies and shipping. The first U.S. bomber deployed as part of this mission arrived at RAF Fairford in March 2026.
On July 22, the U.S. Air Force used B-1B Lancer to strike Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps facilities in Iran. The aircraft performed combat missions using the British RAF Fairford airfield.
On March 2, U.S. B-1Bs were used to strike ballistic missile production and storage facilities in Iran.
The scale of the U.S. deployment at RAF Fairford was so significant that organizers canceled the Royal International Air Tattoo 2026 air show in May.

Ukraine’s Robotic Turrets Record First Shootdowns of Russia’s Jet-Powered Geran-5 Drones
Ukraine has recorded its first confirmed interceptions of Russian jet-powered drones using automated gun turrets equipped with artificial intelligence and machine-vision systems, according to Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on October 5 that Ukraine’s robotic turret systems have already downed jet-powered UAVs, including Russia’s Geran-5. “There have already been shootdowns of even jet-powered UAVs, even the Geran-5, using those same turrets,” Ihnat said during Ukraine’s national telethon.
He said the systems rely on machine vision and artificial intelligence to automate targeting and reduce the role of human error during interception.
“The use of innovative technologies—artificial intelligence—eliminated human error. Machine vision is used specifically in the interception. Artificial intelligence makes it possible to engage even jet-powered UAVs,” Ihnat said.
The turrets have a relatively limited engagement range because their primary weapon remains a machine gun, according to Ihnat.
Russia has increasingly combined conventional Shahed-type attack drones with faster jet-powered UAVs during strikes against Ukraine. Ihnat said Russian forces launched around 50 jet-powered drones per night during each of the previous two nights.
According to figures cited by Ihnat, Ukrainian forces currently intercept approximately 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed-type drones. The estimated interception rate for jet-powered UAVs is lower, at around 50% to 70%.
The automated turrets are being deployed at selected locations, including around bridges, as Ukraine expands a layered defense network intended to protect infrastructure from low-flying attack drones.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on October 4 that more than 12 such turrets had already been deployed in Kyiv, with another eight planned for the surrounding Kyiv region.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine needs a combination of different air-defense systems as Russia adjusts its strike tactics and increasingly introduces faster drones and ballistic missiles alongside conventional Shahed-type UAVs.

articles.title: Ukraine’s answer to Russia’s jet-powered Shaheds: a small new missile named Nika, heading into testing
articles.body:
Ukraine has developed a new missile to knock down Russia's fast, jet-powered Shahed drones, the ones its air defenses catch far less often than older models, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on 4 October, Suspilne reported. The weapon, called Nika, has not yet been tested. He announced it during a visit to Kyiv by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Russia's plants turn out an estimated 3,000 jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones a month, Ukraine's military intelligence estimates, and the jets fly fast enough to outrun the cheap interceptors built for slower, propeller-driven Shaheds. Ukraine plans about 400 units of just one of five interceptor models it is testing by the end of October, as it scrambles to close the gap before winter.
A new missile heads into testing
Both the Ukrainian and German sides have reacted positively to the missile, Zelenskyy said, though he stayed cautious on the result: for now, he said, it only "could be positive." In the same remarks, he announced a successful test of a separate system, the German-Ukrainian interceptor Spys.
Russia adds new weapon to its jet-powered drones, even more dangerous: 40-kilogram charge made to sever high-voltage pylons and iron bridges
Ukraine shoots down 85-92% of propeller-driven Shaheds, Zelenskyy said. Against the jet-powered variants, interception falls to roughly 50-60%, he noted at the press conference with Merz. F-16 fighter jets help close the gap, he said.
From interceptor drones to a new missile
Over the past month, Ukraine tested a new generation of drone interceptors built for the jet-Shahed threat. On 15 September, one struck a Shahed in trials, though Zelenskyy said developers still needed to refine its control system. On 19 September, he said the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) had created its own interceptor drone and used it to down a jet Shahed in combat. Nika adds a purpose-built missile to that mix.

articles.title: As Air Force Goes Big on Autonomy, Are Cargo Drones Next?
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force’s plans to field 1,000 semi-autonomous fighter and intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance drones within just a few years made headlines at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference last month.
But beyond the service’s signature Collaborative Combat Aircraft and Massed Modular Aircraft programs, a half-dozen or so firms are pitching another kind of autonomous aircraft: cargo drones to solve some of the thorniest logistics problems.
Textron Aviation and Merlin Labs unveiled a cockpit-less Cessna equipped with Merlin’s autonomy software and a nose hatch opening to a cavernous cargo bay.
“By pairing a proven aircraft platform with autonomy technology, we’re exploring new approaches to contested logistics operations while also examining how autonomy may enable more efficient cargo aircraft designs that increase usable volume, improve cargo accessibility and support mission sustainment requirements,” Bob Gibbs, Textron’s vice president for defense and special mission sales, said of the company’s Cessna SkyuCourier UX concept.
Reliable Robotics is offering its own modified Cessna 208B Caravan. Its aircraft flew in multiple Agile Flag exercises in 2024, installing actuators, sensors, and other gear in the cockpit and using a human pilot to command high-level direction from a ground station. Reliable announced a $17.4 million deal with the Air Force in 2025 to provide an aircraft for a yearlong test.
In a May blog post, Reliable’s certification flight test lead Chris Baughman wrote that the firm is targeting the start of fiscal 2027 to begin the test, which will focus on the Indo-Pacific region. The company is also seeking FAA certification for its autonomy software to operate in U.S. airspace, targeting 2028 for that certification.
Joby Aviation, which previously acquired autonomy startup Xwing, is also flying a modified Cessna Caravan, racking up 40 hours and 7,000 miles during last summer’s Resolute Force Pacific. Joby did not exhibit at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber, but sought to capitalize on the timing by announcing soon after that it completed 3,199 miles of autonomous flight across the U.S. this summer, including stops at Shaw Air Force Base, S.C., and near Washington D.C. At a press event Sept. 24, Joby’s Head of Defense Policy John Barranco told Air & Space Forces Magazine that the aircraft carried a safety pilot for those flights in case human intervention was needed, but the autonomy software never required a pilot intervention.
Coming at the same time that other vendors are developing autonomous fighters and reconnaissance aircraft with clean-sheet designs, the modified Cessnas might seem like minimalist efforts. But aviation firms see a gap they can fill in the Air Force’s logistics enterprise, a small airlifter that can do jobs that USAF’s workhorse C-130 cannot do as efficiently. The Hercules can haul 40,000 pounds of cargo, and the Air Force has only about 270. A Cessna could be ideal for shorter hops and smaller loads at a fraction of the cost.
“It’s a really robust, reliable existing cargo airframe that’s in the world, and there are many of them, and so we can retrofit a lot of those for the customers,” Barranco said.
USAF officials have spent years talking about Agile Combat Employment—the concept of dispersing small teams of Airmen and aircraft from large bases to operate from remote or austere locations and move quickly to counter adversary long-range missile attacks. But the ACE logistics is complex, especially in the vast and watery Indo-Pacific region.
Having small, unmanned aircraft to island-hop and resupply those forces so they can generate airpower—without taxing manned airlifters—could be a solution.
“Historically it’s about a logistics train where you’re trying to move a really big airframe and move a lot of stuff, and that takes time, and it takes Airmen, and it takes support, and that’s a really important mission,” said Barranco. “Sometimes you need to move a lot less really, really quickly, without standing up a mission, without 24 hours’ notice, without pulling folks together.”
Other concepts are also emerging to chase this possible market. DZYNE Technologies put its autonomous cargo drone, called Grasshopper, on display.
DZYNE and the Air Force Research Laboratory unveiled Grasshopper last May, as a self-guided glider capable of carrying up to 500 pounds after being dropped out the back of a C-130; from there, it could glide tens of miles to resupply troops in “high-risk environments.”
DZYNE has since offered a “Long-Range” powered variant with a turbine engine that can fly “10 times” further than Grasshopper and launched from “standoff” distances.
U.S. Special Operations Command has tested the concept, using the Long-Range Grasshopper in Exercise Trojan Footprint 26 in Romania and North Macedonia, where the drones were launched from a Romanian Air Force C-27J.
But the firms pursuing this niche want more than a narrow special ops use case, focusing on any mission where moving cargo quickly without risking crews could be attractive.
Grid Aero won $6 million in seed funding from the Air Force’s innovation arm, AFWERX, last August. CEO Arthur Dubois compared his company’s drone to a “flying pickup” truck at the time, saying it would be able to carry somewhere between 1,000 and 8,000 pounds from “Guam to Japan,” for example, a trek of some 1,500 miles.
Grid Aero’s Lifter Lite hasn’t made its first flight yet, but the firm was among seven selected in September to compete for the Air Force’s Massed Modular Aircraft program. It’s unclear if Lifter Lite or some other design is what the company envisions as its entry.
Dubois said last year that the idea for Lifter Lite sprang from asking military and commercial air cargo stakeholders about their pain points. For the military, that’s executing logistics in areas where U.S. assets could be attacked.
Lt. Gen. Kenyon K. Bell, deputy chief of staff for logistics, engineering, and force protection, noted as much during the conference: “The era of uncontested logistics is over,” Bell declared. “We will have to continue to fight our way in from a logistics standpoint and be able to sustain and regenerate ourselves while we’re in contact. … That is a concept that we certainly need to think through.”
Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach endorsed the concept of autonomous cargo drones during a media roundtable at the conference, albeit without completely committing to it.
“We believe that there’s some value in that as well,” he said in response to a question. “It certainly could be valuable in the Pacific, with the ranges that we’re talking about. And so we’re looking at several different options and evaluating them, but I would say, no program of record just yet, but certainly taking a look at some demonstrators and the like to see what’s available to us.”
Congress and Pentagon officials are also tuning in. When Undersecretary of Defense for Research and Engineering Emil Michael culled the department’s list of “critical technology areas” from 14 to just six last November, “contested logistics technology” survived the cut.
The House Armed Services Committee directed the the Air Force to present a briefing on the topic in their version of the 2027 defense policy bill. Lawmakers also expect a proposed timeline for developing an acquisition strategy that could include rapid prototyping. They also want a strategy for the use of “low-cost and attritable Group 4 and 5 unmanned aircraft systems in contested logistics operations.”
Staff Writers Matthew Cox and Stephen Losey contributed reporting.

articles.title: Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
articles.body:
Officers involved in strikes on Ukraine were among eight killed in Tu-95MS crash in Russia
Eight military personnel were killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast on 29 September. At least three of them were officers involved in combat missions or their preparation, according to the Book of Executioners, a Ukrainian project documenting Russian war criminals and people who betrayed Ukraine.
Source: Russian media outlets Mediazona and The Insider
Details: Russian media outlets reported that the names of those killed had been posted in the Selskiye Novosti (Rural News) social media group for Seryshevo, a settlement near the Ukrainka strategic air base. OSINT analyst duke garland was the first to flag the post.
A photo featuring the portraits of the eight men killed was also released by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast. He said the local authorities would ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state awards.
Mediazona verified the list and confirmed that all eight served in Russia's strategic aviation.
According to the media outlets, those killed are:
- Andrei Lobanov, 40
- Vladislav Moskovskikh, 31
- Artur Yenokian, 30
- Mikhail Kotyshev, 23
- Sergei, 47, whose surname is reported as Monsevich by Mediazona and Moisevich by The Insider
- Vladimir Kelip, 55
- Fedor Pavlyukov, 43
- Andrei Gerasimov, 36.
The OSINT analyst believes the portraits in the announcement follow the standard order in which Tu-95MS crew members are listed. On that basis, Lobanov was the crew commander, Moskovskikh the co-pilot, Yenokian the navigator, Kotyshev the navigator-operator (responsible for operating the bomber's mission systems), Monsevich the flight engineer, and Kelip the radio operator. Pavlyukov and Gerasimov were likely passengers or inspectors.
Mediazona says the quality of the photograph makes it difficult to establish the military ranks of all those killed with certainty.
The Insider checked the names against the Ukrainian Book of Executioners database and found Lobanov, Pavlyukov and Gerasimov in its records. Details about them had been added before the plane crashed.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as the deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron of the 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at the Ukrainka airfield. According to the project, he directly commanded the unit and personally participated in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as the regiment's deputy commander for flight training. He commanded a Tu-95MS squadron from August 2021 to April 2024. According to the project, he was responsible for preparing flight personnel for combat missions and directly led the unit.
Furthermore, in March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence included Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots who, according to its data, were being prepared to participate in the war against Ukraine.
Andrei Gerasimov is listed in the Book of Executioners as a major and commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. According to the database, he commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions. However, Mediazona's casualty list gives his rank as lieutenant colonel.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatolii Shtefan also reported that at least three of those killed were involved in organising and executing missile strikes on Ukraine. Shtefan did not specify whom exactly he was referring to.
According to Port Amur, cited by The Insider, there were nine military personnel on board. The bodies of two of the crew members were not found immediately. The Russian Ministry of Defence initially reported six dead and one taken to hospital.
Background:
- On 29 September, the Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky district in Amur Oblast.
- The Russian Defence Ministry claimed that the bomber was conducting a training flight without ammunition when it crashed in an unpopulated area. Regional authorities said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential buildings, and no one on the ground was injured.
- The Russian Defence Ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to the site to establish what caused the crash. Kommersant reported that investigators had tentatively attributed it to a technical malfunction. The Insider notes, however, that no conclusions about the cause of the crash have been publicly confirmed.
- According to Mediazona, most of those killed had served at the Engels strategic bomber airbase in Saratov Oblast before moving to the Ukrainka airbase. According to the outlet, Russia began pulling its strategic bombers out of Engels after Ukraine launched its first drone attacks on the airfield.
- After the Security Service of Ukraine carried out Operation Spider's Web, the Ukrainka airbase in Russia's Far East became one of the main bases for its strategic aviation. According to The Insider, a Tu-95MS combat mission from the base, involving stopovers at Engels or Olenya airfield, missile launches and the return flight, can cover more than 12,000 km and last around 23 hours. The outlet notes that flights of this length accelerate wear on the aircraft and their engines, shortening their service life.
