articles.title: Ukraine has largely exhausted its air defense capabilities — military analyst
articles.body:
MOSCOW, October 5. /TASS/. The capabilities of Ukraine’s air defense forces have largely been exhausted, and the Ukrainian armed forces are unable to repel strikes by the Russian Armed Forces, military analyst Igor Korotchenko, editor-in-chief of the National Defense magazine, told TASS.
"To a large extent, the capabilities of Ukraine’s existing air defense forces have been exhausted. But this does not mean that there is no air defense at all. Our capabilities are now much more effective due to the use of new weapons systems, so Ukraine’s existing air defense forces cannot fully counter our strikes, and they are unable to intercept ballistic missiles at all, since they do not yet have the appropriate capabilities," said the military analyst.
He noted that Russia has modernized its Geran family of drones. The new versions feature higher speed and enable high-precision strikes in the final stage of the flight path. According to the military analyst, the enemy currently has no means of intercepting them in the airspace.

articles.title: Geran-5 Gets Kh-101-Like Guidance as Russia Pushes Its Jet Drones Toward Full Autonomy
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Geran-5 Gets Kh-101-Like Guidance as Russia Pushes Its Jet Drones Toward Full Autonomy
Russia has equipped its newer jet-powered Geran drones with an electro-optical navigation system that lets them autonomously fly toward targets by comparing camera imagery with a stored visual map of the route, bringing their guidance concept closer to that used on some Kh-101 cruise missiles, Defense Express reported on October 5.
Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence recently released new details on the Geran-5 K5 and a newer Geran-4 variant that Russian forces began using this fall. Both reportedly carry a system known as Susannin, designed to reduce the drone’s dependence on an external control signal during the flight.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Rather than relying on an operator continuously steering the aircraft through a communications network, Susannin uses onboard imagery. The drone compares what its camera sees below with reference images loaded into the system and uses those visual matches to determine where it is and continue along its programmed route.
In practical terms, the aircraft can navigate by “looking” at the terrain. Defense Express notes that this means mesh modems and airborne mesh repeaters are not necessarily required for the drone to reach its intended target, since the navigation process can continue autonomously without a constant outside command link.
A similar principle has already appeared in more sophisticated Russian long-range weapons. One version of the air-launched Kh-101 cruise missile, known as Izdeliye 504AP, used an optical navigation system called Otblesk-U during Russian missile strikes against Ukraine between 2022 and 2025.
That comparison is important because it shows Russia gradually transferring technologies associated with expensive cruise missiles into cheaper unmanned strike systems. The goal appears to be making jet-powered Geran drones increasingly independent, accurate, and less reliant on vulnerable communications links during their approach to a target.
The change also comes as Ukraine becomes more effective at intercepting Russia’s newer jet-powered UAVs. Defense Express estimates that Ukrainian forces are already destroying roughly 50% to 60% of them, meaning that only around four or five out of every 10 launched may currently reach their targets.
Improving autonomous navigation could therefore be part of Russia’s effort to increase the number of drones that survive long enough to complete their missions, particularly as Ukraine expands dedicated interceptor-drone units and other counter-UAV defenses.
The Geran-5 and newer Geran-4 are part of a broader Russian effort to move beyond the original propeller-driven Shahed concept. Their jet propulsion already gives them significantly greater speed, while systems such as Susannin add another layer of sophistication by allowing the aircraft to navigate visually without depending on continuous external guidance.
The result is a weapon that increasingly sits somewhere between a conventional one-way strike drone and a small cruise missile: cheaper and simpler than weapons such as the Kh-101, but borrowing some of the same ideas in navigation and terminal autonomy.
Earlier, a Geran-type drone equipped with a turbojet engine entered Moldovan airspace and later crashed and exploded near a road in the Orhei district on the evening of September 30.

articles.title: German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
articles.body:
German intelligence head warns of threat of violent conflict with Russia
Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has stated that he sees the danger of a violent conflict with Russia, noting that the confrontation between the countries has acquired a "new, dangerous quality".
Source: European Pravda, citing Jäger's remarks during a hearing in the Bundestag, quoted by Die Welt
Details: The German intelligence head warned that the war in Ukraine, marked by increasingly brutal Russian attacks, is entering a "new, very dangerous phase", while the threat of hybrid attacks against Germany remains real.
Jäger stated that the risk involves Germany being dragged into a conflict with Russia.
The intelligence head emphasised that Russia is visibly escalating the conflict in Ukraine and continues to step up pressure on Europe and Germany. The confrontation Germany is in with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous character. The country risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Russia.
As an example of this escalation, he cited the attempted attack on Leipzig Airport, responsibility for which Berlin attributed to Russia.
Jäger noted that no other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive and concrete threat to Germany. Germany did not seek this confrontation. Russia is imposing it on the country, seeing it as its main adversary because Germany does not tolerate Russia's revisionist, expansionist policy and its war of aggression against Ukraine.
According to Jäger, the Russian leadership seeks to "ensure for the future that no political decisions directed against Moscow are made in Berlin or other European capitals". The consequence of this is "increasingly aggressive actions by Russian intelligence services" against Germany and other states.
Jäger stated that Russia is waging a shadow war against Germany. This undeclared war cannot be characterised using traditional military or legal categories. Germany is not in a state of defence, yet they are still under attack – that is precisely what a shadow war is.
The intelligence head added that Russia sought to undermine Europe's political support for Ukraine and emphasised that they had to be prepared for intimidation attempts and further interference. He noted that nuclear threats would likely be voiced again.
However, according to Jäger, at this time the intelligence agency sees no signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory. Nevertheless, "Russian military actions on a limited scale" are possible, particularly in the Baltic states, specified the head of German intelligence.
Background:
- Chancellor of Germany Friedrich Merz declared that his country is "preparing for major hybrid attacks, including severe ones" and will respond to them "swiftly and very clearly".
- German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt planned a package of measures covering protection against drones and sabotage targeting critical infrastructure and cyberattacks, as well as the detection of spies and potential terrorists.

articles.title: Jetten: Ukraine needs more F-16 spare parts and ammunition; Netherlands to provide assistance
articles.body:
Ukraine requires additional maintenance resources, spare parts, and ammunition for its F-16 fighter jets, and the Netherlands will assist with this, stated Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten.
"President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and I discussed the latest developments in the war. Further strengthening Ukraine's air defense is literally a matter of life and death. To achieve this, Ukraine needs more maintenance, spare parts, and ammunition for its F-16 fleet. I assured him that the Netherlands would help Ukraine with this," Jetten wrote on X following his conversation with Zelenskyy.
For his part, Zelenskyy noted that the F-16s supplied by the Netherlands to Ukraine are responsible for shooting down a significant percentage of jet-powered "Shahed" drones, and that there are opportunities to support their operations with the necessary resources.
“We also discussed other ideas for protecting critical infrastructure and bolstering air defense. I am grateful for the readiness to help,” Zelesnkyy said on X following the talk.
He also informed Jetten about contacts with the U.S. team and potential trilateral meetings at the technical level between Ukraine, the USA, and Russia. “Realistic proposals that can bring peace closer are important. But Russia must take the negotiations seriously and not try to find more and more pretexts to drag the war out further,” Zelenskyy said.
The President of Ukraine thanked the Prime Minister and the Netherlands for their consistent and resolute support.
In his post, Jetten noted that Russian aggression against Ukraine continues to escalate.
"We saw this again this past weekend, particularly with the air strikes on Kyiv. Russia is deliberately targeting civilian sites and energy infrastructure, seeking to make Ukrainian cities uninhabitable and destroy the economy this winter. We cannot allow this to happen," the Dutch Prime Minister wrote.

articles.title: Northrop’s Talon Blue Collaborative Combat Aircraft Makes First Flight
articles.body:
Northrop Grumman’s Talon Blue YFQ-48A Collaborative Combat Aircraft took its first flight Oct. 3, heightening the competition for the Air Force’s future combat fleet.
Talon Blue is Northrop’s so-called “loyal wingman” drone, an autonomous aircraft designed to pair with crewed fighters. The Oct. 3 flight was an important milestone for the firm as it looks to break into the Air Force’s CCA program—thus far, the service has awarded production contracts to General Atomics and Anduril Industries, but more “increments” are expected in the coming years.
Northrop said the drone completed a fully autonomous flight, including taxi, takeoff, “in-flight maneuvers,” and landing from its Mojave, Calif., facilities.
Air Force leadership say they plans to field at least 500 CCAs by 2032. While the service has not selected Talon Blue for production yet, the company has been bullish that the service could be a customer in the future. The Air Force also gave Talon Blue an official Department of Defense Mission Design Series designation, YFQ-48A, last December, signaling that it sees the aircraft as a competitor for future CCAs.
“Our customers made it clear they need autonomous systems that can be fielded faster and more affordably without sacrificing mission effectiveness,” Craig Woolston, Northrop Grumman’s vice president and general manager for research and advanced design, said in a statement. “We listened. Talon Blue’s first flight is one step toward a new generation of autonomous capabilities. Every flight and lesson strengthens our broader autonomy work and sharpens what comes next.”
The company’s CCA is a unique offering. It was first unveiled last December to a small group of reporters, including Air & Space Forces Magazine, as a self-funded effort. The company’s Scaled Composites subsidiary, known for its history of innovative aircraft, built it, and the company has touted how quickly it developed the aircraft. The time between when the aircraft was conceived and when it had “weight on wheels” was roughly 15 months, company officials said. When Northrop announced the aircraft, it said it expected the aircraft to fly around fall 2026, a milestone the company has now met.
Talon Blue falls under the company’s broader Project Talon. The project also includes the Talon IQ, an autonomous testbed for using Scaled Composites Model 437 aircraft. Talon IQ uses Northrop’s Prism mission autonomy software. So far, the Air Force has pursued a “software sold separately” approach to CCAs, running separate competitions for the mission autonomy software and the aircraft themselves.
While General Atomics’ FQ-42 Vengeance and Anduril Industries’ Fury FQ-44 have been awarded production contracts from the Air Force and are undergoing ongoing testing with the service as part of the Increment 1 of the service’s first autonomous wingman, Northrop Grumman is hoping to market Talon Blue for future Air Force purchases and to U.S. allies.
Northrop’s original CCA offering lost out on the Increment 1 contracts due to its cost, president of the company’s aeronautics division Tom Jones said, leading to what became Talon Blue.
“The idea was to see if we could build an aircraft that had all the same capability of our original offering, and do it faster,” Jones said at the unveiling last year. “So the outcome was an aircraft, but the outcome we’re shooting for was the process: How do we design and build things that perform at a high level, but that we can build quickly now and can do affordably?”
The Air Force has yet to spell out the requirements for Increment 2 of the CCA program.
“It’s getting defined as every day goes by,” Gen. Dale White, the Pentagon’s director of critical major weapon systems, told reporters at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference when asked by Air & Space Forces Magazine about the status of Increment 2.
“The challenges I may have in the Indo-Pacific theater could be very different [from those] in the [U.S. Central Command] theater and different again in the [European Command] theater,” White said. “So how do we take all of those different requirements and make sure we have a [CCA] capability that can address many different mission sets across many different requirement centers?”
Whether Northrop’s Talon Blue fits into that picture is still unknown. But the YFQ-48A could also be appealing to U.S. allies, some of which have started rolling out their own CCAs, such as the U.K. government-backed, British-designed Brontanax CCA from BAE Systems. U.S. Air Forces in Europe and NATO Allied Air Command boss Lt. Gen. Jason T. Hinds said other European nations were watching the U.S.’s work on CCAs.
“You’re going to see a lot more interest from other nations inside Europe,” Hinds said at Air, Space & Cyber when asked about CCAs.
When the Talon Blue aircraft was unveiled last December, Jones said multiple U.S. military services and international partners are interested in the drone, and some had visited Mojave to see it.
“We’re still extremely good at making something very complex,” Jones said at the time. “This was really about broadening that paradigm to what it means to be a high-performing engineering, aviation, development, and manufacturing organization to encompass all aspects of it.
Talon Blue is important for Northrop’s future tactical aircraft efforts, as the company recently lost out to Boeing to build the Navy’s future F/A-XX sixth-generation fighter jet. The company is still building major weapons systems for the Air Force: the B-21 Raider stealth bomber, set to enter service next year and a project that will likely be expanded beyond the original program of record of 100 aircraft, and the LGM-35A Sentinel, the next-generation intercontinental ballistic missile.
The CCA market Talon Blue is competing for is crowded, not just by the FQ-42 and F-44, but also by Lockheed Martin’s new Vectis offering. Other possible competitors, such as Boeing’s MQ-28 Ghost Bat and Kratos’s XQ-58 Valkyrie, have been used by the U.S. military in tests and exercises alongside crewed aircraft.
The Air Force sees CCAs as a critical part of the future force.
“I can imagine a day in the future, 10 years [from now], maybe more, where a CCA autonomy algorithm does a better job flying a fighter airplane than I did as a captain,” Lt. Gen. Christopher Niemi, the Air Force’s Chief Modernization Officer, said last month. “That hurts my ego a little bit. But at the same time, I see that this trend is happening, and we’ve got to find a way to do that.”

articles.title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
articles.body:
Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers from the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.
The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before.
Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”.
Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening.
US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.
A report on ITV News said the US feared a multiple drone attack, similar to Ukraine’s Operation Spiderweb, in which cheap small drones launched from trucks destroyed 10 Russian bombers in a coordinated attack in June last year.
But UK sources cast doubt on whether Iran had the capability to launch such a complex operation 2,700 miles away. The Ukrainian operation took about 18 months to plan.
Donald Trump said on Monday that the US had withdrawn the bombers from the base because of “some threats”, without saying what they were.
“There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy – we’ll capture the enemy and beat the enemy, but why should we leave them there? So we moved them around a little bit, not very far,” Trump said.
UK sources indicated they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran could orchestrate a fresh attack, a week after five men from London were arrested late at night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose.
The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely for a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.
Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. Neither the Ministry of Defence nor Gloucestershire police commented when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.
RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target.
The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.
It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran destroyed a US Awacs radar plane on the tarmac during fighting in March. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would be likely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.
Experts cautioned there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute.
Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged.
No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later.
Trump said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited.
A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.

articles.title: Why the U.S. Bomber Withdrawal From a U.K. Air Base Is Significant
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said Monday afternoon that "threats" had prompted the U.S. to remove all of its B-1 Air Force bombers from the RAF Fairford base in southern England over the weekend. The move came a week after several men were arrested nearby in relation to a suspected terror plot, which the U.K. government believes may be linked to Iran.
When asked if there was a specific threat that led to the bombers being moved, Trump told reporters: “Yeah, I think we can say that. They didn’t fly out by accident. There were some threats, and rather than tempting the enemy… why should we leave them there? We moved them around a little bit, not very far.”
He added that Washington “actually knows the people that made the threat.” When asked if they are linked to Iran, Trump responded: “They would be linked to Iran.”
A U.S. Defense Department official had earlier told TIME that all the U.S. bombers had been ”re-deployed to their home stations in the United States,” but did not offer a specific reason behind the move, instead saying that U.S. bombers “routinely operate around the world to support global force readiness and operational requirements.” The official added that America’s bomber force remains “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities… anywhere, anytime.” Hours before Trump's remarks, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio dismissed the idea that the removal of U.S. bombers was directly connected to the foiled Fairford plot, insisting he has “confidence” in the security of U.S. bases.
A spokesperson for British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the RAF Fairford base remains safe, but refused to offer any specific comment on the military operations of “foreign nations.” The British Ministry of Defense directed TIME to the U.S. Air Force when approached for comment.
The move comes after five men, all U.K. nationals, were arrested on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offenses on Sept. 27, following a suspected terror plot nearby RAF Fairford, an airbase used by the U.S. to strike Iran. Officers made the arrests after receiving a tip-off that three "suspicious vehicles" appeared to be heading toward the direction of the base. Amid ongoing investigations, British counterterrorism police arrested a dual British-Iranian national in central London on Oct. 1 on suspicion of terrorist acts in connection with the incident. All arrestees have been released on bail.
David Dunn, a professor of international politics at the University of Birmingham, says the U.S. withdrawal from Fairford is “historic, unprecedented, and an indication of the sense of vulnerability” surrounding U.S. military assets abroad.
“Fairford is normally the place during a crisis where America sends bombers to beef up America's military capability and its formal operating bases, whether that's for operations in Europe, like the Kosovo campaign, or for operations in the Gulf through 2003 onwards, or indeed for operations in Iran,” Dunn tells TIME. “This [removal] is an indication of concerns about the safety of those assets in their forward operating bases.”
Dunn adds “the haste” with which the operation took place over the weekend is also noteworthy, referencing reports that some of the aircraft had only been there for a relatively short period of time, having arrived recently as part of a rotation.
U.K. and U.S. officials suspect Iranian involvement in RAF Fairford plot
Both U.K. and U.S. officials have voiced suspicion of Iranian involvement in the suspected terror plot that has led to several arrests.
Burnham on Sept. 30 said the U.K. believes Iran was likely involved in the incident. “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” he said, adding that British forces were “working closely” with U.S. counterparts.
Iran has vehemently denied any involvement. In the immediate aftermath of the initial arrests, the Iranian embassy in London said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" any attempt to "link Iran to" the arrests made near RAF Fairford. After Burnham’s comments, Iran doubled down on its denial, with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi accusing the U.K. of “barking up the wrong tree.”
Trump previously said the five men arrested at the scene had been under “investigation” prior to the arrests and were looking to cause “big damage.” Asked whether Iran was involved in the suspect terror plot, he said, “it might be,” but did not offer further details.
Dunn says that although Iran “hasn't got the range to [directly] attack bases in the U.K.,” it does not necessarily remove the potential threat to U.S. assets stationed there. “Iran—by doing things via proxies, organized criminal gangs, or hiring people gangs through payments through the dark web—can still have a military effect and a deterrent effect on the operation of a base like Fairford,” he says.
Counter Terrorism Policing has said it is looking at all angles, citing possible foreign-state involvement as one line of inquiry. It has urged against conclusions being drawn in what is a high-profile and active investigation.
How RAF Fairford has supported U.S. military operations for decades
RAF Fairford is a NATO-designated standby deployment and a U.S. forward operating base for U.S. Global Strike Command, according to U.K. government records. The base, which opened in 1944, has been used extensively by U.S. military aircraft in previous conflicts, including "Operation Iraqi Freedom" in 2003.
The U.S. Air Force describes RAF Fairford as its “preferred” European “bomber forward operating location” and previously said it has used Fairford “nearly continuously” since the base was constructed.
Former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer initially refused to allow U.S. access to U.K. military bases in its offensive strikes against Iran—a move that earned him the wrath of Trump. Starmer changed his position in March, authorizing the U.S. to use bombers based at RAF Fairford to carry out strikes on Iranian missile sites used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warned the base could be a target on account of its use by the U.S. military, insisting it makes the U.K. a “participant in aggression” in the war.
Starmer had previously warned the British public of the general threat posed by Iran. On Feb. 28, in an address to the nation hours after the U.S. and Israel launched its initial strikes against Iran, he said: “Even in the United Kingdom, the Iranian regime poses a direct threat to dissidents and the Jewish community. Over the last year alone, they have backed more than 20 potentially lethal attacks on U.K. soil.”

articles.title: Don’t know? Blame Russia: Finnish president takes page from NATO chief’s playbook
articles.body:
Don’t know? Blame Russia: Finnish president takes page from NATO chief’s playbook
Published 5 Oct, 2026 04:09 | Updated 5 Oct, 2026 09:27
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has blamed Russia for a wide range of security concerns facing the EU, including the influx of migrants over the summer into Ceuta, Spain’s enclave in Morocco. He later admitted that he did not know the situation in Ceuta “well enough to take a position.”
Stubb made the remarks in an interview with Spanish newspaper El Mundo over the weekend. Asked about potential hybrid threats posed by Russia, Stubb said the country would try to interfere with the upcoming Spanish election.
Madrid “should expect some form of sabotage or hybrid attack. It could be related to information warfare or a campaign that threatens their democracy,” he claimed.
The president went on to allege that Russian-backed cyberattacks are “happening as we speak against Spanish banks and other targets,” without citing specific evidence.
“They send asylum seekers to our border, as we have also seen in Ceuta,” he said, accusing Russia of committing acts of sabotage throughout the EU.
He also mentioned cases in which Russian-linked ships were accused of cutting undersea telecommunications cables in the Baltic Sea and the recent incident at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport, where explosives-laden drones were found near Ukrainian cargo planes. Germany blamed Moscow and ordered the closure of a Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural center in Berlin. Russia dismissed the accusations as “nonsensical” and denied any involvement.
Pressed further about Russia’s alleged role in the Ceuta crisis in late July, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the enclave, Stubb admitted that he did not “know the matter well enough to take a position.”
Reuters reported at the time that migrants had been encouraged by viral videos and misleading claims about Spain’s asylum and migration rules. Spain later accused Russian- and Israeli-linked networks of spreading disinformation regarding the crisis, which both countries denied.
Stubb’s interview came after NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte encouraged members of the bloc to attribute incidents to Russia whenever they are sure or “almost sure” that Russia is responsible.
“When able, when you are sure it is the Russians, or almost sure it is the Russians, attribute it to the Russians,” Rutte said this week.
Direct conflict unlikely
Asked about the possibility of a direct conflict between NATO and Russia, however, Stubb dismissed it as negligible.
“Do we expect Russia to attack? The answer is no. We have no evidence of that,” he told El Mundo.
According to the Finnish president, EU leaders have a “communication problem,” as some have been “acting in an alarmist way and conflating [hypothetical] scenarios with the perception of the threat.”
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius urged officials this week not to “exaggerate” when making alarmist statements about Russia and said there is no evidence that the country is planning to attack NATO. Rutte has also said there is “no imminent threat to NATO territory.”
Nevertheless, EU officials have argued that the bloc, as well as NATO, should be prepared for a potential clash with Russia. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the country must be ready for a conflict by as early as 2028. The German government amended its constitutional debt brake to fund military spending and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion ($121.5 billion) to defense and €11.5 billion in military assistance for Ukraine.
Russia has stated that it would not attack any NATO country unless attacked first – warning, however, that Western military aid to Ukraine makes a dangerous escalation more likely. President Vladimir Putin has argued that European politicians are stirring tensions with Russia to distract voters from problems at home.

articles.title: Saudi Arabia explored new routes oil export amid Hormuz crisis
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Aramco eyes new oil routes to bypass Strait of Hormuz
Saudi Arabia's Aramco is examining proposals for two new land-based oil export routes that would bypass the Strait of Hormuz, as continued military tensions disrupt shipping, tankers come under attack and freight rates soar.
According to a report published on 27 September by BN Report, a platform specialising in energy intelligence and business economics, the Saudi oil giant is conducting engineering and technical feasibility studies to expand its export routes.
The proposals include connecting pipelines to Oman's coast and the Duqm storage complex, giving Saudi Arabia direct access to Asian markets while reducing its exposure to disruption in the Strait of Hormuz and rising insurance premiums.
US-based Business Insurance magazine, which specialises in risk and insurance intelligence, reported on 1 October that war-risk insurance premiums for Saudi-linked tankers had tripled to 3% of a vessel's value at Yanbu port. At southern ports, premiums had risen to 7%, adding millions of dollars to the cost of individual shipments.
The plans come as the Houthis intensify their attacks on Saudi oil facilities, with the group announcing that it had carried out a "qualitative military operation" using several ballistic missiles and drones targeting Saudi Aramco in the capital Riyadh.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said on Saturday, 3 October, that the operation "comes as part of the response to Saudi Arabia's targeting" of the Yemeni capital Sanaa and other areas under the group's control.
The Houthis also said they would continue to impose the equation of "siege for siege and escalation for escalation".
Investment costs decline
Strategic, economic and infrastructure considerations are increasingly shaping the region's energy transport calculations, according to economic expert Hossam Ayesh.
Ayesh told The New Arab that the huge investment costs and lengthy construction periods involved in building new pipelines must be weighed against rising insurance premiums and the risks facing maritime shipping.
Although shipping oil by sea may theoretically remain cheaper than constructing thousands of kilometres of pipelines, geopolitical tensions and the risk of the Strait of Hormuz being closed are pushing policymakers to look beyond traditional export routes, he said.
These calculations also come amid shifts in international competition.
Bloomberg reported on 29 September that the vulnerability of logistical hubs in the Middle East coincides with rising production in the Americas, which is expected to exceed 32 million barrels per day by 2030. This puts further pressure on Gulf producers to secure reliable export routes and protect their market share in Asia as alternative supplies grow.
Gulf states are also drawing lessons from recent disruptions to international energy infrastructure, particularly the fallout from the Nord Stream pipelines linking Russia and Germany.
The pipelines were sabotaged and subsequently halted amid the war in Ukraine, causing major financial losses.
The precedent shows that new pipelines would not be immune to targeting or sabotage, particularly amid heightened global uncertainty and sharp fluctuations in oil demand, Ayesh said.
Through the proposed routes, policymakers at Aramco and in Saudi Arabia are seeking to diversify oil export options through the Red Sea, domestic pipelines and potential land routes towards Oman, Jordan and Syria.
The aim is to safeguard vital market share and ensure reliable supplies despite mounting security threats, according to Ayesh.
This makes the financial cost a secondary consideration compared with the strategic need to ensure the sustainability and reliability of Saudi oil exports, he added.
The project could also go beyond transporting Saudi oil and play a role in strengthening logistical and economic integration with neighbouring countries, particularly Oman.
Its scope could eventually expand to include the transport of Qatari liquefied natural gas towards the Arabian Sea, according to Ayesh, who said shared infrastructure could generate additional economic benefits across the region.
Riyadh-Muscat partnership
Aramco's study of new export routes represents a major strategic investment aimed primarily at strengthening the security and resilience of Saudi oil exports and protecting them from future shocks, according to economic expert Ali Metwally, who works at a London-based consultancy.
Metwally told The New Arab that the project could be implemented in stages over several years, particularly if one of the routes includes a direct connection to Oman's Arabian Sea coast.
The estimated cost of building a major regional pipeline with a capacity of between 1.5 million and 2.5 million barrels per day ranges from $8 billion to $15 billion for a single route.
Costs could rise further with the addition of major pumping stations, storage facilities, maritime export terminals and advanced protection and operating systems.
Metwally stressed that the figures remain preliminary until Aramco announces official details on the project's approved capacity and final budget.
The case for alternative routes is being strengthened by continued disruption to seaborne oil flows.
Lloyd's List, a London-based maritime data and intelligence provider, reported on 2 October that congestion affecting ship-to-ship oil transfers in the Gulf of Oman was prompting tanker owners to bypass bottlenecks around the strait in favour of alternative ports.
The shift reflects growing expectations that the shipping crisis could persist for years.
The project's economic value lies partly in avoiding soaring insurance premiums and maritime shipping costs, which could rise to tens of dollars per barrel during periods of heightened tensions and clashes around the Strait of Hormuz.
Rather than comparing pipeline construction costs with ordinary shipping costs during periods of stability, Metwally argues that the pipeline's fixed capital costs would be spread across long-term contracts and millions of barrels transported each day, potentially making the project financially viable as maritime risks increase.
A route linking Saudi Arabia and Oman would also provide additional strategic value by giving Saudi oil direct access to major Asian markets without passing through the Strait of Hormuz, using Duqm port and other terminals on the Arabian Sea, according to Metwally.
It would draw on Oman's developed logistics infrastructure and large storage facilities, potentially creating deeper regional integration in oil handling, tanker shipping and strategic stock management.
Aramco's commercial gain
For Aramco, the main commercial benefit would be greater supply reliability for major importers and a reduced risk of losing its established market share in Asia to competing energy suppliers.
The proposed routes would create a more flexible export network, allowing the Saudi oil giant to redirect shipments between the Gulf, Red Sea and Arabian Sea depending on security risks, insurance costs and global demand, according to Metwally.
However, one of the biggest obstacles would be constructing a route stretching more than 1,000 kilometres across harsh desert environments, including the Empty Quarter.
This would pose significant technical challenges, including extreme temperatures and shifting dunes, as well as the need to establish electricity networks, maintenance infrastructure and secure access routes.
The project would also require Riyadh and Muscat to reach comprehensive bilateral agreements governing ownership and operating rights, tariffs and security arrangements.

articles.title: Ukraine touts gains from Operation Vivaldi as Russia claims major encirclements. What’s really happening on the battlefield?
articles.body:
Ukraine touts gains from Operation Vivaldi as Russia claims major encirclements. What’s really happening on the battlefield?
The Russian and Ukrainian armies continue their offensives in different sectors of the front. Because these operations have coincided with a new burst of activity in the negotiations mediated by Donald Trump, they have been accompanied by loud public relations campaigns. The Russian command describes its offensive as “destroying encircled groupings,” though in reality it has failed to encircle any major Ukrainian forces. Ukrainian military officials claim they have already moved on to the third phase of “Operation Vivaldi” near the city of Lyman in Donetsk region. Judging by open-source videos, however, they are still working — successfully — to push Russian forces off their first line of defense. In reality, the nature of the fighting has not changed. The Russian army is trying to break through to the Kramatorsk-Sloviansk urban area from different directions, while Ukrainian forces are trying to stop this advance with counterattacks. This battle is of decisive importance for the course of the war even without the additional public relations campaigns, which are more likely to mislead.
Vladimir Putin, speaking last week at a meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club, said “the authorities in Ukraine and Europe themselves believe they’ll be able to hold Donbas for only a year and a half to two years.” Russian forces, he said, will capture it “much sooner.” Putin assured the experts gathered at the event that the pace of the offensive is “accelerating.”
In reality, the Russian army captured Pokrovsk and Siversk by early 2026 and Kostiantynivka that summer, but over the following nine months failed to break through into the cities defending the Kramatorsk urban area from the south, northeast, and southwest. In the northeast, around Lyman, Russian forces lost much of the territory they had captured the previous year.
‘Operation Vivaldi’ and fighting on the Siverskyi Donets
- Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps, who recently took charge of all forces defending Kramatorsk and Sloviansk from the north, east, and south (the newly formed “Center” grouping), said troops have begun the next phase of “Operation Vivaldi.” The goal of the operation — which, like the Italian composer’s famous work, is supposed to have four parts — remains unclear. Ukrainian forces are likely planning to push Russia’s 20th and 25th armies back across the Chornyi Zherebets, a tributary of the Siverskyi Donets. As a result, Russian forces risk losing all the gains they have made in this sector since the summer of 2025, when they crossed the Chornyi Zherebets along a broad front.
- Biletskyi has described the operation’s progress only in general terms, but many in Ukraine, unofficially, see it as something close to a harbinger of a new tactic that could help Ukrainian forces defeat the Russian army. The pace of “Vivaldi” so far shows no sign of such a shift: Ukrainian troops, who began the offensive in mid-summer, have advanced no more than 10 kilometers (6 miles) in different sectors.
- Videos that surfaced in recent weeks were meant to confirm Ukrainian successes. They show Ukrainian forces liberating several villages on the perimeter of the Russian salient around Lyman — Novoselivka, Shandryholove, and Nove — and attempting to gain a foothold in Serednie, Karpivka, and Katerynivka, villages that had been on the line of contact for months.
- Russia’s 20th Combined Arms Army, which faces Ukrainian forces in this sector, was previously thought to have largely withdrawn across the Chornyi Zherebets. Now, if the published videos mark the farthest extent of the Ukrainian advance, the 20th Army appears to still hold positions on the western bank of the Chornyi Zherebets near Zarichne and in the surrounding forests and ravines. The Russian position is worsening, however: Ukrainian assault troops have pushed deep into the flanks at Nove and Kolodiazi.
- To the south, meanwhile, Russia’s 25th Army continues to hold positions on the outskirts of Lyman. One video shows Russian assault troops back in the city center, which had largely been cleared of them earlier in the summer after a failed assault. Problems facing the neighboring 20th Army are worsening conditions on the 25th Army’s northern flank, and if Ukrainian forces capture the Chornyi Zherebets crossings at Torske and Zarichne, the 25th Army will have to withdraw from Lyman.
- The Russian offensive on Lyman was meant to support the 3rd Combined Arms Army’s advance along the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets toward Sloviansk. That plan worked until Russian forces were stopped near Lyman and on the approaches to Sviatohirsk, farther west. Problems facing its neighbors on the northern bank have recently forced the 3rd Army to fight its way toward Sloviansk alone. By late summer, its troops had reached the city of Mykolaivka, 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Sloviansk, but failed to take it in a quick assault, though Russian assault troops did reach its eastern outskirts.
- In recent weeks, Ukrainian forces have tried to eliminate the threat to Mykolaivka through counterattacks near Rai-Oleksandrivka, reaching the village center, where heavy fighting has broken out. Russian forces still control the southeastern approaches to Mykolaivka, though, and are trying to outflank the Ukrainian units advancing on Rai-Oleksandrivka near the Siverskyi Donets–Donbas canal in the Yurkivka and Orikhuvatka area.
- These battles will determine whether Russian forces get closer to Sloviansk’s outskirts in 2026. Biletskyi’s troops are likely to try a larger counterattack on the southern bank of the Siverskyi Donets.
Dobropillia and Druzhkivka
- Russian forces are trying to go around the Kramatorsk urban area from the west. In their path is one of Ukraine’s “fortresses”: the city of Dobropillia. Russian troops spent the first half of the year covering the 10 kilometers (6 miles) from Pokrovsk, which they had already captured, to Dobropillia’s southern outskirts. Forces in this sector needed significant reinforcement: the 76th Airborne Assault Division was redeployed to the area from other sectors first, followed by the 90th Tank Division.
- In September, the Russian Defense Ministry unexpectedly announced that Dobropillia had been encircled. A month earlier, Putin had expressed displeasure with the slow pace of the advance to the commander of the 76th Division. Judging by that conversation and the place names mentioned in it, Russian forces were only about five kilometers (3 miles) from the city at the time and were not even contemplating an encirclement.
- In the two weeks since the encirclement announcement, no evidence has emerged that Dobropillia has been outflanked from the west or east. Ukrainian forces, judging by published videos, managed to regain control of Hannivka, the city’s northeastern outskirts. Russian assault troops did enter Dobropillia itself from the south, however, beginning an assault on the city.
- At the same time, Russian forces are widening the front of their offensive around Dobropillia. The 90th Tank Division and its neighbors advanced several kilometers north in the sector between Dobropillia and Druzhkivka, while units of the 2nd Combined Arms Army pushed southwest of the city in the Hrushynka River valley.
- Although Dobropillia isn’t encircled, the situation around it is growing increasingly difficult for Ukrainian forces. Russian forces, after redeploying large reserves, now hold a significant advantage in the area.
- In September, Biletskyi described Russia’s plan for the Donbas offensive this way: the Russian “northern pincer” was meant to cut supply routes to Kramatorsk and Sloviansk by crossing the Siverskyi Donets near Sviatohirsk and Lyman and blocking the roads to Izyum and Kharkiv, while the “southern pincer,” advancing through Dobropillia, was meant to cut the road out of Kramatorsk near Barvinkove and complete the encirclement of the Kramatorsk urban area. The “defeat of the northern pincer” near Lyman, Biletskyi said, eliminated that threat. Russia’s plan now appears far more modest, however: after capturing Dobropillia, Russian forces want to push directly along the Dobropillia–Kramatorsk road toward the center of the urban area, as well as from Chasiv Yar toward the heights south of Kramatorsk. Defending Dobropillia and the territory east of the city will require Ukraine’s military command to urgently redeploy additional forces.
The ‘Vovchansk encirclement’
- The Russian command has announced another “encirclement” far beyond the Donbas front. In May 2024, when Russia launched a new invasion of the Kharkiv region using forces of the Leningrad Military District (the “Sever” grouping), the Russian General Staff likely planned to combine this offensive with the assault on Donbas: after capturing Vovchansk, troops were supposed to push through Velykyi Burluk into the rear of Ukrainian forces defending Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. This mirrored the Russian operation in 2022, when Russian forces reached Izyum within the first days of the full-scale invasion, crossed the Siverskyi Donets after heavy fighting, and advanced almost to the northern outskirts of Sloviansk. Russian forces lost all of this territory in the Kharkiv region in the fall of 2022.
- The 2024 offensive was stopped in the center of Vovchansk itself, after which it lost any connection to plans for capturing Donbas. The “Sever” grouping’s forces, however, maintained contact with the “Zapad” grouping, which had spent years unsuccessfully attacking nearby Kupyansk. The top priority became reaching Velykyi Burluk, in the rear of the Ukrainian grouping defending Kupyansk.
- In the fall of 2025, Ukraine’s command decided to push Russian forces back from Kupyansk, using units that had been defending Vovchansk. Ukrainian forces managed to temporarily liberate central Kupyansk, but at the cost of a sharp escalation around Vovchansk: Russian forces crossed the Vovcha River in the city center and, by year’s end, had begun a slow advance toward Velykyi Burluk.
- In the summer of 2026, Russian forces unexpectedly launched an offensive across the state border east of Vovchansk. At the same time, groups of Russian assault troops began infiltrating south from Vovchansk toward the village of Bilyi Kolodiaz. In September, the Russian Defense Ministry announced that its troops had “closed the encirclement of a major Ukrainian grouping near the border” east of Bilyi Kolodiaz.
- Since then, no evidence has emerged that this encirclement actually exists. Russian assault troops have been spotted in Bilyi Kolodiaz (more precisely, a single assault trooper with a Russian flag). Russian units advancing from east of the border have reached Blahodatne, but a 17-kilometer (11-mile) “gap” remains between Bilyi Kolodiaz and Blahodatne, where no Russian troop presence has been recorded so far.
- Ukrainian forces haven’t experienced any supply shortages so far at the positions supposedly encircled. Judging by published videos, Ukrainian armored vehicles are still operating inside the hypothetical “pocket” even a month after Russia announced that supply lines had been cut.
- Despite all the Russian command’s exaggerations, the situation for Ukrainian forces in this sector continues to deteriorate: they clearly lack the strength to eliminate the Russian assault troops that have broken through into their rear. Ukrainian troops periodically counterattack with small groups of two or three tanks — a pattern that, given how this war is being fought, may point to a serious shortage of infantry and even drones.
- About 15 kilometers (9 miles) separate Velykyi Burluk from the positions where Russian assault troops have been recorded. Because fighting here is taking place without a stable front line, Russian forces could break through to this city, which is critical for supplying Ukrainian forces on the Vovchansk and Kupyansk fronts.

articles.title: NATO Uses Lessons-Learned in Ukraine to Plan Russian Defeat in 3D+ Battlespace
articles.body:
NATO is drafting a strategy designed to defeat a potential Russian attack on its eastern flank quickly and decisively by combining conventional military power with drones and artificial intelligence.
The document, titled “Theory of Victory,” is being developed under NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR) Gen. Alexus Grynkewich and is expected to be presented in Poland on Monday, Oct. 12, Bloomberg reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Bloomberg reviewed an unclassified version of the document, which is intended to clarify how NATO would respond if Russian forces entered the territory of an alliance member.
The strategy remains a planning document rather than an indication that NATO believes a Russian conventional attack is imminent.
“The Supreme Allied Commander Europe’s theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO’s advantage,” Grynkewich’s spokesperson, Col. Martin O’Donnell, told Bloomberg.
O’Donnell declined to discuss operational details but said the alliance needed to prepare now to deter aggression and prevail if attacked. He also stressed that NATO remained a “purely defensive” alliance.
Drones and AI would support conventional forces
Under the proposed strategy, NATO would initially seek to stop an incursion using land forces and capabilities developed through its Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
These would include low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-assisted targeting integrated with conventional weapons and military units.
Russian Authorities Won’t Confirm Pneumonic Plague Outbreak in Central Siberia
After securing freedom of movement, allied forces would attempt to disrupt and destroy the enemy’s command-and-control structure, with the aim of defeating the attacking forces before they could establish a lasting foothold on NATO territory.
The plan emphasizes avoiding unintended provocations while demonstrating enough military readiness to convince an adversary that an attack could not succeed.
It also covers hybrid threats – hostile actions such as sabotage, cyberattacks, interference with infrastructure and covert operations that remain below the threshold of open warfare.
Russia has reportedly ordered its intelligence services to intensify hybrid operations across NATO and EU countries, including possible sabotage against military facilities, critical infrastructure and communications systems.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has said there are currently no indications that Russia is preparing a conventional assault on the alliance. However, European governments expect Moscow’s hybrid campaign to continue and potentially intensify.
NATO applies lessons from Ukraine
The strategy reflects lessons from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, where inexpensive drones, electronic warfare and rapidly updated software have transformed even frontline 2D battlefield operations into 3D-plus battlespace operations.
NATO has already been testing drones, unmanned ground vehicles, counter-drone equipment and new communications systems under the Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative.
The alliance has also explored an AI-assisted automated defensive zone along its borders with Russia and Belarus. The proposed system would use interconnected sensors, drones and weapons to detect hostile movements while reducing the number of soldiers required to monitor exposed areas.
In July, NATO members agreed to invest more than $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over five years. The alliance is also developing a counter-drone marketplace and plans to train five times as many military drone operators by the end of 2027.
Allies face spending and force decisions
The proposal comes as European NATO members sharply increase defense expenditure but debate how to divide funding between tanks, artillery and other conventional weapons and newer technologies demonstrated in Ukraine.
The US reportedly sent allies a questionnaire during the summer asking about their defense spending and support for President Donald Trump’s policies as Washington considered reducing some American military assets assigned to Europe.
The questionnaire also asked whether NATO members could contribute additional forces to Grynkewich’s defense plans.
“Theory of Victory” is therefore intended not only to describe a possible military response but also to show governments what forces and technologies they would need to finance before a crisis begins.
The initiative comes amid growing concern about Russian drone incursions, sabotage and airspace violations along NATO’s eastern flank. Rutte has said the alliance deliberately keeps the precise threshold for activating Article 5 ambiguous, preventing adversaries from calculating how far they can escalate without triggering a collective response.

articles.title: America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
articles.body:
America’s bomber withdrawal points to wider UK-US friction
The Pentagon’s decision to relocate B-1 bombers from the British air base comes after months of frustration in the Trump administration over Britain’s defense spending.
LONDON — Britain and the U.S. sought to ease friction Monday after American bombers were suddenly moved amid major security concerns at the base that hosted U.S. aircraft used to strike Iran.
The U.S. move is the latest stumbling block in the special relationship between the allies and underscores reservations in Donald Trump’s administration about how the U.K. is handling its defense and security commitments.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday that it had removed all B-1 bombers from the RAF Fairford air base — where they were deployed to conduct what have been termed as "defensive" strikes against Iran — and sent them back to their home stations in America.
Advertisement
Trump went further, telling journalists Monday evening: "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why would I leave them there? ... If we're going to be threatened we're just going to move them, and that sort of alleviates that."
It comes as Britain's counter-terrorism agencies investigate a suspected terror plot against the air base, which the U.K. government believes involves Tehran.
Trump on Monday added: "We actually know the people that made the threat, and they've got themselves a big problem," adding in response to a follow-up question: "They would be linked to Iran."
He later said that he believes the U.K. is still a safe place for U.S. forces.
Downing Street had earlier insisted that the base was safe, but refused to comment directly on America’s decision to remove the bombers from the area.
The move comes as the Trump administration has grown increasingly frustrated with the U.K.’s defense spending and the White House's continuing anger that the U.K. didn’t send warships to the Middle East to help with the American blockade of Iranian shipping.
Advertisement
Something deeper is wrong
London has yet to outline a path to meet the NATO standard of spending 3.5% of GDP on defense by 2035 — up from its current level of around 2.7%. It has also been shut out of a subgroup within the alliance convened by Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby. The group is slated to meet again in Poland some time later this month.
Late last month, Colby hinted at that frustration with London, saying the countries' long history will continue to bind them, but the British government needs to make the case to its people for spending more on defense.
“There's this incredible legacy, and that's what we want to rekindle,” Colby said. “Exactly how you convince the British people [to spend more on defense] I would not presume to say, but … there's probably sort of a degree of reconciliation between what the U.K. wants to be doing, what it spends, and what it spends on, because you know a modern military is not cheap.”
The U.S. is also conducting a sweeping review of its posture in European NATO countries — including the U.K. — which will determine the number of American troops and military assets on the continent.
Sophia Gaston, a senior national security researcher at King’s College London, said: “The Trump administration is undeniably sensitive to the costs of the Iran conflict as they head into the midterms next month, so their caution is understandable.
An armored vehicle is seen at RAF Fairford on Sept. 28, 2026. | Ben Stansall/AFP via Getty Images
“It’s also hard not to, at some level, perceive a degree of uncertainty about the capacity of the British services to currently prevent such an attack. That partly reflects the innate challenge drones and other aspects of modern warfare pose to the sitting ducks of expensive kit.
Advertisement
“But it also speaks to the American wariness towards the pressured state of Britain’s military capabilities. Not only does Washington no longer wish to be solely responsible for allies’ protection, its expectations for the security allies offer its bases has also increased.”
Trump on Monday praised his relationship with new U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He said: "He's liberal, very liberal, but I hear he's going to open up North Sea oil if he does that in Aberdeen. If he does that, you're going to have a rich country. If he doesn't, you're going to have a bankrupt country."
Britain’s security concerns
In May, the U.K. raised its terrorism threat level to “severe” — meaning a terrorist attack is highly likely — after its MI5 security service said the U.K. had been “experiencing a gradual increase in terrorist threats for some time” including from hostile states like Iran.
In Britain, police and the security services are dealing with a three-fold threat from Iran-backed groups: attacks against Iranian dissidents, attacks against the country’s Jewish population, and the targeting of U.S. assets such as those used for strikes against Tehran.
Counter Terrorism Policing is currently investigating potential Iranian state involvement in a major incident at RAF Fairford on Sept. 27, when police were alerted to three suspicious vehicles near the base.
Six men — including a British-Iranian national — have so far been arrested on suspicion of terror offenses. All have subsequently been released on bail while police continue their investigation.
Advertisement
US strike capability
Though the Pentagon stressed that bombers remain “ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities” — including from the U.S. mainland — removing them would make any further American strikes on Iran more complex, since the bombers would have to double their flight path from the continental U.S. to the Middle East.
There is a fresh U.S. buildup in the region, with a third aircraft carrier currently steaming across the Pacific along with several large amphibious ships carrying 2,500 Marines, joining the 2,500 already at sea in the Middle East, giving President Donald Trump more options should he restart the bombing campaign after the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
Christoph Bergs, a research analyst at the RUSI defense think tank, said: “The basing of US B-1 bombers at RAF Fairford for operational employment against Iran was based on the UK stipulation that these were only used for defensive strikes. This likely included a more modest targeting list. Their withdrawal reduces the capacity to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat.”
The Pentagon declined to comment on whether it will, or is considering, the removal of other aircraft from British bases used to support operations against Iran.
This article has been updated with comments from Donald Trump.

articles.title: Yemen's Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Yemen's Houthis claim striking Riyadh airport, other Saudi sites
Iran-backed Houthis on Monday said they had struck Riyadh's international airport, an Aramco refinery and several other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.
Pakistan and Turkey meanwhile pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.
The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said on X that its naval forces had hit "military targets" belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
They "destroyed weapons depots, facilities storing booby-trapped boats and naval mines" and had "thwarted a planned attack" targeting waterways in the southern Red Sea, he said.
Loud explosions rattled Riyadh on Monday evening as the fighting escalated, and a Houthi spokesman said the group had hit the Saudi capital's King Khalid International Airport as well as an Aramco refinery and other targets in the kingdom's south.
The government announced on Sunday the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory, home to most of Yemen's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
Last month the Iran-backed group seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping, in Yemen's deadliest fighting in years.
The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen's civil war flared back to life, and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
On Monday, representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other's aid in the event of any attack.
They also agreed "to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom".
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
A spokesman for UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said he was "deeply concerned by the sharp escalation in fighting", and condemned "the continued Houthi cross-border attacks" on Saudi Arabia.
Global oil system 'straining'
Houthi attacks have also targeted Saudi oil infrastructure, as well as its tankers in the Red Sea.
A source in the Saudi energy sector told AFP that an attack on Sunday had again halted pumping by the East-West pipeline to the Red Sea, a key conduit for the kingdom's exports since Iran blockaded the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the wider Middle East war.
Crude prices had already been soaring as a result of the Middle East war, before the Houthis began targeting the world's largest oil exporter.
Saudi Aramco chief executive Amin Nasser warned on Monday that global oil stockpiles were "scarily thin" owing to the war.
"The system is already straining," Nasser told the Energy Intelligence Forum in London.
Mocha fighting
Yemeni military sources said Monday that pro-government forces had cut off the only supply route to the Houthi-held city of Mocha, but stopped short of confirming an official announcement of the port's recapture.
While the war in Yemen predates the broader Middle East war that began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran, it has become its most active front in recent weeks. According to UN figures, the fighting has displaced more than 184,000 people.
Yemen's civil war broke out in 2014, with the Saudis intervening the following March, but fighting was paused by a 2022 ceasefire that held until July of this year.

articles.title: Can Yemen's divided coalition turn the tide against the Houthis?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Can Yemen's divided coalition turn the tide against the Houthis?
When the Houthis launched attacks along Yemen's western coast on 3 September, internationally recognised government-aligned forces were unprepared for what was the largest offensive since the ceasefire signed in 2022.
Their response revealed a series of operational failures that allowed the Houthis to advance across 5,000 square kilometres, seizing the port city of Mocha, several coastal positions, and the islands of Mayyun and Hanish to gain control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.
Reported accounts of the initial Houthi offensive show that the fragmented government-aligned forces lacked military coordination and timely support from Saudi Arabia, which backs Yemen’s internationally recognised government.
The Houthis penetrated opposition communications, tracked troop movements, and cut off frontline units from command. They reportedly relied on Iranian advisers, who provided direct support for their blitzkrieg.
Over the following days, Saudi airstrikes and Yemeni government-aligned counterattacks sought to reclaim lost ground, including areas along the Taiz–Aden route.
Combat is currently concentrated in Taiz province, where the Houthis are attempting to consolidate control over captured territory.
"Their objective is to consolidate gains by securing the mountainous areas overlooking Bab al-Mandeb and blocking the road between Taiz and Lahej and Aden to cut off military support," Yemeni political analyst and journalist Mohammed Al-Qadhi told The New Arab.
"By recapturing these zones lost in 2017, the Houthis shield themselves from government and Saudi counter-offensives, avoiding exposure in the flat coastal areas."
Reports also suggest Houthi troop movements towards Saada province on the Saudi border.
The fault lines in Yemen's anti-Houthi camp
Regional and Western officials told Reuters last week that Saudi Arabia was planning a large-scale offensive against the Houthis, including a possible coastal push to secure Red Sea shipping, or an assault on multiple fronts.
On Sunday, Yemen’s government then announced the ambitious goal of retaking all Houthi territory, with operations beginning at dawn.
So far, according to the Saudi-led coalition, the military has carried out over 1,000 airstrikes using 100 warplanes as part of Operation 'Dawn of Yemen'.
The Houthis effectively encircled the city of Taiz the same day, cutting off the main supply route linking the city to Aden, the capital of the government.
As the war unfolds, the Houthi offensive could expose the limits of Yemen’s anti-Houthi coalition, with Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government struggling to overcome fractured command structures and competing political agendas threatening to undermine their campaign.
Yemen's anti-Houthi camp has never been a single bloc, with the Saudi-backed government, represented by the Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), an uneasy coalition of rival factions.
Among them is the Southern Transitional Council (STC), a UAE-backed separatist movement that had been represented on the council until January and seeks an independent southern Yemen.
Its offensive to expand control, launched in December 2025, was rapidly reversed by Saudi-backed forces in January, prompting the UAE to withdraw its remaining forces from Yemen.
Tareq Saleh, nephew of the late president Ali Abdullah Saleh, meanwhile, commands the National Resistance Forces (NRF), which favour a unified Yemen but were long backed by Abu Dhabi.
Islah, the Sunni Islamist party with historical ties to the Muslim Brotherhood - an association it denies - has long opposed the southern separatist project and supports a unified Yemen.
The UAE-backed Giants Brigades and National Resistance Forces (NRF) retain distinct command structures, even as Riyadh seeks to bring Yemen's fragmented armed groups under a more unified state command through the Nation's Shield and other security and military structures.
Operationally, the NRF, Giants Brigades, and National Shield Forces (operating under the PLC) maintain separate command structures and logistics rather than a unified field command, while the PLC itself has yet to establish an integrated military leadership.
Coordination is made even harder by lingering anger in the south after the STC's contested dissolution in January, the rise of the southern region of Hadhramawt as an independent political force, and Islah’s mistrust of UAE-backed groups.
"On this basis, a unified front under a single command with a shared offensive objective appears unlikely in the coming months," Ahmed Alshargabi, a research analyst at the Yemen Policy Centre, told The New Arab.
“The more probable outcome is defensive coordination aimed at blocking further Houthi advances toward Lahj, Aden, Bab al-Mandeb and Marib, without any real integration of forces.”
He added that a real alliance depends on an understanding between Riyadh and Abu Dhabi, unified funding, southern political guarantees, and an empowered field command.
Rival regional visions for Yemen
The Saudi-UAE rivalry plays a critical role in the anti-Houthi coalition’s internal fragmentation.
As Andreas Krieg, associate professor in Security Studies at King’s College London, explained to The New Arab, Saudi Arabia and the UAE have different interests and cultural approaches to Yemen.
Abu Dhabi does not see a unified Yemen as a necessity, while Riyadh favours a unified sovereign state. The result is a fragmented landscape in which few Yemeni forces have a stake in fighting beyond their own regions.
“It’s unrealistic to think that the southerners will fight in the north against the Houthis, which most southerners see as a problem for northerners,” he told The New Arab.
“Even if there is a reconciliation between the UAE and Saudi Arabia, it’s very unlikely the southerners will volunteer to take the war into northern Yemen. They have no stakes there. So ultimately what we end up with is a shifting stalemate.”
Last week, UAE Vice President Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed visited Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Riyadh. It was the first visit by a senior Emirati official since a diplomatic rift erupted between the two Gulf states in January.
Alshargabi said the meeting reflects a tactical rapprochement driven by Houthi advances and Riyadh’s reliance on UAE-backed forces, but Abu Dhabi’s potential demands could fuel new instability and leave their rivalry unresolved.
Krieg added that potential UAE support is unlikely to alter the war’s trajectory, given the fragmented command structures and the limited reach of southern forces.
In early 2026, Yemen's government attempted to consolidate southern forces by integrating former STC units into the Interior Ministry, reshuffling commanders, and tolerating hybrid arrangements. Some experts argue that a state monopoly on force is unlikely given Yemen’s tribal loyalties, whereas reducing the number of non-state armed actors is more realistic.
Forging military cooperation among anti-Houthi forces is far easier than achieving political unity, according to Anas Alqaed, director of programmes at the Gulf International Forum, because battlefield coordination requires no formal political agreement.
“The coalition lost ground mainly due to a breakdown in command and control, and fixing that could take anywhere from a few months to two years,” he told The New Arab.
“However, I do not believe the anti-Houthi coalition is ready to reverse the Houthi advance, and we will not see a joint Saudi-Emirati or global coalition form against them until they actively move to close the Bab al-Mandeb Strait.”
After the US declined Saudi Arabia’s request for military support, Riyadh turned to Pakistan and Turkey, signatories of the recent Mecca defence pact. Both have limited their commitments to technical support, while their defence and foreign ministers and military chiefs are due to meet in Riyadh this week.
Riccardo Gasco, foreign policy coordinator at InstanPol Institute, said expectations around the Mecca Pact are inflated, particularly over the prospect of automatic military support.
“Turkey has a clear interest in stopping the Houthis in relation to Bab al-Mandeb Strait as a trade corridor, but strictly automatic military support remains highly improbable,” he told The New Arab.
Among Saudi Arabia's other allies, Britain offered air refuelling, while France announced the deployment of military personnel to the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.
Unconfirmed reports say Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has offered to help Gulf states in a wider campaign against the Houthis. But Krieg argued that "the Israeli intelligence networks in Yemen are very poor", with Riyadh and Abu Dhabi far better placed.
"That is not something the Israelis can deliver," he said, adding that Israeli involvement could further fracture the anti-Houthi camp and fuel Houthi propaganda, while Tel Aviv may use its assistance as a card to play in its push for normalisation.
A new stalemate?
While the fragmentation of the anti-Houthi camp benefits the Houthis and Iran - exerting pressure on a second strategic chokepoint after Hormuz and handing Tehran greater leverage in US negotiations - it also strengthens the Houthis' position against Riyadh.
As the trajectory of the Yemen war remains uncertain, experts lay out several scenarios. One is containment, with the Houthis consolidating gains as far as Bab al-Mandeb and front lines settling around Lahj, Taiz, and Marib.
This would leave Yemen de facto partitioned and Riyadh entering negotiations from a position of weakness.
Alternatively, a limited counter-offensive could see coalition forces retake ground around Dhubab and Mokha, though this would require unified command and Saudi–Emirati coordination.
Other possibilities include regional escalation via attacks on Saudi infrastructure or shipping, or a return to UN-led diplomacy.
Dario Sabaghi is a freelance journalist interested in human rights

Iran-backed Houthis said Monday they had struck Riyadh's international airport and an Aramco refinery as Saudi-led forces intensified attacks on Houthi positions in Yemen. Iran-backed Houthis on Monday said they had struck Riyadh's international airport, an Aramco refinery and several other sites in Saudi Arabia, as the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said they had destroyed Houthi targets on the Red Sea coast.
Pakistan and Turkey meanwhile pledged to deploy troops to Saudi Arabia under a new mutual defence pact following weeks of Houthi attacks, as Riyadh and its Yemeni government allies began an ambitious push aimed at retaking all territory held by the group.
The Yemeni military said it carried out more than 1,000 strikes and began an offensive against the Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while the Saudi-led coalition supporting the internationally recognised government said 100 warplanes flew sorties at dawn.
Turki Al-Malki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition said on X that its naval forces had hit "military targets" belonging to the Houthis in Hodeida on the Red Sea coast.
