Loud explosions rattled Riyadh on Monday evening as the fighting escalated, and a Houthi spokesman said the group had hit the Saudi capital's King Khalid International Airport as well as an Aramco refinery and other targets in the kingdom's south.
The government announced on Sunday the lofty goal of retaking all Houthi territory – home to most of Yemen's population, and much of it held for more than a decade.
Last month the Iran-backed group seized swathes of coastline along the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandab Strait, a chokepoint for oil and cargo shipping, in Yemen's deadliest fighting in years.
The Houthis have also been attacking neighbouring Saudi Arabia since Yemen's civil war flared back to life, and have declared a maritime blockade on its ships.
On Monday, representatives of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey held an emergency meeting in Riyadh under the auspices of a joint defence agreement signed in August committing them to come to each other's aid in the event of any attack.

articles.title: DIU reveals new version of Russian Geran-4 with optics and compass
articles.body:
DIU reveals new version of Russian Geran-4 with optics and compass
According to Ukrinform, the Main Intelligence Directorate reported this.
According to intelligence reports, the upgraded “Geran-4” incorporates a new “MOH” unit, which is based on a high-precision magneto-inductive sensor (magnetometer) PNI5GA manufactured by the American company PNI Sensor. This module works in conjunction with the SADRA inertial navigation module to reduce the drift of its gyroscopes, thereby improving the accuracy of the drone’s autonomous navigation.
In addition to satellite and inertial navigation, the Russians have added another autonomous navigation system—the “Susannin” optoelectronic correlation system, which compares images from an optical sensor with a reference image stored in the computer’s memory, to ensure the drone’s route aligns from the launch point to the target point. A similar system is also used on the new “Geran-5” K5 version.
1 / 5
To effectively destroy (by cutting with a cumulative jet) bridge structures and power line towers, Russian invaders have begun using a new warhead for the KRSN—a special cumulative-cutting payload.
The Russians have replaced the Chinese Telefly turbojet engine with a domestically produced counterpart manufactured in Alabuga.
The rest of the electronic units and components remain unchanged and are identical to those of previous “Geranium” models.
As reported by Ukrinform, thanks to the deployment of their own satellite communications, Russian troops have changed their tactics for jet drone strikes on Kyiv and are now controlling the drones in real time instead of following pre-programmed routes.

Ukraine Develops New Nika Missile to Shoot Down Jet-Powered Shahed Drones
Ukraine has developed a new small missile called Nika to intercept jet-powered Shahed drones, while additional anti-drone turrets are being deployed in Kyiv and the surrounding region, Suspilne reported on October 4.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the new interceptor while speaking with journalists ahead of talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The new systems come as Ukraine works to improve interception rates against faster jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy previously reported that Ukraine was intercepting around 85% to 92% of conventional Shahed drones, while the interception rate for jet-powered UAVs stood at approximately 50% to 60%.
“We now have a new small missile, Nika, against jet-powered Shaheds,” Zelenskyy stated. “The Germans and we are responding positively. There will be testing. For now, we are looking at what could prove successful.”
Zelenskyy also reported a successful test of Spear, a new Ukrainian-German drone interceptor.
“It is important that today we heard about the test of our new interceptor, the German-Ukrainian Spear interceptor,” Zelenskyy added. “The test was successful.”
Ukraine is also expanding the use of specialized turrets against jet-powered drones. Zelenskyy reported that more than 12 had already been installed in Kyiv, with another eight due to be deployed across the Kyiv region.
“There will be dozens of these turrets at different facilities, and we will defend ourselves as best we can,” Zelenskyy stated.
The expansion of Ukraine’s air defenses comes as Russian drone and missile strikes continue hitting Ukraine’s critical civilian infrastructure. articles.title: Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border under ‘active defense’ program
articles.body:
Estonia is preparing for possible Russian provocations by moving troops closer to its border with Russia and buying weapons capable of striking deep inside Russian territory, the Financial Times reported.
Under its new “active defense” strategy, Estonia has expanded and modernized a base in Jõhvi, 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the border with Russia. The headquarters of the First Brigade has relocated there from Tapa, Estonia’s main military base, about 150 kilometers (93 miles) from the border.
Estonia is also building a new base in Narva designed to house 1,000 troops. The plan calls for 200 troops to be stationed there permanently, while the base could accommodate another 800 in the event of a crisis on the border.
Estonian military officials believe Russia is unlikely to try to seize the border town of Narva but do not rule out provocations meant to test how NATO’s collective defense clause functions.
As part of the “active defense” strategy, Estonia signed contracts in 2025 to buy nine American-made HIMARS systems with missiles that have a range of up to 300 kilometers (186 miles), as well as nine South Korean Chunmoo multiple rocket launchers with a similar range, the Financial Times reported.
Military and intelligence officials believe Russia is not ready for a full-scale war with NATO, at least not within the next couple of years, the FT reported, but they intend to do everything possible “to make aggression against us unthinkable.” “Our aim is clear: to keep the enemy and the destruction of war away from Estonian territory,” the Defense Ministry said.
European countries, especially those bordering Russia, have said repeatedly in recent months that they fear Russian provocations designed to pressure NATO into abandoning its support for Ukraine. Latvia’s intelligence services made a similar statement in the summer of 2026.

articles.title: Russia Upgrades Geran-4 Drones With Better Navigation and New Warhead, Ukraine Says
articles.body:
Russia has upgraded its Geran-4 attack drones with technology designed to make them harder to disrupt and more accurate, Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) agency said.
The new version, which Russia has started using this autumn, can navigate more precisely without relying entirely on satellite signals and carries a new warhead designed to damage bridges and power infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
One of the upgrades is a small magnetic sensor made by US company PNI Sensor. It helps the drone understand changes in its position and correct errors in its onboard navigation system, improving its ability to stay on course.
Russia has also added an optical navigation system called “Susanin.” In simple terms, the system uses a camera to compare what the drone sees below with images stored in its computer.
This allows the drone to recognize where it is and follow its planned route even without relying on GPS or other satellite navigation.
A similar system is being used on the newer Geran-5 drone, according to Ukraine’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
The upgraded Geran-4 also carries a new warhead designed specifically to attack infrastructure. It can use a powerful shaped charge to cut through bridge structures and supports carrying high-voltage power lines.
Russia has also replaced the Chinese-made engine previously used on the drone with a Russian-made version produced at the Alabuga industrial facility in Russia’s Tatarstan.
Guterres’s Successor Will Need Russia’s Blessing
Most of the drone’s other electronic components remain unchanged, HUR said in a report published on its War&Sanctions portal.
What is the Geran-4?
The Geran-4 is a relatively large, jet-powered attack drone designed for long-range strikes. It is about 3.6 meters (11.8 feet) long, has a 3.05-meter (10-foot) wingspan and can carry a warhead weighing up to 50 kilograms (110 pounds).
It has a maximum takeoff weight of about 450 kilograms (992 pounds). Its cruising speed is around 320 km/h (200 mph), while its maximum speed is 350 km/h (217 mph).
The drone has a reported range of about 770 kilometers (479 miles) and can fly at altitudes of up to 4 kilometers (2.5 miles).
Geran-4 vs. Geran-5
The Geran-5 is a larger and more powerful member of the same family.
It is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and weighs up to 850 kilograms (1,874 pounds) – almost twice as much as the Geran-4. It can carry a warhead weighing up to 90 kilograms (198 pounds).
The Geran-5 has a cruising speed of 450–600 km/h (280–373 mph) and a range of about 950 kilometers (590 miles). It can fly at altitudes of up to 6 kilometers (3.7 miles).
In simple terms, the Geran-4 is smaller and lighter, while the Geran-5 is a much larger platform capable of carrying a heavier warhead and flying faster and farther.

articles.title: US nuke test detection experiment bid to assert its hegemony: Ex-nuclear chief
articles.body:
MUMBAI: Former chief of Atomic Energy Commission of India, Anil Kakodkar, who played a key role in the Pokhran nuclear weapons tests, said the main aim of the US conducting what is called a non-proliferation experiment last week was to assert its global nuclear hegemony and prevent other nations from conducting atomic tests.On Sept 30, the US conducted an experiment which will enable it to detect whether countries are carrying out low-yield nuclear explosions.Kakodkar told TOI, “The US is attempting to get more sensitivity in terms of nuclear tests detection. There is a generic understanding that nuclear tests will not be carried out. But what if a country executes a test camouflaged?”Asked whether the motive of the test jeopardised nuclear sovereignty of countries, he said the main aim was to assert global US nuclear leadership and stop other countries from carrying out atomic weapons tests.A recent study by Federation of American Scientists says that currently India has 190 nuclear warheads and has enough military plutonium for 140 to 225 nuclear warheads.Anil Anand, considered the father of India’s nuclear submarine programme, quoted US National Nuclear Security Administration (NNSA) and told TOI that in the experiment researchers gathered measurements using a broad suite of advanced sensors, including accelerometers, seismometers, chemical and radiotracer samplers.
He said, “Together these measurements will improve scientists’ understanding of the signatures produced by underground explosions and strengthen US’ ability to detect and characterise nuclear explosive events.”According to NNSA, it “conducted a subsurface, non-nuclear chemical high-explosive experiment” at the Nevada National Security Site. An FB post by NNSA states, “If foreign countries test in secret, we will know.
The goal? Keeping the US one step ahead.” It further said the experiment assumes significance in the context of China supposedly having conducted a nuclear test in June 2020 secretly.“It takes nuclear expertise to detect nuclear activities, and experiments like these ensure America remains unmatched in detection,” said Brandon Williams, NNSA administrator. “Trump Administration has made it clear that the US will lead from a position of strength. You cannot evade American innovation. With this experiment, we are sending a clear message that under this administration, America will never be outmatched.”

articles.title: Russia’s Tu-95MS Goes Down With Three Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine
articles.body:

Russia’s Tu-95MS Goes Down With Three Officers Linked to Missile Strikes on Ukraine
Three Russian strategic aviation officers linked to missile strikes against Ukraine were among those killed when a Tu-95MS strategic bomber crashed in Russia’s Amur region in late September.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Militarnyi on October 4, the officers were identified as Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov and Majors Andrey Gerasimov and Andrey Lobanov. A photograph of the deceased crew was published by Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District in the Amur region.
The Tu-95MS crashed near the village of Krasnoyarovo on September 29 during what the Russian Defense Ministry described as a training flight. Russian authorities said six crew members were killed and one person survived with injuries.
Pavlyukov served as deputy commander for flight training with Russia’s 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment and previously commanded one of its Tu-95MS squadrons, according to data cited by Militarnyi from the Ukrainian database Book of Executioners. Ukrainian researchers linked him to the preparation and execution of missile strikes against Ukraine.
Gerasimov was a Tu-95MS squadron commander with the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, which is associated with Engels-2 airbase in Russia’s Saratov region. According to the same database, he participated in combat sorties and may have been involved in organizing cruise missile launches during strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Lobanov served as deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in Russian military unit 75715. Militarnyi, citing previous reporting by 24 Kanal, said Lobanov commanded a Tu-95MS during a May 29, 2023 combat sortie in which its crew launched six air-launched missiles at Ukrainian critical infrastructure.
The crash occurred as Russia continued moving Tu-95MS bombers between Engels-2 and Ukrainka airbase in the Amur region following Ukrainian strikes against strategic aviation facilities.
According to Militarnyi, Engels-2 is used to prepare aircraft and load Kh-101 air-launched cruise missiles, while the more distant Ukrainka base allows Russia to disperse its strategic aviation fleet. Such deployments can require flights exceeding 12,000 kilometers and lasting close to 24 hours.
The Soviet-designed Tu-95MS remains one of Russia’s primary strategic missile carriers and has been repeatedly used to launch Kh-101 cruise missiles against Ukraine.
Earlier, on October 1, a Russian Mi-8 military helicopter crashed in the Voronezh region, killing all three crew members. The helicopter was reportedly shot down by a Russian Su-35 fighter after being misidentified as a Ukrainian drone during a large-scale drone attack.

articles.title: Ukraine using AI-enabled robot guns to counter Russian drones
articles.body:
Ukraine commenced using artificial intelligence-enabled robot guns to bring down Russia's new and fast-moving jet-powered drones, according to its air force on Monday.
For months, Kyiv has been seeking a way to intercept the new Russian drones pounding the Ukrainian capital, even as it faces a dire lack of suitable ammunition to take them out.
Russia has been deploying newer jet-powered drones that move faster and are harder to intercept than the traditional models, which are based on Iranian Shahed drones.
As part of Ukraine's efforts to respond, "robotic turrets are now being installed on bridges," air force spokesperson Col. Yuri Ignat told national television.
"There have already been shoot downs," of the drones, including the bigger, faster and more powerful Geran-5 version, he told national television.
Speaking to Agence France-Presse (AFP), Ignat explained that the new turrets, which have been seen by AFP journalists in the Ukrainian capital, use "optical vision and artificial intelligence to eliminate the human factor and deliver strikes."
Sergiy Beskrestnov, a technology adviser to the Ukrainian defense ministry, explained on Telegram over the weekend that the new automated turrets were "an innovative Ukrainian solution that shoots down (drones) using machine guns controlled by artificial intelligence."
He said that 12 of the turrets had been installed in Kyiv, adding that "more turrets will be installed in the future."
Ignat acknowledged that the new system had a small operating radius.
"It can operate at about one kilometer plus (0.6 miles). And it works when conditions are favorable, when the attack approach angle is suitable," he told AFP.
"This is not some kind of panacea," he said, stressing that the turrets were part of "an integrated air defense system that provides engagement of these targets at different tiers."
"Of course, we rely on all available assets."
Ukraine has been accelerating the integration of artificial intelligence into its defense capabilities and is already using the technology on the frontlines to guide drones, detect targets for strikes and coordinate large-scale operations.

articles.title: Cambrian Patrol expands for largest exercise yet
articles.body:
Exercise Cambrian Patrol has expanded to its largest edition since the event began in 1959, with 140 patrols taking part in a demanding two-day assessment across the Welsh mountains, according to the British Army.
Running from 2 to 13 October, the 2026 exercise has been increased to meet demand from British units and international partners, with additional phases and patrols added to the programme.
The field includes 75 Regular Army patrols, 15 Reserve teams and 13 from University Officer Training Corps units, alongside 35 international patrols and two combined British Army and international teams. More than 350 personnel are supporting the exercise.
Each eight-person patrol begins near Builth Wells after an initial equipment inspection at Beulah, before receiving orders and completing its battle preparation. Teams then cover up to 40 miles across the Welsh mountains over roughly 48 hours before finishing at Sennybridge. Performance is assessed throughout the route, with teams competing for gold, silver and bronze medals or a completion coin.
According to a news update from the British Army, Major Darren Pridmore, Officer Commanding Exercise Cambrian Patrol 2026, said: “This is all designed to test the skills that soldiers need to survive and fight on the modern battlefield. It is a demanding assessment of leadership, resilience, tactical judgement and teamwork under pressure.”
The exercise is delivered by 160th (Welsh) Brigade on behalf of Commander Land Forces, with training direction provided by the Director Land Warfare Centre. Tasks this year include casualty evacuation, intelligence gathering, artillery fire planning, vehicle recognition, simulated chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear incidents, reconnaissance, minefield crossings and attacks on enemy positions.
Organisers have also increased the emphasis on small-unit leadership, placing junior officers and non-commissioned officers in situations where they must make tactical decisions while managing fatigue and maintaining the momentum of their patrol. The 2026 exercise has been adjusted to incorporate lessons associated with contemp rary conflicts, particularly the increased prevalence of persistent surveillance and unmanned aircraft.
Patrols will be tracked by both ground forces and unmanned aerial systems, requiring teams to consider concealment, routes and movement patterns while completing their assigned tasks. Mobility and survivability assessments include crossing the Forward Line of Own Troops, river crossings and navigating minefields during reconnaissance missions.
The exercise also includes a greater emphasis on the collection and integration of battlefield information. Patrols will use safe houses, static sensors and unmanned aerial systems to build an intelligence picture, combining information gathered from several sources before identifying and reporting targets.
Major Pridmore said: “We’ve preserved the spirit of Cambrian Patrol while adapting it to reflect the realities of contemporary conflict.
“From drones and persistent surveillance, to intelligence integration and CBRN readiness, this year’s exercise better reflects the challenges soldiers can expect to face on operations.”
Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear readiness will also receive greater scrutiny during the exercise, with teams assessed on whether they arrive with the necessary equipment and can continue operating in a simulated contaminated environment.
The changes reflect the Army’s wider effort to adapt training to battlefield conditions in which small units can face persistent observation, widespread use of drones and a greater requirement to combine information from distributed sensors.
Pridmore added: “The battlefield is evolving rapidly and success increasingly depends on close collaboration between operators, innovators and industry.
“Cambrian Patrol provides a unique opportunity to bring those communities together, helping us adapt faster, exploit emerging technologies and maintain operational advantage.”
International participation remains a major part of the event, with 35 overseas patrols taking part alongside British teams this year.
Cambrian Patrol has long been used by foreign armed forces as an opportunity to test their troops against British units in difficult terrain, while exposing participants to different tactical methods and operating procedures.
Major Pridmore said: “The United Kingdom does not fight alone. Future operations will be conducted alongside allies and partners, making interoperability and mutual understanding essential.”
The exercise takes place over terrain around the Brecon area of Wales, where weather, elevation and distance add to the tactical assessments faced by teams. Patrols must continue completing military tasks while carrying their equipment across the route and operating with limited rest.
Once the field phase is complete, teams undergo a detailed debrief and reporting process before their overall performance is assessed and the final medal standard determined.

articles.title: Zelensky: Ukraine prepares new contracts for air defense systems and missiles as infrastructure protection remains key challenge
articles.body:
Zelensky: Ukraine prepares new contracts for air defense systems and missiles as infrastructure protection remains key challenge
According to Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky made this statement during an evening video address, as reported by Ukrinform.
“Today, I spoke with Ukrainian Prime Minister SerhiyiKoretskyi about additional security measures. The Minister of Defense, the Minister of Infrastructure, and the Armed Forces of Ukraine all provided important briefings today. And we are increasing our level of protection every day. This applies to both turrets and special units tasked with shooting down ‘Shaheds.’ “We expect manufacturers to move quickly with the interceptors. The tasks have been defined, and funding is in place,” Zelensky noted.
According to him, Ukraine is preparing new contracts for air defense systems and missiles. The President emphasized that there are currently no public details regarding these agreements, but there may be “positive developments,” and he stressed that having the right solutions in place is crucial.
“It is important for us that these decisions exist. And I also ask our partners: we need more anti-ballistic systems to protect our infrastructure—that is the main challenge right now,” the President noted.
At the same time, he emphasized that world leaders understand the situation and recognize that Russia has no intention of shifting from escalation to negotiations.
Zelensky called on Ukraine’s leaders and partners in Europe and the United States to maximize protection against Russian strikes and diplomatic efforts in October following Russia’s attack on Kharkiv.
“Rescue operations continued all day today in Kharkiv following the Russian bombing. More than 50 people were injured. Searches were conducted for people trapped under the rubble, and, unfortunately, there have been fatalities. My condolences go out to all the families and loved ones,” Zelensky said.
The president emphasized that all of Ukraine’s leaders and partners in Europe and the United States need to focus their efforts specifically in October to maximize protection against Russian strikes and utilize all diplomatic avenues.
“Thank you to everyone who is truly helping out! And please, take care of yourselves,” he concluded.
As reported by Ukrinform, President Volodymyr Zelensky held a meeting with the team from the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine and the diplomatic team from the Office of the President regarding the schedule for arms deliveries from partners, and also set new tasks for long-range operations.

articles.title: NATO Drafts "Theory of Victory" Plan Using Drones and AI to Repel Russian Attack
articles.body:
- Category
- World
NATO Drafts "Theory of Victory" Plan Using Drones and AI to Repel Russian Attack
NATO’s top military commander is preparing a strategy to quickly defeat any Russian attack on the alliance’s eastern flank, using drones and artificial intelligence alongside conventional forces.
Bloomberg reported the plan on October 5 after reviewing an unclassified version of the document and speaking with senior officials and diplomats familiar with the initiative.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The document, titled "Theory of Victory," is being developed under Supreme Allied Commander Europe General Alexus Grynkewich. He is expected to present the strategy in Poland on October 12.
The plan is intended to clarify how NATO would respond to a potential Russian incursion into allied territory. It places particular emphasis on integrating emerging technologies, including drones and AI, with NATO’s existing conventional military capabilities.
Rather than replacing traditional forces, the strategy seeks to integrate technological systems with established military power to accelerate decision-making on the battlefield and strengthen NATO’s ability to stop an attack before Russia can achieve its initial objectives.
The document comes amid heightened tensions between NATO and Russia and growing concern among allied governments about Moscow’s intentions toward the alliance’s eastern members.
The outlet noted that officials have been assessing repeated reports suggesting Russia could consider military action against NATO territory.
The strategy also reflects NATO’s broader effort to absorb lessons from Russia’s war against Ukraine, where drones, automated targeting, electronic warfare, and rapidly changing battlefield technologies have become central to combat operations.
The alliance has increasingly focused on integrating such capabilities into its eastern defenses while retaining conventional forces as the foundation of deterrence.
NATO's shift toward automated warfare has already begun taking shape along the alliance's eastern flank.
Earlier reports indicated that the alliance plans a unified surveillance and defense system stretching from Finland to the Black Sea, built on drones, satellites, sensors, and AI to detect and help repel incoming attacks.
The approach draws on Ukraine, where AI-guided drone swarms can identify targets and strike autonomously even when Russian electronic warfare severs human control.
During the Freedom Shield 2026 exercises near the Belarusian border, Germany's 45th Armored Brigade fitted its Leopard 2 tanks and Fuchs carriers with anti-drone screens modeled on Ukrainian combat experience.

articles.title: Estonia Moves Troops Toward Russian Border, Prepares 300-Km Deep Strikes Under New Defense Strategy
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Estonia Moves Troops Toward Russian Border, Prepares 300-Km Deep Strikes Under New Defense Strategy
Estonia is moving key combat units closer to its border with Russia and expanding its long-range strike capabilities under a new “active defense” strategy aimed at confronting a potential attack from forward positions.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 5, the headquarters of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade—the country’s main combat formation—is being permanently relocated from Tapa to Jõhvi, about 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the Russian border, where new military facilities are under construction.
“We have to start at the border and win the first battles,” Colonel Tarmo Kundla, commander of the brigade, told the Financial Times.
The move represents a shift from Estonia’s previous strategy, which envisioned slowing an invading force while waiting for NATO reinforcements. Under the new approach, Estonian forces intend to defend territory from forward positions and strike military targets deep behind enemy lines from the beginning of an attack.
Estonia is also building a military base in Narva, directly on the Russian border. The facility is expected to permanently host about 200 troops and accommodate up to 1,000 personnel during a crisis.
At the same time, Tallinn is expanding its long-range firepower. Estonia is set to field nine US-made HIMARS and nine South Korean K239 Chunmoo launchers, with available munitions capable of reaching approximately 300 kilometers. The Financial Times noted that St. Petersburg is about 260 kilometers from Estonia’s eastern military positions.
“To make deterrence credible, we have to make aggression against us unthinkable. Our goal is clear: keep the enemy and the destructive consequences of war away from Estonian territory,” Estonia’s Defense Ministry said, according to the Financial Times.
The shift comes as Estonia increases defense spending to approximately €2.4 billion in 2026, or about 5.4% of GDP, with €1.27 billion allocated to weapons and other defense procurement.
Estonian intelligence does not currently assess a Russian attack on NATO as imminent. Officials cited by the Financial Times said they do not expect Moscow to seek a full-scale war with NATO within at least the next two years, but warned that Russia’s military restructuring could increase the threat in the longer term.
Earlier, Estonian security officials warned of a pro-Russian influence campaign promoting the creation of a so-called “Narva People’s Republic.” The campaign, reported by BILD in March, included calls for sabotage and armed resistance, with Estonian intelligence warning that it could be intended to prepare the ground for a scenario similar to Russia’s actions in eastern Ukraine in 2014.

articles.title: The case against Bortko, who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine, has been brought to court — what punishment does the Russian director face
articles.body:
The case against Bortko, who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine, has been brought to court — what punishment does the Russian director face
Kyiv • UNN
The SBU has completed its investigation into Volodymyr Bortko, who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine and its capture. He faces up to 8 years in prison.
The indictment against Vladimir Bortko, the director of "Bandit Petersburg," who called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine, has been sent to court, UNN reports, citing the Office of the Prosecutor General and the Security Service of Ukraine.
Details
The Security Service of Ukraine has completed its pretrial investigation into Russian director, screenwriter, and former State Duma deputy Vladimir Bortko, who promotes Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine.
The SBU investigators have now submitted the indictment to the court. The offender faces up to 8 years in prison with confiscation of property.
The investigation established that the suspect publicly calls for the continuation of the war, denies Ukrainian statehood, and advocates the use of tactical nuclear weapons against our country.
The SBU recalled that Bortko is known for the Russian television series "Bandit Petersburg" and "Streets of Broken Lanterns." He combined his work in cinema with political support for the Kremlin regime.
During the investigation, Security Service officers documented numerous episodes of his provocative statements between 2017 and 2026.
Thus, on the air of the "Komsomolskaya Pravda" radio station, he once again called for a nuclear strike on Ukraine. In addition, he advocated seizing Kyiv and then the entire territory of our country.
On the basis of the evidence collected, Bortko has been charged under two articles of the Criminal Code of Ukraine:
▪️ Article 436 (propaganda of war);
▪️ Part 3 of Article 436-2 (the production and dissemination of materials in which Russia’s armed aggression against Ukraine is justified, recognized as lawful, or denied, committed repeatedly and using the mass media).
Since the suspect is located in Russia, comprehensive measures are underway to bring him to justice.
The investigation was conducted under the procedural guidance of the Office of the Prosecutor General.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukrainian pilots to start training on French Rafale jets soon
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian pilots will soon start training in France on French Rafale fighter jets, and also announced the preparation of a new package of defense supplies from France.
"A good conversation with President Emmanuel Macron. Thank you for France's full support. We discussed Russia's terrorist escalation and our defense needs. New defense supplies are currently being prepared, and we expect the new package to arrive in Ukraine soon. We discussed its contents," Zelenskyy said in a post shared on Facebook on Monday.
According to him, Ukrainian pilots "will start training on French Rafale aircraft in France in the very near future."
"This is a significant step for Ukrainian combat aviation," the president said.
Zelenskyy also said Ukrainian and French teams are continuing to work on localizing the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine.
"We are actively preparing the FREYJA system. We discussed where we can speed things up. We agreed to discuss everything in more detail during the meeting," he said.
Ukraine and France have agreed on the purchase of 16 Rafale fighter jets for the Ukrainian Armed Forces as the first batch of 100 aircraft, the acquisition of which was provided for in an agreement between the two countries in November 2025. The presidents of Ukraine and France, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Emmanuel Macron, signed a joint declaration to that effect on July 14, 2026.
According to the agreement, the first four Rafale jets are to be handed over to the Ukrainian military upon completion of the training cycle for Ukrainian pilots and mechanics. Training was scheduled to begin in France in 2026.
The French side said the first Rafale jets could appear in Ukrainian skies in 2028-2029. At the same time, the agreement provides for the supply of weapons for the aircraft, including AASM bombs, MICA and Meteor missiles, as well as laser-guided missiles to counter drones.
The President of Ukraine also said that training for Ukrainian pilots and mechanics in France will begin as early as this year, after which the Ukrainian Armed Forces are set to receive the first four Rafale jets.

articles.title: Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking
articles.body:
Ukraine says Russian drones behind Turkish ship sinking
October 5, 2026
Romanian authorities said on Monday that two people were killed and another one was wounded after a fire broke out in a commercial vessel on Romanian waters in the Black Sea.
The Turkish-owned civilian vessel subsequently sank. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the incident was caused by a Russian drone attack.
Romania's Interior Ministry said the Coast Guard was alerted at around 11 a.m. local time (14:00 UTC) and the afflicted vessel was in Romania's exclusive economic zone, some 30 nautical miles (55 kilometers) south of Sfantul Gheorghe in Tulcea County.
"Eleven crew members have been rescued. Two deceased individuals have also been located," the ministry said, adding that a helicopter had airlifted the injured.
Zelenskyy accuses Russia of 'horrific strike'
Authorities did not identify the cause of the fire, but Romanian media reported that the ship was carrying grain and was hit by a drone.
"A horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Türkiye. Azerbaijani and Indian citizens were on board," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on X.
"As of now, unfortunately, we know that the ship's captain was killed ... The fate of one other person is still being established," he added.
The Ukrainian government says it has repeatedly proposed taking steps to de-escalate the situation in the Black Sea, which is putting maritime trade at risk.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian vessels instead of normal maritime navigation," Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
Rising threat to Black Sea maritime traffic
The Black Sea is a major commercial shipping route, which connects Ukraine's grain exports with the rest of the world. The waterway has faced heightened security concerns since Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine in 2022.
There has been an increase in war-related objects found in the Black Sea, mostly in Romanian, Bulgarian and Turkish waters, with analysts saying the trend is expected to continue.
The incident is the latest to take place on Romanian waters. In August, a Romanian F-16 fighter jet destroyed a marine drone near an offshore gas project in the Black Sea.
Two months before, a Ukrainian maritime drone exploded in Romania's Black Sea port of Constanta, with Ukraine saying the drone had been knocked off course by Russian electronic interference.

articles.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
articles.body:
On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.
Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.
Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.
“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”
Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.
When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”
The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.
In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.
“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”
With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

articles.title: Russia says it’s fighting scammers. Its latest proposals would push VPN services off Russian servers, tie eSIMs to devices, and expand telecom data retention.
articles.body:
Russia says it’s fighting scammers. Its latest proposals would push VPN services off Russian servers, tie eSIMs to devices, and expand telecom data retention.
Fighting fraud has been a major focus of Russian lawmaking in recent years. The country has already adopted two sweeping packages of anti-fraud measures, and the authorities often use the fight against fraud as a pretext to push through repressive measures. This was their justification, for example, for banning voice and video calls on Telegram and WhatsApp. This week, Russia’s Digital Development Ministry published provisions from a third package aimed at telephone and online fraud. It includes another set of major proposals that could impose much tighter restrictions on internet use in Russia. Meduza reviewed the document and breaks down its key proposals.
VPN services would find it harder to use Russian hosting providers
Roskomnadzor, Russia’s communications regulator, would create a separate registry of Russian hosting providers’ customers who use rented computing resources to run proxy or VPN services that help circumvent internet censorship. Individuals or companies found to be circumventing blocks would be barred from signing new contracts with any hosting provider in the country for a full year.
The government would have to establish a procedure for Roskomnadzor and hosting providers to exchange this information.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 10²⁻¹. Special rules governing hosting providers
5³. The federal executive authority responsible for regulating and overseeing the media, mass communications, information technology, and telecommunications shall maintain, under a procedure established by the Government of the Russian Federation, a registry of persons who use hosting providers’ computing resources to host information and telecommunications networks or information resources (a website and/or webpage on the Internet, an information system, or a computer program) that provide access to information resources or information and telecommunications networks blocked within the Russian Federation under this Federal Law, and whose owners have failed to comply with the requirements of paragraph 1 of part 7 of Article 15⁸ of this Federal Law. The Government of the Russian Federation shall determine what information must be included in this registry.
5⁴. A hosting provider may not supply computing resources for hosting information in an information system permanently connected to the Internet to persons listed in the registry provided for in part 5³ of this Article who apply to the hosting provider within one year of being added to the registry.
Russian hosting providers would have to disconnect customers at the FSB’s request
It is unclear whether, in practice, the security service, which oversees internet blocking, would use this power solely to combat cyberattacks or also against VPNs. The amendment reads:
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 10²⁻¹. Special rules governing hosting providers
12. A hosting provider must cease supplying computing resources upon receiving a request to that effect from an agency conducting criminal intelligence operations or from the organization specified in paragraph 2 of part 2 of Article 5 of Federal Law No. 187-FZ of July 26, 2017, “On the Security of the Russian Federation’s Critical Information Infrastructure,” where necessary to counter cyberattacks.
Related reading
Companies would have to report their VPN use to Roskomnadzor
The authorities currently allow companies to use VPNs capable of circumventing Russian blocks, provided they meet two conditions:
The company needs the VPN “for technical purposes necessary to its operations”
The company determines in advance which employees will use the VPN
Under the proposal, companies would have to notify Roskomnadzor that they are using VPNs to circumvent blocks, though the notification process remains unspecified. There would also be unspecified requirements for employees with VPN access, along with rules governing its use. The government would draw up these requirements and rules subject to the FSB’s approval.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 15.8. Measures to counter the use within the Russian Federation of information and telecommunications networks and information resources that provide access to information resources and information and telecommunications networks blocked within the Russian Federation
17. The provisions of this Article shall not apply to operators of state information systems, government bodies, or local government bodies, or to the use of software and hardware that provide access to blocked information resources and information and telecommunications networks, provided that the owners of that software and hardware determine its users in advance and that it is used for technical purposes necessary to the operations of the person using it.
18. The Government of the Russian Federation, with the agreement of the federal executive authority responsible for security, shall establish requirements and rules governing the use of software and hardware that provide access to blocked information resources and information and telecommunications networks in the circumstances specified in part 17 of this Article and by the persons specified in that part. These shall include the procedure for notifying the federal executive authority responsible for regulating and overseeing the media, mass communications, information technology, and telecommunications of the use of such software and hardware, and the content and format of the information to be submitted.
All websites and apps would have to give the FSB users’ registration and login data
The proposed requirement would apply to both Russian and foreign services. They would have to keep records of users’ registrations and every account login for three years. They would also have to give this information to the FSB, with “the information to be supplied and the procedure” still to be determined by the government:
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 8. The right of access to information
10. The owner of a website and/or webpage on the Internet, and/or an information system, and/or a computer program, operating on the Internet within the Russian Federation, where access to information on that website and/or webpage, and/or in that information system, and/or computer program is provided to users who have logged in, must:
2) retain information on users’ account registrations, logins, and account closures for three years after those actions have been completed, and provide that information to authorized government agencies conducting criminal intelligence operations or ensuring the security of the Russian Federation, with the information to be supplied and the procedure determined by the Government of the Russian Federation.
Related reading
Foreign websites and apps would have to authenticate Russian users exclusively by phone number
Currently, authentication requirements apply only to websites, information systems, and programs owned by Russian citizens or legal entities. They can choose how to authenticate users: by phone number, through the Gosuslugi government services portal, through the Unified Biometric System, or through another Russian system.
Article 13.55 of the Code of Administrative Offenses already allows fines of 500,000 to 700,000 rubles for companies that violate this requirement.
Federal Law “On Information, Information Technology, and the Protection of Information”
Article 8. The right of access to information
10¹⁻¹. A person specified in part 10 of this Article who is neither a Russian legal entity nor a citizen of the Russian Federation must authenticate users located within the Russian Federation using a mobile phone number.
Sole proprietors and private individuals would no longer be able to sell SIM cards on telecom operators’ behalf
Currently, private individuals, sole proprietors, and legal entities can all sell SIM cards if they have an agency agreement with a telecom operator.
The bill proposes removing that right from the first two groups. Only employees of those legal entities, working under employment contracts, would be allowed to sell the cards. Telecom operators would have to verify the information provided about those employees.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
7. Legal entities that are not telecom operators may enter into mobile telephone service contracts and process subscribers’ payments for those services only if they have written agency agreements authorizing them to act on a telecom operator’s behalf. The powers granted under those agency agreements may not be delegated to third parties. Such agency agreements may not be concluded with sole proprietors or private individuals.
For legal entities that are not telecom operators, employees working under employment contracts with those entities shall enter into mobile telephone service contracts and process subscribers’ payments for those services.
A telecom operator must verify the accuracy of information about an employee of the telecom operator or a person acting on its behalf who arranged the signing of a mobile telephone service contract, using the procedure and methods established in paragraph 6 of this Article.
Telecom operators would have to store additional information alongside the traffic data and metadata required by the Yarovaya law
Operators would have to store information “on network addresses and ports” used by a customer when signing a contract for communications services. They would have to keep it for three years. The government has yet to determine “the procedure for storage and the amount of information to be stored.”
It is hard to say exactly why the authorities want this information. Most likely, it would allow them to determine after the fact whether a subscriber had masked their IP addresses with a VPN or proxy servers when signing a contract.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 64. Telecom operators’ obligations and restrictions on communications service users’ rights during criminal intelligence operations, measures to ensure the security of the Russian Federation, investigative actions, the detention of criminal suspects and defendants, and the enforcement of prison sentences
1. Telecom operators must store the following within the Russian Federation:
3) information on network addresses and ports used by the subscriber and the telecom operator when concluding a communications service contract over the Internet, including the time the contract was concluded — for three years after those actions have been completed. The Government of the Russian Federation shall establish the procedure for storage and the amount of information specified in this subparagraph to be stored.
Embedded SIM cards would be tied to specific devices
When someone buys an eSIM, their contract with the telecom operator would include the identifier (IMEI) of the specific phone, tablet, or smartwatch they use. When an eSIM is reissued for another device, the contract would apparently be amended at the same time. Most likely, this is intended to deter fraudsters from even attempting to clone their victims’ eSIMs (which is no easy task).
Roskomnadzor would monitor telecom operators’ compliance with this requirement.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
1.1. To conclude mobile telephone service contracts, a telecom operator or a person acting on its behalf must use the following, which must meet requirements established by the Government of the Russian Federation:
Where user equipment (terminal equipment) has an embedded identification module whose information can be modified through software, and that information is needed to identify an individual subscriber and/or user equipment (terminal equipment) on a mobile carrier’s network, the mobile telephone service contract must include information about the user equipment (terminal equipment) in which that identification module will be used, including its identifier.
Where user equipment (terminal equipment) has an embedded identification module whose information can be modified through software, and that information is needed to identify a person using communications services under a subscription held by a legal entity or sole proprietor, and/or user equipment (terminal equipment) on a mobile carrier’s network, information about that equipment’s identifier must be entered into the Unified Identification and Authentication System by the subscriber that is a legal entity or sole proprietor, or, at that subscriber’s discretion, by the communications service user. Before providing communications services using that equipment, the telecom operator must verify that the information is present and accurate by submitting a query to the Unified Identification and Authentication System through the Unified System of Interagency Electronic Interaction.
Max would let users lift self-imposed restrictions and buy a new eSIM
Russians can currently bar themselves from obtaining a new phone number by visiting a telecom operator’s office in person or applying remotely through Gosuslugi. Beginning March 1, 2027, they will be able to block calls from abroad in the same way.
For now, the only way to lift these self-imposed restrictions is to visit a government services center in person. The Digital Development Ministry proposes allowing people to lift them remotely, including through the Max messaging app.
Users would also be able to buy a new eSIM through Max.
Federal Law “On Communications”
Article 44. Provision of communications services
1. Within the Russian Federation, telecom operators provide communications services to subscribers under communications service contracts concluded in accordance with civil law, this Federal Law, and the rules governing the provision of communications services.
Communications service contracts may be concluded over the Internet, except in the circumstance specified in the fifth paragraph of paragraph 1.1 of this Article, provided that an individual, including a sole proprietor, or a legal entity expresses consent through one of the following methods:
[…]
using an enhanced unqualified electronic signature and, in accordance with paragraph 4 of part 3 of Article 1 of Federal Law No. 156-FZ of June 24, 2025, “On the Creation of a Multifunctional Information Exchange Service and Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Russian Federation,” providing information contained in documents establishing a Russian citizen’s identity through the multifunctional information exchange service, provided that, to enable the submission of that information through the multifunctional information exchange service, a photograph of the citizen submitting the information has previously been matched to that citizen’s biometric personal data held in the Unified Biometric System
Article 45. Special rules for providing communications services to citizens
7². The restrictions specified in paragraph 7¹ of this Article on concluding mobile telephone service contracts and on allowing user equipment (terminal equipment) to receive telephone calls originating from a foreign telecom operator’s network and bearing numbers corresponding to a foreign numbering system and plan may be lifted through one of the following methods:
3) using an enhanced unqualified electronic signature and, in accordance with paragraph 4 of part 3 of Article 1 of Federal Law No. 156-FZ of June 24, 2025, “On the Creation of a Multifunctional Information Exchange Service and Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Russian Federation,” providing information contained in documents establishing a Russian citizen’s identity through the multifunctional information exchange service, provided that, to enable the submission of that information through the multifunctional information exchange service, a photograph of the citizen submitting the information has previously been matched to that citizen’s biometric personal data held in the Unified Biometric System;
Foreigners would be able to buy SIM cards online in some cases

Zelensky discusses strengthening air defenses and protection against Shahed drones with Dutch PM
According to Ukrinform, the head of state announced this on Telegram.

articles.title: Turkey, Pakistan agree rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
articles.body:
Turkey, Pakistan agree rapid troops deployment in Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks
RIYADH - Turkey and Pakistan will undertake a “rapid deployment” of troops to Saudi Arabia as part of a new mutual defence alliance, the three countries said on Oct 5, as the Gulf kingdom faces escalating attacks from Yemen’s Houthis.
The three countries in August signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement committing them to come to each other’s aid in the event one were attacked.
The pact unites NATO’s second-largest army, that of Turkey, with the Islamic world’s only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power, Saudi Arabia.
Their representatives held an emergency meeting in Riyadh on Oct 5 where they noted recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, in particular ones targeting the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, without mentioning the Iran-backed Houthis by name.
The trio “reaffirmed their unequivocal rejection of any attack or threat against the Kingdom’s security and territorial integrity”, they said in a joint statement.
They also agreed “to move immediately to the practical implementation of the collective defence commitments and to take the necessary measures to provide the agreed military forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the Kingdom”.
The statement did not specify what sort of role the troops would fill once in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced repeated Houthi attacks targeting its cities, oil infrastructure and ships ever since Yemen’s civil war flared back to life in July.
In September, the group launched a new offensive that seized swathes of territory from Yemen’s Saudi-backed government, which on Oct 5 launched a counteroffensive with Riyadh’s support seeking to retake all Houthi territory, some of it held for more than a decade. AFP

articles.title: Ukraine says its strikes have knocked out more than 51% of Russia’s oil refining capacity
articles.body:
Ukraine's Security and Defense Forces have "put out of action" more than 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity through recent long-range strikes, Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said in a statement published by the Defense Ministry on 4 October. These "carefully thought-out" actions were aimed at "bleeding the Russian war machine" and "destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
Ukraine treats Russia's refineries as a priority target because their revenue helps fund the war. Even Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed on 1 October that the strikes had cost Russia 1% of its GDP and had "partially" achieved their goal, Interfax reported.
The ministry did not publish how it calculated the figure.
"The consequences of Ukrainian operations are not always visible immediately. But the effect accumulates and produces a tangible result," the ministry said.
Ukrainian deep strikes continue to bring the war to Russian territory
The ministry named eight recently struck facilities, among others. One of them is the Moscow Oil Refinery, which Ukraine targeted in a massive drone attack on the night of 20 September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. The refinery, operated by Gazprom Neft in Moscow's Kapotnya district, supplies about 40% of Moscow's fuel market and 70% of the Moscow region's demand for gasoline and aviation fuel, according to Russian news Telegram channel Astra.
Another was KINEF, which Ukraine has attacked repeatedly. It is Russia's second-largest oil refinery by capacity, and the Ukrainian military struck it on the night of 30 August, setting off a fire at the facility.
The ministry also named the Yaroslavl, Perm, Ilsky, Saratov, and Syzran refineries and the Ust-Luga port complex.
Ukraine triples production and procurement of long-range drones—and this is not the end
This year, Ukraine has tripled the production and procurement of long-range attack drones, the ministry said.
"This is not the limit. We will continue to scale up deep-strike capabilities," the statement said.
International cooperation is part of that push. Berlin will fund the production of additional DeepStrike-class long-range drones in Ukraine, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said after a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on 15 April. The sides also agreed to jointly develop and produce a medium- and long-range drone system.
Ukraine and Germany also signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on 8 July. The Bars' modular design allows it to be used for deep strikes, among other missions.
Oil refinery output has fallen
Russian refineries cut crude oil processing by 14% in the first nine months of the year compared with the same period last year amid Ukrainian drone attacks, according to calculations by two industry sources.
Experts' estimates of the decline differ widely. In August, Serhii Vakulenko of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center put it at 25–28%, while Russian economic commentator Vyacheslav Shiryaev put it at 65–70%, according to Defense-Aerospace.
Fuel production data give a more concrete picture: in July, Russia's gasoline and diesel output was about a quarter to a third lower than in March 2026, the outlet reported.

articles.title: Geran-4 Gets Russian Engine and New Navigation System — DIU
articles.body:
Russia’s Geran-4 jet-powered drone has received a locally produced engine and a new optical navigation system.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine reported this on the War&Sanctions portal.
Russian forces began using an upgraded version of this UAV in the fall of this year.
A new MOKH module based on the high-precision PNI5GA magneto-inductive sensor manufactured by U.S. company PNI Sensor has been integrated into the Geran-4 design.
The sensor operates together with the SADRA inertial module, reducing gyroscope drift and improving the accuracy of autonomous navigation.
In addition to satellite and inertial navigation, the enemy has added the Susanin electro-optical correlation system.
It compares images from an optical sensor with a reference image stored in the computer’s memory to adjust the route from the launch point to the target.
Instead of the Chinese Telefly TF-TJ2000A turbojet engine, Russians installed a locally produced equivalent manufactured in Alabuga.
According to Oboronka, engines assembled in Russia undergo additional testing and modifications due to poor manufacturing quality in China. Among the debris, investigators found a turbocharger impeller with Russian markings and drilled holes for weight balancing. Such modifications reduce the centrifugal force acting on the component at high rotational speeds and lower vibrations that can lead to engine failure.
To effectively strike bridge structures and power transmission line towers, the enemy has equipped the drone with a new KRSN shaped-charge cutting warhead.
The remaining electronic modules and components of the UAV remain identical to those used in previous versions of the Geran drones.
The Geran-4 jet-powered attack UAV features a flying-wing aerodynamic configuration and is designed to strike targets at medium and long ranges. The fuselage is approximately 3 meters long, the wingspan exceeds 2.5 meters, and the launch weight is estimated at 200–250 kg, with a warhead weighing up to 50 kg.
The drone is equipped with a turbojet engine that enables it to reach a flight speed of 400–500 km/h and provides an effective range of 400–600 km. Its onboard control system combines satellite navigation, an inertial module, a magnetometric unit, and an electro-optical correction system for autonomous guidance to the target.

articles.title: Russia names eight fatalities in Tu-95MS crash in the Far East, The Insider confirms three officers linked to combat missions in Ukraine
articles.body:
Eight Russian service members — rather than the six initially reported by the Ministry of Defense — were killed on Sept. 29 when a Tu-95MS long-range bomber crashed in the Amur Region. The Insider has established that at least three long-range aviation officers were among the dead: Andrei Lobanov, Fedor Pavlyukov, and Andrei Gerasimov. Ukraine links all three to Tu-95MS combat missions.
On Oct. 4, the local outlet Port Amur was the first to report that the death toll had risen to eight, adding that nine service members had been on board and that two of the dead had not been found right away. Mikhail Piven, head of the Mazanovsky District in the Amur Region, soon published a photograph featuring portraits of those killed. The Ministry of Defense had initially reported six dead and one hospitalized.
According to the captions under the portraits, the dead include Andrei Lobanov, Vladislav Moskovskikh, Artur Enokyan, Mikhail Kotyshev, Sergei Moisevich, Vladimir Kelip, Fedor Pavlyukov, and Andrei Gerasimov. Piven said local authorities intend to ask the long-range aviation command to put the crew forward for state honors.
Three of the dead appeared in a Ukrainian database
The Insider cross-checked the data on those killed against the Ukrainian database Russian Torturers, a project launched in 2022 on the initiative of President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its creators say the entries are verified by Ukrainian law enforcement or intelligence agencies.
As of November 2025, Major Andrei Lobanov was listed in the database as deputy commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in Russia’s 182nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment, based at Ukrainka airfield. The database claims that he directly commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions.
Lieutenant Colonel Fedor Pavlyukov is listed as deputy commander for flight training for the same 182nd Regiment. From August 2021 to April 2024, he commanded a Tu-95MS squadron. The database’s creators say Pavlyukov was responsible for preparing flight crews for combat missions and directly commanded the unit. As early as March 2022, Ukrainian intelligence had placed Pavlyukov on a list of Russian long-range aviation pilots suspected of direct participation in the war against Ukraine.
Major Andrei Gerasimov is listed as commander of a Tu-95MS squadron in the 121st Heavy Bomber Aviation Regiment. The database claims he directly commanded the unit and personally took part in combat missions.
Ukrainian serviceman and blogger Anatoliy Shtefan (“Stirlitz”) also claimed that at least three of those killed were involved in organizing and carrying out missile strikes on Ukraine, though he did not specify which of those killed he had in mind.
The Sept. 29 plane crash
The Tu-95MS crashed on Sept. 29 during a training flight near the village of Krasnoyarovo in the Mazanovsky District. The Ministry of Defense said the plane had been flying without weapons and went down “in an uninhabited area.” The local government in the Amur Region said the crew steered the aircraft away from residential areas in order to avoid causing further casualties, and no one on the ground was hurt. The ministry sent an Aerospace Forces commission to investigate the crash. No publicly confirmed findings have established its cause.
Ukrainka airfield, where the 182nd Regiment is based, has taken on particular importance for Russia’s long-range aviation over the past year. The Insider previously reported that most of Russia’s long-range bombers (that are still able to fly) were redeployed from the western part of the country to the Far East following Ukraine’s behind-the-lines Operation Spiderweb.
As a result, Ukrainka became the main base for operational Tu-95MS aircraft, significantly complicating combat missions. In order to launch missiles at targets in Ukraine, the aircraft must fly upwards of 12,000 kilometers round-trip, refueling at the Engels or Olenya air bases in western Russia. A typical mission thus lasts around 23 hours, putting significant strain on the aging aircraft.

articles.title: Swiss scammed out of millions by Ukraine-linked call centers – media
articles.body:
Ukraine’s scam-call networks targeting Swiss – anti-fraud squad
Swiss police are investigating a sprawling fraud operation with suspected links to Ukrainian scam call centers, an industry said to be worth billions to corrupt officials in Kiev, Neue Zurcher Zeitung (NZZ) has reported, citing law enforcement officials.
According to a report on Sunday, NEDIK, the police network coordinating Switzerland’s fight against digital crime, recently recorded an increase in fraud offenses suspected of having links to Ukraine. The network declined to provide nationwide figures “for tactical reasons,” but noted that at least four fraudulent call centers in Ukraine have been identified in international investigations involving Swiss authorities, with Swiss and German citizens among their main victims.
One investigation by Bern authorities, reportedly underway for years, concerns a man suspected of operating several call centers in Kiev. On just one platform allegedly linked to the operation, reported losses in Switzerland amounted to nearly 4 million Swiss francs ($4.8 million).
Several Ukrainian nationals have also recently been arrested in Swiss cantons for allegedly acting as cash collectors in telephone scams. In St. Gallen in early September, a person posing as a bank employee called a 93-year-old man and instructed him to withdraw and hand over a large sum of money. Police later arrested a 38-year-old Ukrainian who allegedly collected the cash.
Police in Aargau have similarly reported a growing number of suspected cash collectors holding Ukrainian citizenship. Authorities, however, have not established whether they are being directed by call centers in Ukraine or acting independently. NZZ noted that it remains unclear to what extent Ukraine-based operations are connected to fraud networks and cash collectors operating in Switzerland.
While Russians have long been portrayed as the main targets of Ukrainian scammers, sources cited by NZZ challenged that narrative. Brian Lee, head of the Eurasia Observatory at the Geneva-based Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), said Russians accounted for just 10%-15% of targets even at the height of the so-called “patriotic fraud” narrative, under which young Ukrainians were recruited into scam networks on the pretext of taking revenge for Moscow’s military operation against the Kiev regime. Victims have been identified in at least 29 countries, with scam centers increasingly targeting Europe and the US, according to a GI-TOC report published earlier this year.
Lee also reported that bribing Ukrainian officials for protection is central to the business model, saying GI-TOC investigations found that criminal elements “operate seamlessly and efficiently alongside law enforcement agencies, public officials and the private sector.” Such protection reportedly costs scam operators $10,000-$15,000 per month.
Scam networks and state structures
Corruption has long plagued Ukraine, with high-level scandals including last year’s $100 million Energoatom kickback scheme, reportedly led by Timur Mindich, a former business partner of Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky. Western-backed investigators have since uncovered further graft involving Ukrainian officials.
The scam call center network reentered the spotlight last month after Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko – a key pillar of Zelensky’s increasingly fragile governing structure – resigned amid the exposure of an industrial-scale network across the country with alleged links to senior figures in Kiev. Ukraine’s Western-backed National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) accused Sergey Kropiva, head of the cybercrime unit at the Prosecutor General’s Office, of leading a ring that collected protection payments from notorious Ukrainian scam call centers. NABU said it identified assets worth almost $1 million allegedly purchased with proceeds from the scheme.
The sums involved in Ukraine’s wider scam industry are reportedly far larger. Ukrainian media earlier estimated that roughly 2,000 scam offices were operating nationwide as of early August, about half paying protection money to corrupt officials. Such payments were estimated at $240 million annually, while the industry itself has been valued at up to $1 billion a month.
The scam industry has also been linked to powerful security structures under Zelensky’s government. In September, personnel from the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) and military intelligence (HUR) exchanged fire in Kiev in a confrontation that left three servicemen injured. The clash centered on Stepan Kaplunov, a member of an HUR-linked armed unit detained by the SBU. A law enforcement source cited by Ukrainian outlet Strana said Kaplunov may have been involved in operating scam call centers, pointing to a broader struggle between rival security agencies over the lucrative industry. Ukrainian journalists have also reported that proceeds from criminal operations help finance parts of the HUR’s activities.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has described phone scams as a key tactic employed by Kiev to extract money from Russian citizens, suggesting the practice has effectively become state policy. Moscow considers the industry a national security threat and claims Ukrainian scam networks operate in coordination with the country’s intelligence services.
Russian forces have recently intensified strikes on Ukrainian telecommunications infrastructure, mobile operators, and data centers in response to Kiev’s botched “pressure campaign” of drone attacks on civilian infrastructure deep inside Russia. The strikes have disrupted internet access, digital television, and other services, including by hitting data centers in Kiev that Moscow says were used by Ukrainian military and intelligence services. Media reports late last month also claimed a Russian strike hit one of the scam call centers in Dnepropetrovsk.

articles.title: India is one of Russia’s biggest energy buyers. Can it also help broker peace with Ukraine?
articles.body:
India is one of Russia’s biggest energy buyers. Can it also help broker peace with Ukraine?
India is beginning to take a more active role in efforts to reach a settlement between Russia and Ukraine, Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said. Bloomberg reported that his explicit statement signals New Delhi’s shift toward a more active stance after years of caution over the war, driven partly by its close economic ties with Russia.
Speaking at a Munich Security Conference meeting held away from its usual venue, Jaishankar said India had become “a little bit more involved” in the peace process in recent months. He said New Delhi is now in talks with both Russia and Ukraine:
We are trying to be helpful, starting with the Black Sea safety of shipping issue, but going beyond that to cover some immediate concerns which both of them have on grain exports, on energy exports, on non-attack possibilities. So those are ongoing conversations right now.
Jaishankar gave no details about the progress of the talks. He also said India sees Russia, as the Soviet Union’s successor, as a partner that has traditionally helped it in its conflict with Pakistan.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has discussed the war twice in meetings with Vladimir Putin over the past few weeks — first at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Bishkek, then at the BRICS summit in New Delhi. After the latest meeting, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Modi had “actively offered his good offices” to help secure a peaceful settlement.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on October 1 that four international mediators, including India, had put forward proposals for a peaceful settlement. “We have four proposals. India’s is the most comprehensive. For the first time, India has offered to play a role,” Sybiha said. He did not specify what India’s proposals involved.
India and China are currently the biggest buyers of Russian energy, and Russian energy’s share of India’s imports has risen sharply since the war began. The U.S. has repeatedly pressured India to stop buying Russian oil in exchange for lifting tariffs. In early 2026, Donald Trump said an agreement had been reached. But India later resumed purchases after war broke out in the Middle East and energy shortages emerged.
Negotiations over a trade deal between India and the U.S. are ongoing. In recent weeks, the talks have been complicated by the U.S. passage of the so-called “sanctions from hell” law. It allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries buying substantial amounts of Russian oil — above all, India.

Discussion on whether to shoot down Russian drones over Ukraine is ongoing, Polish foreign minister says
A discussion is still underway over whether Poland should agree to Ukraine's request to shoot down Russian drones over Ukrainian territory.
