However, as you know, NATO has established an integrated defence system for the entire eastern flank. This means that the decision does not depend on Poland alone. So the discussion is ongoing, but we have not yet reached the decisions that would satisfy you."

articles.title: Bloomberg: NATO developing "Theory of Victory" over Russia using drones and AI
articles.body:
Bloomberg: NATO developing "Theory of Victory" over Russia using drones and AI
NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe Alexus Grynkewich is developing a strategy for achieving a swift victory in the event of a Russian attack on the Alliance's eastern flank, with a particular focus on integrating new defence technologies such as drones and artificial intelligence.
Source: Bloomberg, which obtained an unclassified version of the document titled Theory of Victory, as reported by European Pravda
Details: Grynkewich is due to present the document in Poland on 12 October. Officials and diplomats familiar with the matter said it is intended to explain how the Alliance would respond to a potential invasion of NATO territory.
The document is also intended to show allies how NATO will integrate conventional weapons with new capabilities that have emerged since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, as well as to encourage greater defence investment and better preparedness, the sources said.
The strategy emphasises NATO's defensive nature and the need to avoid unintended provocations, while making clear the need for a collective response to hybrid threats.
The strategy stresses that by demonstrating its readiness, NATO aims to convince an adversary that victory is impossible.
However, if NATO is attacked, the Alliance would seek to halt the invasion using a combination of ground forces and other assets under the NATO Eastern Flank Deterrence Initiative – a concept based on the use of low-cost drones, minimally crewed systems and AI-powered targeting.
Grynkewich's spokesperson, Colonel Martin O'Donnell, declined to discuss the details of the plan but stressed that the Alliance is "purely defensive".
"The Supreme Allied Commander Europe's theory of victory is simple: maintain NATO's advantage. Given the unsettled and complex global security environment, we need to set conditions now to deter aggression and, if necessary, win if attacked," he said.
Background:
- Martin Jäger, head of Germany's Federal Intelligence Service, has said he sees a risk of violent conflict with Russia and that the confrontation has taken on a new and dangerous quality.
- Media reports have also indicated that Estonia is relocating a key brigade from the town of Tapa to Jõhvi, 50 kilometres from the Russian border, as part of the launch of an "active defence" strategy in preparation for possible Russian aggression.
- Meanwhile, Lithuania and Poland are jointly developing an international civilian evacuation plan that could be implemented if some residents of Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia need to be evacuated across the border.

articles.title: Russia burned 628,000 new school textbooks in Kharkiv at the peak of back-to-school season
articles.body:
Russian missiles and drones destroyed 13 million Ukrainian books this summer, The Guardian reported. That is about a third of all books printed in Ukraine this year, the government estimates.
Russia is striking civilian warehouses, including those where publishers store their books. The uncertainty is pushing publishers toward safe international bestsellers, Publishers Weekly reported. "We'll all end up fed up with safe, non-risky books—if there are still publishers around to publish them," said Iryna Baturevych, co-founder of the publishing news outlet Chytomo.
Millions of Ukrainian books on fire
Ranok is one of Ukraine's largest publishing houses and a leader in children's literature and school textbooks. On one day in August, Russia destroyed more than 85% of its stock, The Guardian reported.
Viktor Kruhlov, the publisher's co-founder and chief executive, was on the warehouse floor at its headquarters in Kharkiv. The facility, built on the site of a former bread factory, covered about 10,000 m².
Together with five senior colleagues, he was discussing plans for the upcoming school year, the peak of the distribution season. Moments after the meeting began, a strike hit about 30 meters from where the staff had gathered. Kruhlov heard an explosion and almost at once saw a huge fire. As colleagues tried to put out the flames, a second strike came, and he realized there could be a third and a fourth, so the staff evacuated. Fifty people were on shift that day, and no one was injured, Kruhlov told The Guardian.
Eight million books, including 628,000 new school textbooks, were in the warehouse at the time. None could be saved. Firefighters battled the blaze for a week.
Several editorial staff members who saw the remains of the warehouse for the first time looked shaken as they recognized fragments of books they had helped create.
"When you see what was produced with your brain, with your hands, with your imagination, spoiled by Russia, it's an awful feeling," Kruhlov said.
He predicted shortages at Ranok's stores this fall, when the books in stock run out and there is nothing to replace them.
Literature is part of Ukrainian identity
Kruhlov is convinced that Russia deliberately targeted the book warehouse, but Bohdana Laiuk, Ukraine's deputy culture minister, sees the strikes as part of Russia's broader campaign against warehouses, The Guardian wrote.
"They cannot occupy Kyiv. So they target warehouses around Kyiv to take the possibility of everyday life from us—and books are part of everyday life," she said.
Books also matter to Russia's occupiers, Laiuk said.
"When the Russians occupy, the first thing they do—and we know this from the areas that were occupied and then liberated in 2022 in the Kherson and Kharkiv regions—is to go to the libraries, take the Ukrainian language books out, and destroy them," Laiuk said.
Before 2022, about 70% of the Ukrainian book market consisted of Russian-language titles, most of them imported from Russia.
Russian dominance in Ukrainian publishing developed over centuries, from tsarist bans on publishing in Ukrainian in the 19th century to Soviet Russification. Ukrainian writers were purged, and Ukrainian literature stayed in the shadow of Russian literature, the article notes.
Laiuk calls the dominance of Russian books a form of colonialism. Russia deliberately built its own information space in Ukraine through books, media, and television, she argues, so that everything would be ready for it once its tanks arrived.
Even after independence, a commercially successful Ukrainian-language novel was long seen as unlikely. But at the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukrainian bookstores stopped selling Russian imports, and interest in Ukrainian literature grew, from 1920s classics and poetry to contemporary authors and translations.
"So people are asking: what does it actually mean to be Ukrainian? Literary culture gives us the place to understand who we are," Laiuk told The Guardian in 2023.
The future of Ukrainian literature is uncertain
Ranok is now rushing to reprint textbooks and bestsellers: schools need the former, while sales of popular titles will help the publisher make up for lost revenue.
For debut authors and writers of less commercial or experimental books, the situation is particularly difficult. Even before the strike on Ranok's warehouse, some publications had been delayed by attacks on printing infrastructure.
Ksenia Shpak's debut novel, an urban fantasy about a girl displaced from eastern Ukraine to the Carpathians, was due out in February 2025 but was published only that November, the article says. Half of the print run was in Ranok's Kharkiv warehouse when it was attacked.
It was her first published book, and Shpak fears the publisher will now focus on bestsellers and reprint her novel only if money allows. The Ukrainian book market is also feeling demand level off and the cost of living rise, she said.
Despite the loss of 8 million books, Kruhlov remained optimistic. Looking over the ruined warehouse in Kharkiv, he said he planned to rebuild everything—and to do it better.

articles.title: Germany facing potential ‘violent conflict’ with Russia – spy chief
articles.body:
Germany facing potential ‘violent conflict’ with Russia – spy chief
Germany could become “embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia,” the country’s foreign intelligence chief has warned, claiming that a mysterious drone incident at Leipzig airport is an example of the “real and imminent” threat posed by Moscow.
Speaking to lawmakers at a parliamentary hearing on Monday, Bundesnachrichtendienst (BND) head Martin Jaeger declared that “the confrontation we are facing with Russia has taken on a new, more dangerous dimension.”
“Germany is in danger of becoming embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia – the attempted attack in Leipzig is just one example,” he continued, referring to the discovery of an explosive-laden drone next to a Ukrainian transport plane at the city’s airport in August.
German authorities have not released any evidence linking the incident to Russia, and Moscow has described the episode as a “hastily cobbled-together provocation” serving “exclusively the aims of Kiev and the militaristic wing of the European political class.” It is “obvious that Germany is pursuing a further course of escalation,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said last month.
Nevertheless, Jaeger claimed that Russia is “waging a shadow war,” and that there is a “real and imminent” threat of attacks against targets in Germany. “No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany,” he added.
Jaeger is one of dozens of Western political, military, and media figures to accuse Russia of waging a “hybrid war” or “shadow war” against Europe in recent weeks. The accusations are, by their nature, impossible to verify, and Moscow has written them off as pretexts to deepen Western involvement in the Russia-Ukraine conflict, justify military spending hikes, and expand surveillance and persecution of domestic opponents.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has explicitly and without evidence described the country’s most popular political party, the right-wing AfD, as “Russia-backed.” Martina Rosenberg, the head of Germany’s Military Counterintelligence Service (MAD), alluded to this claim during Monday’s briefing, telling lawmakers that the country is “threatened by diverse dangers from both outside and within.”
Jaeger, Rosenberg, and domestic intelligence (BfV) chief Sinan Selen all praised Merz’s recent efforts to grant the BND greater offensive powers, and called for further strengthening of the MAD and BfV’s capabilities.
Despite their allegations of “hybrid war,” European leaders have repeatedly stressed that they do not believe Russia to be planning any actual attacks on NATO territory. The BND has seen “no indication of an imminent large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory,” Jaeger added on Monday.
Amid an unprecedented escalation in the West’s rhetoric toward Russia, RT is tracking the statements, accusations, and threats in our ongoing ‘Escalation Watch’ special. Keep an eye on it here as we sort the facts from the propaganda and debunk the psyops in real time.

articles.title: American rocket artillery opens fire in joint drill
articles.body:
US Army rocket artillery has opened fire during a joint live-fire exercise with the Singapore Armed Forces, with M270 Multiple Launch Rocket Systems used during Exercise Daring Warrior 2026 at Fort Sill in Oklahoma, according to the US Army.
Soldiers from Bravo Battery, 3rd Battalion, 13th Field Artillery Regiment, 75th Field Artillery Brigade conducted the firing on 21 September alongside Singaporean personnel as part of the bilateral training event.
Imagery released by the US military shows an M270 launching rockets across the Fort Sill training area, with American and Singaporean troops also working together around artillery equipment and command systems during the exercise.
The US Army said the live-fire was designed to synchronise American and Singaporean launch crews, allowing the two forces to practise delivering coordinated precision fires while testing their ability to operate together on the range. Exercise Daring Warrior brings together artillery personnel from the two countries for training involving weapons operation, command and control and the coordination required to employ long-range fires as part of a combined force.
The M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System is a tracked rocket artillery platform operated by the US Army and several allied militaries. Its launcher carries interchangeable rocket and missile pods, allowing it to employ different types of ammunition depending on the mission.
Unlike conventional tube artillery, multiple launch rocket systems are intended to deliver fires over greater distances and can engage targets using guided munitions. The M270 shares ammunition with the wheeled M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System, better known as HIMARS, although the tracked M270 carries two launch pods rather than one.
The system has also gained renewed prominence during the war in Ukraine, where M270 and HIMARS launchers supplied by Western countries have been used extensively by Ukrainian forces for long-range precision strikes.
For the American and Singaporean troops at Fort Sill, the emphasis was on operating the systems as part of a combined artillery force rather than simply conducting individual launcher firings.
Photographs from the exercise show personnel from both armies working together during equipment familiarisation and planning activity, as well as operating observation and targeting equipment in the field. Other imagery shows American and Singaporean troops positioned around command posts and tactical vehicles before the live-fire phase, reflecting the wider chain of activity required to identify targets, pass firing information and coordinate launch crews.
The Singapore Armed Forces operates its own M142 HIMARS rocket artillery systems, giving its personnel experience with a weapons family that shares ammunition and elements of fire-control architecture with the M270.
Fort Sill is the US Army’s principal artillery training centre and home to the Field Artillery School, making the Oklahoma installation a regular location for both domestic and multinational artillery exercises. The 75th Field Artillery Brigade is also based at Fort Sill and provides long-range precision fires capabilities to US forces, with subordinate units operating rocket and missile artillery systems.

articles.title: US warns foreign financial institutions over business with Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US warns foreign financial institutions not to do business with Iran
The United States on Monday warned foreign financial institutions that if they do business with Iran or its banking sector, Washington could sanction them.
"Foreign financial institutions continuing to transact with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions could be targeted at any time without advance notification and should take immediate action to terminate such activity and relationships," the US Treasury said in an "alert" statement.
The United States launched its war on Iran in late February, killing the country's leadership and demanding it cease any nuclear-related activities.
The war has plunged the Middle East into violence, with Tehran's retaliatory action targeting Washington's Gulf allies and sending global energy and fertiliser prices skyrocketing after it virtually shut a key trading route.
Since late August, Washington has stepped up its campaign to isolate Tehran economically, warning its allies that secondary sanctions would hit them if they continued to conduct transactions with the country's government.
The US Treasury has also announced a slew of new sanctions as part of that push, targeting Iran's financial, cryptocurrency, rail, automotive and manufacturing sectors.
It has also taken action against two banks, one in the United Arab Emirates and another in Turkey, over their alleged aid to the authorities in Tehran.
In Monday's statement, the Treasury said Iran's government operated so-called "shadow banking" channels to circumvent US sanctions, and that foreign financial institutions should aim to identify and avoid any such activities.

articles.title: Estonia to Move Troops to Russian Border Under “Active Defense” Strategy
articles.body:
Estonia is moving some of its troops closer to the Russian border as part of a new “active defense” strategy.
The Financial Times reports that the main units of Estonia’s 1st Infantry Brigade, the country’s main combat force, will be permanently stationed in Jõhvi instead of Tapa.
Jõhvi is located about 50 km from the Russian border, while Tapa is approximately 130 km away.
To accommodate the troops in Jõhvi, Estonia is building new military facilities. The country is also constructing a military base in Narva that will be able to accommodate up to 1,000 troops.
Around 200 troops are expected to be stationed there in peacetime, with up to 800 more deployed in the event of war.
The changes are part of a broader review by Estonia’s Ministry of Defense of its military strategy, as the country shifts to an “active defense” concept introduced in May 2026.
The concept calls for defending the country directly from the border and attempting to stop an enemy at the earliest stage of an attack. As part of this approach, Estonia is acquiring modern weapons and long-range artillery, including HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems.
Militarnyi previously reported that, after four months of training, Estonian troops carried out their first live-fire exercises using the country’s own HIMARS rocket systems.
The wartime structure of the Estonian Defense Forces includes more than 43,000 positions. About 4,200 are assigned to active-duty personnel, while the rest are reservists and members of the Estonian Defense League (Kaitseliit).
As of 2026, the Estonian Division forms the core of the land component of the Estonian Defense Forces. It is the country’s largest land formation, reports directly to the Commander of the Defense Forces, and is integrated into NATO’s command structure.
The division includes the 1st and 2nd Infantry Brigades, a headquarters and signals battalion, an ISTAR reconnaissance battalion, and artillery, engineering, and logistics battalions.
The division’s main maneuver unit remains the 1st Infantry Brigade. It comprises the Scouts Battalion, the Kalev and Viru infantry battalions, an air defense battalion, a combat support battalion, headquarters and signals companies, and an anti-tank company.
The brigade also trains conscripts, who are later transferred to the reserve.
The 2nd Infantry Brigade is primarily responsible for the southeastern part of the country. In peacetime, it consists of a headquarters in Tartu, the Kuperjanov Battalion in Võru, a combat support battalion, and a support and communications company. In wartime, the brigade is expanded with reserve units.
In addition to the division, the Estonian Defense Forces include the Cyber Command, Support Command, Military Police, Special Operations Forces, and other units.

The size of the order indicates Russia’s intention to use Pechora-2M systems or air defense systems compatible with them.
Against the backdrop of a shortage of air defense capabilities, a return to Soviet-era systems is a practical step due to the availability of significant stockpiles of corresponding ammunition.
The system is a major upgrade of the S-125M air defense system and is designed to engage air targets at ranges from 3.5 to 32 km and at altitudes from 20 meters to 20 km.

articles.title: Trump blames Democrats and Ukraine for soaring US fuel prices, not Iran war
articles.body:
Trump blames Democrats and Ukraine for soaring US fuel prices, not Iran war
Trump shifts blame for fuel price hikes to Democratic-led states such as California and Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries.
With the United States midterm elections approaching, President Donald Trump has attempted to shift blame for high fuel prices from the US-Israel war on Iran to Democrats and Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries.
“What’s driving up Gasoline is no longer the Strait of Hormuz, because Record Numbers of Barrels are coming out now on an almost daily basis, but the word, ‘Refineries,’ where Russia’s are being blown up by Ukraine, and where ours are being closed up, in Blue States, like California, by the Dumocrats,” Trump said in a Truth Social post on Monday.
While Trump claims domestic refinery closures are driving the spike, daily exports through the Strait of Hormuz have actually plunged 97 percent since the war began, choking global supplies.
Petrol prices are continuing to climb for consumers. The average price for a gallon (3.79 litres) is $4.36, up from $4.14 a month ago and up from $2.98 on February 28, when the US and Israel first struck Iran, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA), which tracks daily petrol prices.
“The ongoing conflicts with Iran and Russia’s war with Ukraine are reinforcing each other, impairing oil product markets, but Middle Eastern flows are far from normal,” Rachel Ziemba, senior adjunct fellow at the Center for a New American Security, told Al Jazeera.
On Friday, G7 countries agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude from emergency reserves amid pressure from the White House. Meanwhile, the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve hits its lowest level since 1982.
“US tells some [European Union] members to release ‘strategic reserves’ or face a potential US diesel export ban, pushing France and Germany to do so, oil prices, along with gasoline and diesel futures strongly lower as a result,” Patrick DeHaan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a post on X.
Global pressures
Ukraine’s attacks on Russia’s energy infrastructure have also driven up prices, particularly diesel fuel. On Sunday, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence claimed that it has disabled more than half of Russia’s oil refining capacity.
“The damage to Russia’s refineries – and risk of more US sanctions on those who process Russian oil – are exacerbating the situation, but the underlying issue is still the volatile flows from the Middle East, the greater difficulty getting oil products out and the lower buffers in place,” Ziemba added.
The latest strikes come amid ongoing attacks since the war between Russia and Ukraine began in 2022. In June, Russian refinery throughput hit its lowest level in two decades, according to an analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA). The analysis also found that diesel production has fallen 30 percent over the past 18 months.
Trump has also blamed price increases on refining cuts in Democratic-led states such as California, where two refineries have shut down over the past year. The closures reduced the state’s refining capacity by 17 percent, creating some supply gaps, according to an analysis by S&P Global.
However, Trump’s effort to shift blame to Democrats comes ahead of consequential midterm elections that could shape the balance of power in Washington. At the same time, most Americans appear to blame Trump for rising prices. A recent AP-NORC poll found that 65 percent of Americans blamed Trump’s policies for higher prices, while 61 percent said the US economy is worse off than when Trump returned to office.

articles.title: Lithuania proposes special status for Ukrainian ammunition project
articles.body:
A project by Baltic Metal Foundry, the Lithuanian subsidiary of Ukrainian defence company Dnipro Electromechanical Plant (DEMZ), to manufacture ammunition and munitions components in Lithuania is being proposed for special status.
The Economy and Innovation Ministry has drafted a government resolution that would designate the project as meeting urgent state security and defence needs. The status would allow the company to benefit from special investment and business conditions beyond those provided under Lithuania’s Investment Law.
The ministry said the decision would contribute to improving the business environment and increasing investment.
Baltic Metal Foundry signed an investment agreement with the ministry in mid-August. Under the agreement, the company plans to manufacture ammunition and munitions components in Alytus and the Prienai district, with the project expected to create up to 450 jobs.
The value of the investment was not disclosed when the agreement was signed. Alytus Mayor Nerijus Cesiulis said at the time that the Ukrainian company planned to invest tens of millions of euros in the town.
Lithuania’s list of major investment projects shows that the company has committed to investing at least 93.3 million euros in the project.
An ammunition assembly plant is planned for the Prienai district, while existing infrastructure at the Alytus industrial park will be used to manufacture metal munitions components.
Construction of the plant near Balbieriškis was expected to begin this autumn, with production scheduled to start late next year or in the autumn of 2027. The facility is planned on a 30.6-hectare site in the village of Ąžuolai.
The company has said its products will meet NATO standards. Its primary market will be the Ukrainian armed forces, while production will also serve the defence needs of allied countries.
DEMZ is a major supplier of defence products to Ukraine’s military. Following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the company shifted its operations from civilian to military production. It has branches across Ukraine and employs about 4,000 people.
Baltic Metal Foundry was registered in Vilnius just over a year ago and currently has one employee, according to Lithuania’s State Social Insurance Fund, Sodra.
Data from the Centre of Registers shows that the company’s beneficiaries include two Polish citizens and one Ukrainian citizen.

articles.body:
That has left the work of identifying these men to local communities and journalists, such as a consortium led by the Latin American investigative outlet CLIP that was able to collect the names, or at least some information, about 19 men killed between September 2 and May 5.
When reached for comment, the U.S. Southern Command declined to discuss how they identify targets, but said that “every narco-terrorist neutralized” as part of the campaign “was an affiliated member of a Designated Terrorist Organization, actively transporting illicit material along known trafficking routes in international waters.” 
In their update on Operation Southern Spear one year in, U.S. officials were less bullish than their president, but said the campaign had driven a 60 percent reduction in illicit maritime activity in the Eastern Caribbean region that includes La Guajira. They also touted a 65 percent reduction in the Western Caribbean and a nearly 50 percent reduction in key areas of the Eastern Pacific.
The Trump administration does not disclose how it measures success, but a July report issued by the Washington Office on Latin America, a rights advocacy group, noted that available evidence suggested the military campaign was having little to no impact on the supply of cocaine reaching the U.S. 
Catalina Niño, a project coordinator at the local branch of the German pro-democracy non-profit Friedrich Ebert Stiftung, noted that “there is nothing to indicate that the strategy is achieving its supposed objective.”
“There is no evidence that the strategy works, not even in terms of physical proof, because destroying the boats leaves no evidence behind. There are no individuals to prosecute, and there is no verifiable evidence that there were drugs on those boats in the first place,” she said. “It is impossible to obtain evidence in this regard.”
When reached for comment, White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said that “all of these decisive strikes have been against designated narcoterrorists bringing deadly poison to our shores, and the President will continue to use every element of American power to stop drugs from flooding into our country and to bring those responsible to justice.”
Colombia’s presidency did not respond to requests to comment. The country’s deputy ombudsman, Paula Aponte, said in a statement that her office has sought further information from other state agencies on the Colombian nationals believed to have died in the attacks, but with little success. 
Searching for a Body 
Down one dusty dirt road in Riohacha sits a single-story brick home where a grief-stricken Wayúu family has been waiting for a boatman to return since May. The family, who lives without running water, has traveled across the peninsula to look for his corpse. They also constantly scan social media, where graphic videos of casualties from decimated boats circulate.
“He hasn’t appeared. They have asked about him even in the Dominican Republic,” said a distraught woman who answered the door to the family’s home and identified herself as a neighbor.
The woman explained that without a body, the man’s mother refuses to accept his death. 
But many believe the moment his life ended was captured in the video accompanying a Southern Command press release announcing a May 4 missile strike on a vessel “operated by Designated Terrorist Organizations” in the Caribbean Sea.
“Two male narco-terrorists were killed during this action,” the press release declared. 
After that announcement, word quickly spread in La Guajira that the men might be from the Wayúu community that has inhabited this desert for hundreds of years.

articles.title: From making interceptors to guarding sky: Ukrainian drone maker gets its own private air defense unit and will pay for it from weapon sales
articles.body:
A Ukrainian drone maker just got its own air defense unit, and says it has already downed Russian jet-powered drones. Ukraine's Defense Ministry has issued an order granting the Night Hornets, the anti-Shahed unit of interceptor maker Wild Hornets, the status of a private air defense, and the company announced it is starting to build its own network of remotely launched interceptor drones.
Russia has sharply increased its use of jet-powered Shahed drones, which cuts the reaction time of Ukraine's mobile fire groups from about a minute to as little as six seconds. Now, a private company joins the air defense line, while Ukrainian military intelligence says Russia is producing up to 500 Geran-4 and Geran-5 jet drones a month.
The planned network will combine remote-control centers, a grid of remote interceptor launches built on the company's Hornet Vision Ctrl technology, and field positions. Wild Hornets will not sell protection for individual sites and will pay for the unit from drone sales profit.
"The unit has more than 50 downed Shaheds to its name, including jet-powered ones. We create technologies that work. We use them ourselves to protect our country," the company says.
Air Force commanders will direct the crews
The crews already go on daily combat duty alongside the military and will take orders from the Air Force command. The unit draws on Wild Hornets instructors and test pilots, including veterans of the war and pilots who rose from beginners to instructors. The company wants to fold private air defense into the country's overall system, including over Kyiv.
Air alerts now swallow nearly a third of mall hours
Due to Russia's jet-powered drones, air-raid alerts covered 30.8 percent of shopping-center operating hours across Ukraine in September, a record, up from 22 percent in August and 14.1 percent a year earlier, the Ukrainian Council of Shopping Centers reports. The average mall has now lost 176.5 working days since the full-scale invasion, including 9.6 in September alone.
Kyiv shows the sharpest jump. The share of alert time during mall hours in the capital rose from 11.6 percent in August to 32.7 percent in September, the council said.
The damage reaches well beyond the malls. Ukraine's Economy Ministry expects losses from Russian strikes to reach up to $10 billion this year, Economy Minister Oleksandr Kravchenko said on 12 September.
